HELD: Modvat - Denial not sustainable where non-levy was not due to default by input manufacturer and proper records were kept. ".......where the initial non-levy was not due to any default or irregularity on the part of the manufacturer and duty is recovered later on by the department, it will be totally iniquitous to deny the benefit of modvat, particularly where the records maintained are amenable to scrutiny and verification."

HEADNOTE: Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 read with Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and Section 35G of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Demands duties not levied or not paid or short paid - Reference - Modvat--Use of soft paper for manufacture of paper product is not a question of law--Modvat--Limitation applicable under ceased to be a question of law after incorporation of limitation in Central Excise Rule 57-I

FACT: The applicants utilised Modvat credit under Rule 57A CE Rules on kraft paper used for packing the final product Linoleums. The Department held that under Notification No. 177/86-CE dt. 1.3.1986 credit in respect of paper used "in the manufacture of final product" was to be restricted to Rs. 800/- per tonne. The applicants' case is that they used the kraft paper "in relation to the manufacture of the final product", as "packing material" is recognised as an input under Explanation to Rule 57A. The Tribunal upheld the Department's view but found the Notice time-barred. In this Reference Application, the main question raised by applicants for reference is whether the expression "in relation to the manufacture" used in Rule 57A is synonymous to the expression "in the manufacture" used in the abovesaid notification. By the Cross Objection, the Department wants reference of the question whether the time limit prescribed in amended Rule 57-I is applicable in respect of an offence committed earlier to the amendment.

HELD: Reference--Question of law--The question whether the expression "in or in relation to the manufacture of final products" used in Rule 57A, and the expression "in the manufacture of final products" used in Notification No. 177/86-CE are synonymous does not arise from the Tribunal's order which examined the statutory definition of "manufacture" and concluded that kraft paper has been used in this case "in the manufacture" of the final product, as wrapping paper. (Ratio of Supreme Court's judgment in CCE v. East End Paper Industries Ltd. and in J.K. Cotton Spg. Wvg. Mills Co. Ltd. v. S.T.O.). "In view of the categoric finding in the order in question that Kraft Paper has been used in the manufacture of final product, linoleum, rejecting the contention to the contrary that it is not so used but only in relation to the manufacture of such final product, the questions of law suggested for reference lose their significance. Thus, for example, Question A in the application is as to whether the two expressions "goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products" appearing in Rule 57A and the expression "goods used in the manufacture of final products" appearing in the 3rd proviso to Notification 177/86 dated 1.3.1986 are synonymous is an academic question with the answer self-evident. It does not arise from the Tribunal's order which also did not proceed on the basis that the two expressions were synonymous. The order also did not seek to apply the restriction in the quantum of modvat benefit applicable under the Notification in question to inputs used only in relation to the manufacture by equating both the expressions. It was, on the contrary, held on the strength of the statutory definition of the expression "manufacture" that the use was only in the manufacture and their contention was rejected on this score only".

. Inputs used for generation of electricity would qualify for MODVAT credit only if they are used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product, such as cement, caustic soda, etc. Therefore, it is not correct to state that inputs used as fuel for generation of electricity captively consumed will not be covered as inputs under rule 57A. [Para 8] However, in some of the cases, electricity generated was consumed by the residential colony of the factory’s workers’ families, schools, etc., to that extent MODVAT credit would not be admissible. [Para 9]

Therefore, there was no merit in the civil appeal filed by the department and accordingly it was to be dismissed. [Para 10]

Therefore, the benefit of Modvat credit is not permissible (ratio of Tribunal Order No. 299/90 SRB dated 4.4.1990). "We observe that the two items are used in the paper machine section of the paper mill and the use of these two items in the paper machines is to make the machine functional. This Bench of the Tribunal, as pointed out by the Ld. Consultant at the very outset, has given detailed reasons as to why these items have to be precluded from the benefit of Modvat credit."

rule 57G and rule 57T. [Para 9]

Applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in various cases to the facts of the instant case, it was to be held that the amendment made in rule 57G of the Rules by insertion of sub-rule (11) vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 relates to procedure for availing Modvat credit and does not effect any substantive right. [Para 35] From the conjoint reading of rules 52A, 57G and the amendment made by Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 by which sub-rule (11) was inserted in rule 57G, of filing of the documents for availing Modvat credit is only a procedural matter and the amendment made vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 which inserted sub-rule (11) in rule 57G the position was made clear that Modvat credit should not be denied only on the ground that the documents referred to in sub-rule (2) does not strictly comply with the said rule but contains the details of payment dues, description of goods, assessable value, name and address of the factory or warehouse etc. This position has also been clarified by the Central Board of Excise and Customs by issuing a circular in exercise of its power under section 37B of the Act and made it applicable to all pending cases. [Para 36]

The submission of the revenue that the Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 would come into effect on the date of its publication i.e., 9-2-1999 only, may be correct but the benefit of that Notification as directed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs has been extended to all the pending cases. The provision of sub-rule (2) is procedural for availing Modvat credit, the benefit of sub-rule (11) is available to the assessee. [Para 39]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - Modvat - Limitation - Runs Relevant from the date of credit and not of utilisation for payment of duty or submission of RT-12 return

HELD: Modvat - limitation--The relevant date for computation of limitation under Rule 57I(1) is the date of credit and not the one of its utilisation for payment of duty or date of submission of RT-12 return which will be subsequent to the date of credit The contention of the Department that the limitation period of six months is to be computed from the date of submission of monthly RT-12 returns filed .....and not from the date of taking credit, is without force, in view of the finality of the matter as expressed by the Tribunal in the case of Arunachal Plywood Industries v. CCE ... and CCE, Patna v. Asia Insulated Wires (P) Ltd. .....--it has been held therein that the relevant date for computation of limitation under amended Rule 57-I(1)(1) the date of credit and not the one of its utilisation for payment of duty or date of submission of RT-12 return which will be subsequent to the date of credit."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Input - Lancing pipe used for passing oxygen into furnace for melting of metal, comes into contact of molten steel and is wholly consumed in process - Tribunal held that these were eligible for Modvat credit - Whether no question of law arose out of order of Tribunal - Held, yes

FACT: The Tribunal held that the product ‘lancing pipe’ used for passing oxygen gas into molten metal for rapid melting of scrap into liquid steel was to be considered as input and was eligible for Modvat credit.

On application :

HELD: The Tribunal had observed that the lancing pipes are used for discharge of oxygen into the furnace to cut open the top holes provided in the furnace to draw out metals from furnace. Lancing pipe while cutting open the holes, comes into contact with the molten steel in the furnace. On account of the high temperature in the furnace, these pipes melt and join the steel. While so the lancing pipe gets wholly consumed in the process. The pipe so consumed form part of the molten metal which is being taken out of the furnace. Since this pipe gets so consumed in the process, it was entitled to Modvat credit. [Para 3]

In view of the aforesaid facts, no substantial question of law arose in the instant application. The application was to be dismissed. [Para 7]

(xi)

PVC Pipes

The Tribunal allowed credit on aforesaid 11 items.

The department argued that the assessee is not entitled for such credit as the inputs are not used directly or indirectly for the manufacture of final products and they are not eligible for credit under rule 57A.

The assessee argued that the precedent judgments had allowed credit.

Issue Involved

Whether aforesaid 11 items were eligible for credit ?

HELD: The item-wise treatment is as follows : Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules deals with credit of duty paid on the excisable goods used as inputs. Rule 57Q relates to credit of duty paid on capital goods used by the manufacturer of specified goods. The Tribunal had relied on assessee's own case in Madras Aluminium Co. Ltd. v. CCE 2001 (136) (ELT) 182 (Tri-Chennai). The said order deals only with 57A of the Central Excise Rules, where many of the inputs were considered for credit. Therefore, the Tribunal is correct in holding that the inputs are used directly or indirectly for the manufacture of final product as per rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules during the relevant period. [Para 18]

Therefore, the assessee is entitled for credit for the above said items. [Para 19]

Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Caustic soda lye - used for neutralising gases before their escape into air for pollution control purposes - eligible input as used in relation to manufacture of final product - appeal allowed (Paras 4  5)

facts.text: The appellants receive duly paid bi-metal strips for use in the manufacture of I.C. Engines and parts thereof. They avail of Modvat Credit for the inputs. The appellants cleared certain parts like plain shaft bearings at nil rate of duty by following Chapter X procedure. The Assistant Collector held that credit could not be allowed on inputs used in the manufacture of parts cleared at nil rate of duty as per provisions of Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. This was upheld by the Collector (Appeals).

The assessee used Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) and furnace oil as fuel for generating electricity which in turn was captively consumed for production of final products such as caustic soda and cement. The assessee claimed MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) of rule 57A on LSHS. In civil appeal challenging the entitlement of assessee to MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

Besides manufacturing chlorine, the appellant company also manufactures hydrochloric acid, essential for the treatment of effluents generated during the process of manufacture of chlorine. The appellants claimed Modvat credit under Rule 57A on hydrochloric acid in terms of Notfn. 217/86-CE, as hydrochloric acid used has to be considered as an input for the finished product (chlorine).

The appellants manufacture metal containers claiming Modvat benefit for lacquered sheets used us input. Duty-paid plain tin sheets were bought and sent direct for lacquering. They were charged for having taken credit in RG-23A register without declaring plain tin sheets as inputs and getting them lacquered without following the procedure under Rule 57F(2) till January 1987, in contravention of Rule 57G. The credit of Rs. 2,28,521.64 was negatived. The Collector (Appeals) upheld the order.
The Department ordered reversal of Modvat under Explanation to Rule 57A, CE on wire netting and felt as the items are parts of paper making machine.

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of paper and was availing the benefit of the Modvat Scheme under rule 57A. The assessee was also manufacturing pulp which was chargeable to nil rate of duty. The said pulp was captively consumed for the manufacture of paper. A small quantity of said pulp was sent to its sister unit without payment of requisite duty thereon on the ground that it was the case of stock transfer and not a sale and, therefore, rule 57CC was not applicable in its case. The department was of view that the assessee should have taken into account 8 per cent of the selling price of pulp sold by the assessee’s sister units in other States for reversal of Modvat credit on inputs on which credit was taken by applying rule 6(b)(i ) of the Central Excise (Valuation) Rules, 1975. The department issued show-cause notice alleging that if comparable prices obtained by the sister units were taken into consideration, then the total duty payable at the rate of eight per cent would work out to Rs. 4.58 lakh (approx.) whereas the assessee had paid duty of Rs. 2.67 lakh (approx.) and, therefore, the assessee had evaded payment of duty and was also liable to pay penalty under rule 57-I(4), read with rule 173C of the 1944 Rules. However, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s contention that in the case of ‘stock transfer’ there is no ‘sale’ and, therefore, rule 57CC was not applicable.

On revenue’s appeal to the Supreme Court :

The applicants utilised Modvat credit under Rule 57A CE Rules on kraft paper used for packing the final product Linoleums. The Department held that under Notification No. 177/86-CE dt. 1.3.1986 credit in respect of paper used "in the manufacture of final product" was to be restricted to Rs. 800/- per tonne. The applicants' case is that they used the kraft paper "in relation to the manufacture of the final product", as "packing material" is recognised as an input under Explanation to Rule 57A. The Tribunal upheld the Department's view but found the Notice time-barred. In this Reference Application, the main question raised by applicants for reference is whether the expression "in relation to the manufacture" used in Rule 57A is synonymous to the expression "in the manufacture" used in the abovesaid notification. By the Cross Objection, the Department wants reference of the question whether the time limit prescribed in amended Rule 57-I is applicable in respect of an offence committed earlier to the amendment.

The respondent are manufacturers of electrical stampings and laminations out of hot-rolled and cold-rolled electrical steel and silicon steel sheets etc. and availed deemed Modvat credit in respect of the inputs as specified under Rule 57A, which were purchased from market and were not covered by any duty paying documents. The G.O.I. modified its earlier instructions and respondent's inputs became illegible with effect from 2.11.1987 for deemed Modvat credit without production of duty paying documents.

Iron & Steel products are manufactured by the appellants. They filed a declaration under Rule 57G of CE Rules for availing MODVAT benefit in respect of inputs used in relation to their manufacture of finished products. The Assistant Collector held that the refractory products are not covered by the explanation in Rule 57A of CE Rules. This order was upheld by Collector (Appeal).

The appellants manufacture duplicating paper, stencil paper, etc. and avail proforma credit under Rule 56A for tissue paper, maplitho paper, printing paper etc. used as inputs in their manufacture. While continuing to avail of proforma credit they opted for Modvat credit in respect of inputs used, other than those on which the Modvat scheme had been extended from 1.3.1986. This was objected to by the department on the ground of sub-rule (9) of 56A which totally bars an availment of benefit under 56A if Modvat credit is availed of under 57A hence they filed the appeal claiming the amount of proforma credit taken under Rule 56A. In 1988, this Bench held that sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A as it stood prior to 15.4.1987 indicated two categories of manufacturers, one under the purview of Rule 56A and the other opting for Modvat credit and that it was not applicable only in respect of the very same inputs on which Modvat credit had been availed of. That if the manufacturer avails Modvat credit under Rule 57A, proforma credit under Rule 56A shall not apply. Reference application has been filed against this decision for referring certain points of law before the High Court.

The appellants manufacture welding electrodes for which they receive wire rods as inputs. Modvat scheme was availed in respect of these goods after filing the requisite declaration. During the period 1.3.1986 to 30.9.1986, the inputs were received against gate passes indicating that the goods were cleared at 'nil' rate of duty under Notfn. No. 208/83. However, the supplier subsequently paid duty on the subject goods on 6.4.1987. Thereafter, in December 1987, the appellants filed a claim for refund of duty in cash as provided for under Rule 57E. The Asstt. Collector rejected their claim. On appeal, the Collector allowed their appeal holding that the appellants were entitled to avail Modvat credit of the duty paid subsequently on the said inputs under Rule 57A and that Rule 57E was inapplicable in their case. Since the appellants' factories have been sold, their object is to get a cash refund as provided for under Rule 57E. Hence this appeal.

The appellants are manufacturers of vegetable product They receive Tin Sheets as packaging material, in respect of which they were taking Modvat Credit. Tin Sheets are converted without the aid of power into metal containers which in turn are used for packing their product. The Collector held that credit taken in respect of Tin Sheets was inadmissible as the sheets were used for conversion into exempted metal containers. He confirmed the demand for Rs. 6,44,906. under Rule-57-I read with S. 11A(1) of CESA, and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 50,000.

Rule 57I is a special provision under the Modvat scheme for the recovery of wrongly availed credit. Prior to its amendment with effect from 6.10.1988, no specific period of limitation was prescribed, for such recovery. Dismissing five Revenue appeals directed against the order-in-original of the CCE (Appeals), the Bench vide its common order No. 2310-14/90-WRB dated 24.10.1990, held that Rule 57I being complementary to CESA S. 11A, the time limit prescribed under S. MA is to be imported into Rule 57I. Through this application, the Department has sought reference to the High Courts of Bombay and Gujarat as a point of law, the question whether for the recovery of irregular credit relating to a period prior to the amendment of Rule 57I, a show cause notice was required to be issued within the period of limitation prescribed under section 11A, CESA, 1944.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the respondents holding that they were entitled to avail of Modvat credit in respect of tinplate used by them for manufacturing tins used for packing their final product, vegetable product for paying duty on the said final product. Revenue have submitted a Reference Application raising the point as to whether the Tribunal's interpretation is legal and proper in view of the fact that Rule 57A, C.E. does not include raw materials for packaging materials if the final product is not container for packaging but some other goods which require a container for packaging. The Department's stand is that Modvat credit is available only on ready to use containers and not on raw materials to be used for containers.

Without filing a declaration under Rule 57G, CER, the respondents were paying duty on the final product "Cables complete" through RG-23A, Part II, by utilising Modvat credit taken on the input, cables. The product was, however, being made through job workers with the permission taken under Rule 57F(2). Classification lists and price lists filed. The department held that in the absence of declaration under Rule 57G, duty could be paid only through PLA or in cash and not through RG-23A Demands were therefore raised taking the clearances as made without payment of proper duty.

The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

In this background, on 1-11-1997, a show cause notice was issued to the Appellant/Assessee raising a demand in the sum for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 2-5-1997, along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent to be calculated on the said amount for the period commencing from 12-8-1997 and ending on the date of payment. Furthermore, via the very SCN, a proposal was also made for imposing penalty.

In the reply, the assessee took stand that, for the period falling between 3-5-1997 and 19-6-1997, it had already 'expunged' MODVAT credit, in consonance with Notification No. 14/97 CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. In so far as the demand for interest was concerned, it was stated that it was premature, as under section 87(2)(c) of the Finance Act, interest would be payable, only, if, the amount demanded was not paid within ninety (90) days of the enactment of the Bill.

The stand, which, the Appellant /Assessee appeared to have taken with respect to penalty was that the alleged infraction was not an offence prior to the enactment of the Finance Act.

The Adjudicating authority sustained the demand in sum, equivalent to the excess credit availed of by the Appellant/Assessee for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 to 3-5-1997. Furthermore, the Appellant/Assessee was directed to pay interest at the rate of 18 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals), allowed the appeal of the Appellant/Assessee, albeit, partially. While the Commissioner (Appeals), confirmed the demand of duty for the period 23-7-1996 to 28-2-1997, along with interest, he set aside the demand of duty for the period spanning between 1-3-1997 and 3-5-1997.

The appellants manufacture aluminium conductors and double paper covered aluminium strips falling under heading 8544.02 of CET 1985. They use aluminium rods as raw material and availed proforma credit under Rule 56A and also benefit of MODVAT Scheme simultaneously for the period 1.3.1986 to 31.7.1986. They paid duty on the intermediate product i.e. bare aluminium strips used captively which was exempt under Notification No. 217/86 dated 2.4.1986. Notional credit under Rule 57B of MODVAT Scheme was taken. Both these practices were objected to by the department and recovery of erroneously availed MODVAT benefits ordered and penalty imposed.

The respondents claimed the benefit of Modvat credit in respect of Graphite rods and A.P.C. Powder, used for the manufacture of castings etc. The original authority denied the claim on the ground that Graphite rods are in the nature of appliance or equipment and the other is not an input under CE Rule 57A. But the Collector of Central Excise (Appeals Madras ordered that the Graphite rods and the A.P.C. Powder are eligible for the benefit of Modvat credit. The Department is in appeal.

The appellants had availed modvat credit for the full amount of duty paid on Kraft Paper used as packaging material for their final product linoleum. The Collector ordered reversal of the credit in excess of Rs. 800/- per mtr. The issues involved in this appeal were (i) interpretation of the terms 'Manufacture' used in Notification No. 149/87-CE vis-a-vis the expression "in relation to" figuring in Rule 57A, and (ii) applicability of extended limitation under Rule 57I when notice was issued after amendment of the Rule and there was no suppression.

The question for consideration in this appeal is whether plaster of paris for moulds used by the appellant for the manufacture of ceramic insulators could be considered to be an 'input' within the meaning of Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 for eligibility of Modvat credit.

The appellants manufacture paper and paperboards and availed of Modvat credit on gum tapes received as inputs from an SSI Unit, availing concession in terms Notification No. 175/86 dated 1.3.1986. The Department held that by virtue of Notification No. 177/86 dated 1.3.1986 the Modvat credit shall be restricted to Rs. 800 per MT and demanded repayment of credit availed in excess of that amount. The appellants' plea that Notification No. 177/86 dated 1.3.1986 was not applicable in their case was not accepted. The order was confirmed by the Collector (Appeals). In this appeal it has been submitted that with non-obstante clause inserted in Rule 57B, its provisions has overriding effect over the provisions of Rule 57A or notification issued thereunder.

The appellants manufacture electric wires and cables. They claimed MODVAT credit under Rule 57A on inputs for their finished products. On an examination of their record in respect of the duty-paid inputs, the Superintendent of Central Excise held the credit availed as inadmissible and ordered a reversal of benefit availed. The modified orders of the Asstt. Collr. were held void by Collector (Appeals) as being without jurisdiction, as the orders of the Superintendent were final, not having been appealed against.

The petitioners sought slay of the order of the Collector holding that the benefit of rule 57D(2) is not admissible to them on the inputs used by them in the manufacture of paints are in the stage of resin. According to them, the fact that resin is exempted from duty is no bar to the availment of modvat credit.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of a variety of industrial textile fabrics and all the final products were manufactured from an intermediate product, i.e., grey fabric (unprocessed fabric). The assessee, in 1994, availed Modvat credit on certain capital goods which were used, during the said period, for the manufacture of grey fabric which, in turn, was captively consumed in the manufacture of final products. Grey fabric was exempt from payment of duty during the said period while the final products were dutiable. As the intermediate product (grey fabric) was not specified as final product under rule 57Q, the adjudicating authority denied the benefit of rule 57R(2) to the assessee in respect of the capital goods holding that availment of credit on such capital goods was barred by the proviso to rule 57R(2). He, therefore, disallowed the Modvat credit availed by the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

Invoking the provisions of CE Rule 57C, the Assistant Collector asked the respondents to reverse MODVAT Credit amounting to Rs. 6,99,966.91 in respect of inputs which were used in the manufacture of Calcined Alumina which in turn was captively consumed without payment of duty in the manufacture of Aluminium. The Collector (Appeals) however, allowed their appeal, holding that credit was admissible on intermediate goods in terms of Rule 57D(2). Revenue are in appeal.

The appellants took Modvat credit in respect of certain inputs. The gate pass covering these goods showed nil rate of duty. The duty had been paid on a later dale by the suppliers upon realising that the notification exempting these goods had since been rescinded. The appellants have filed this appeal aggrieved by the Collector's order reversing the Modvat credit on the grounds that the provisions of Rule 57E had not been met.

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of yarn. It availed MODVAT credit on ‘capital goods’ described in the Table given below rule 57Q in respect of Steel Plates and M.S. Channels used by it for erection of chimney for the diesel generating set. The Assistant Commissioner disallowed the said credit on ground that since Steel Plates and M.S. Channels were not used as input in the manufacture of final product, these could not be covered under any of the Chapter Headings in the Table under rule 57Q. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld said order. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that since the chimney was used as an accessory to the diesel generating set, and Steel Plates and M.S. Channels were used in the fabrication of chimney, these items also fall within the ambit of serial No. 5 of the Table below rule 57Q and, therefore, MODVAT credit on these items could not be denied.

On appeal :

Two final products manufactured by the appellants became exempt from duty w.e.f. 1.3.1988. Consequently, the Assistant Collector disallowed Modvat credit to the tune of Rs. 2,28,323.49 on account of duty on inputs which were in stock on that date, basing his decision on the provision contained in Rule 57C. The Collector (Appeals) upheld the Assistant Collector's order. Hence this appeal before the Tribunal.

In terms of an order issued by the Central Government deemed credit of Rs. 2,300/- per tonne was allowed on aluminium alloy ingots subject to the fulfillment of certain conditions--one of which was that the inputs should be duty paid. Since the aluminium ingots used by the appellants as inputs in the manufacture of aluminium pistons, pins and rings is totally exempted from duty under Notification No. 183/84-CE, the Department alleged that the appellants had wrongly availed Modvat credit and demands were made for recovery of the same in terms of Rule 571. The extended period of limitation was also sought to be invoked alleging that the appellants had suppressed the fact that the inputs received and used by them had been assessed to 'nil' rate of duty. The order of the Collector (Appeals) confirming these demands is under challenge in this appeal.

The Revenue have filed this appeal being aggrieved by the Collector's order holding that the inputs used for the manufacture of caustic soda lye and caustic soda flakes which are finally used in the manufacture of PVC resins and are covered by the exemption notification, are eligible for Modvat credit.

The respondents are manufacturers of tyres. After filing a declaration under Rule 57G, they took Modvat credit for inputs specified in Rule 57A. Part of the finished goods were cleared free of duty under a notification. The issue for consideration is whether credit on the inputs going into that portion of the finished product, which is cleared free of duty under exemption notification has to be reversed.

The appellants manufacture electric lighting bulbs and fluorescent tubes and parts thereof, and availed of modvat credit of duty paid on the inputs. In the impugned orders, the Collector had held that oxygen gas, hydrogen and molybdenum wires were not inputs, but only tools or appliances, and confirmed reversal of credit of Rs. 6,12,005/- and 6,08,888/-, invoking the proviso to Section 11A, CESA, read with Rule 57I.

The appellant-manufacture of cement claimed Modvat credit of duty paid on machinery, equipments and parts and accessories thereof used in the mines of limestone. The claim of appellant was disallowed on ground that the goods were not ‘inputs’ within the meaning of Explanation to rule 57 and in respect of certain items credit had been availed after the expiry of six months.

On appeal :

The assessee installed in its factory duty paid imported capital goods which were to be used in manufacture of dutiable final products. The assessee availed Modvat credit. Subsequently, CBI conducted investigation in the assessees’ premises and seized various documents. The revenue sought to recover the credit of Rs. 12.85 crores on the grounds that (i) declaration filed under rule 57T(1) and 57T(2) were fabricated, (ii) original and duplicate copies of the invoices had fabricated defacements, (iii) the RT-12 returns were pre-dated modified and substituted, (iv) RG-23C PT I and PT II accounts were alleged to be written in January 1997 for capital goods received earlier in December 1994, (v) No installation certification was filed as it was fabricated, and (vi) Credit was taken only in or around January 1997. The assessee placed installation certificate. However, the revenue denied the credit and imposed penalties along with fine.

On appeal :
The issue in dispute is whether Modvat taken and used prior to utilisation of inputs for the manufacture of final products which have become exempt can be recovered under Rule 57C of CE Rules.

The Appellants/Petitioners manufacture Ingots, Billets, Bars, Rounds, Rods, flats etc. of Steel from waste and scrap of steel/iron. On introduction of Modvat scheme w.e.f. 1.3.1986, Govt. by its order dated 7.4.1986, issued directions under the 2nd proviso to Rule 57G(2), allowing deemed credit in respect of specified inputs purchased from outside and lying in stock on or after 1.3.1986, with the manufacturers of specified final products Without production of documents evidencing payment of duty. On 29.8.1986, the Govt. issued another order directing that deemed credit shall not be admissible in respect of waste and scrap of steel which are exempt from payment of duty or are chargeable to nil rate of duty. The Central Excise authorities disallowed the deemed credit in respect of such waste and scrap and directed deposit of the credit already availed. Hence these petitions.

Facts

The assessee, The Madras Aluminium Company, was a manufacturer of Aluminium and Articles and took credit of duty paid on various inputs.

The Department denied credit in respect of the 15 items but Commissioner (Appeals) upheld disallowance only in respect of following 11 items —

(i)

Alfoc Power

(ii)

Agromore rodine

(iii)

Aquachem

(iv)

Steel Wire rope

(v)

MS Plates various sizes

(vi)

Oxygen Gas

(vii)

Acctyne gas

(viii)

MS Welding electrodes

(ix)

Aluminium Welding wire

(x)

CI Welding wire

(xi)

PVC Pipes

The Tribunal allowed credit on aforesaid 11 items.

The department argued that the assessee is not entitled for such credit as the inputs are not used directly or indirectly for the manufacture of final products and they are not eligible for credit under rule 57A.

The assessee argued that the precedent judgments had allowed credit.

Issue Involved

Whether aforesaid 11 items were eligible for credit ?

The Tribunal by its order No. A 722-723/Cal/91 dt. 31.10.1991. had allowed the respondents the benefit of modvat credit in respect of (i) Wire netting of stainless steel and phosphor bronze and felts (articles of textile material) which are not machine, machinery etc. and (ii) Chemicals and resins used in water treatment treating them to be inputs for paper. The Collector has filed these applications under Rule 35 G(1) for reference to High Court of certain questions of law as arising out of Tribunal's order.

Aloxide paper is a coated abrasive paper which is used for polishing plywood. The issue for determination is whether the subject goods belong to the excluded category of inputs that are denied Modvat credit in view of the Explanatory clause under Rule 57A.

The appellants claimed Modvat benefit for Nitrogen Gas as an input used in relation to their final product MMA Monomer. The gas was used as it was inert, did not react with other chemicals, and was an essential technological necessity to create an inert atmosphere. The Assistant Collector held that such a use of Nitrogen gas cannot be held to be in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product and therefore disallowed the credit. The Collector (Appeals) concurred with this view.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing under known as 'H'.

During the set up of 'H', the assessee purchased the complete Single Point Mooring System [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc.

SPM system was located by the assessee outside the factory.

It availed Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system stating that it was capital goods in terms of rule 57Q.

The lower authorities including the Tribunal disallowed the Modvat credit.

On appeal to High Court:

The assessee-company was a manufacturer of motor vehicles. It availed modvat credit on differential duty paid during the period from 21-4-1986 to 2-4-1987 in respect of inputs received in its factory during the year 1986-87 and utilized between the period 16-8-1987 and 30-12-1987. According to the department, rule 57E underwent an amendment with effect from 15-4-1987 and, consequently, the assessee was not entitled to avail modvat credit on differential duty paid during the period 21-4-1986 to 2-4-1987. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to avail modvat credit.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :
The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

The respondents, vide their letter dated 14.3.1988, had filed a declaration in terms of Rule 57G(1), CE Rules, 1944 for availing Modvat credit. The said letter also contained an application under Rule 57H(1) to the concerned Asstt. Collector for availing credit of duty paid on inputs received by them (now lying in stock/consumed) between 27.4.1984 and 29.2.1988. The issue for determination is whether Modvat credit is available to the respondents on all the inputs that were received prior to filing the declaration and thereon, or whether it is limited to the last consignment dated 29.2.1988, that was received immediately before filing the declaration under Rule 57G(1).

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of carbon black. It was availing the facility of modvat credit under rule 57A. On scrutiny of RT-12 returns, filed by the assessee, it was noticed that the assessee had taken modvat credit on the strength of original copies of invoices without taking/applying for permission from the competent authority under rule 57G(2A). Hence, the adjudicating authority disallowed the modvat credit and confirmed the demands under rule 57-I along with penalties. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) remanded the matter to adjudicating authority for de novo proceedings. In remand proceedings, the adjudicating authority allowed the modvat credit, holding that there was no dispute regarding the duty paid character of the inputs and their receipt/utilization in manufacture of final product. Being aggrieved, the revenue successfully took the matter in appeals to the Commissioner against which assessee preferred appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed.

On appeal :

Facts

The assessee was manufacturing Chloromethane Product, TCE Product, STC etc., and took credit on pumps, iron and steel, motor, cables, electrical appliances etc.

The Department denied credit on MS Tanks on ground that MS Tanks (Heading No.73.09 of the CETA Schedule) were brought within the scope of 'capital goods' for credit purpose only with effect from 01-03-2001.

The Tribunal held that MS Tanks is a part of manufacturing plant and therefore, clause (a) of Explanation 1 of rule 57Q would stand attracted and MS Tanks being a capital goods, are eligible for modvat credit.

Issue Involved

Whether MS tanks are eligible for credit as 'capital goods' ?

The Collector (Appeals) rejected the appellants' claim for Modvat credit in respect of oxygen and acetylene on the ground that these gases were used in the cutting torch which comes under the excluded category in Rule 57A.

The assessee-appellant purchased ‘Loadall’ from manufacturer. The cost element of ‘Loadall’ included excise duty of certain amount. The appellant claimed Modvat credit under rule 57Q in respect of said item. Since the said item had been classified by the manufacturer and supplier thereof, under heading 84.29 and duty had been paid under the said heading, the authority-in-original disallowed the said credit to the assessee by observing that the said heading had been specifically ousted from the definition of capital goods under rule 57Q. Consequently, he also imposed certain amount of penalty upon the assessee on that account.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) being of opinion that said item would properly fall under heading 84.27 and not under heading 84.29, held that the assessee would be entitled to claim Modvat credit.

On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order and restored that of the authority-in-original holding that the ‘Loadall’ having been classified by the Central Excise Officer having jurisdiction over the manufacturer’s factory as falling under heading 84.29, the appellant, who was the consumer of those goods, could not get the classification of the manufacturer changed from 84.29 to 84.27.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The appellant was engaged in the manufacture of Hydrochloric Acid. It used Naphthalene as input. In terms of Notification dated 29-12-1962, credit of duty was available on Naphthalene under Rule 56A and Notification No. 177 of 1986 was issued under Rule 57A, stating that the credit on inputs classifiable under Chapter heading 27 of the Tariff Act would not be available. However, the appellant availed credit of duty on Naphthalene falling under said Chapter 27 in terms of Rule 57A during the period September, 1991 to January, 1992. As the said credit was not available under Rule 57A, a show-cause notice was issued to appellants proposing for denial of credit and imposition of penalty. The appellant submitted that it should not be denied credit of duty on the inputs which was available prior to 1-3-1986 under Rule 56A. The claim was rejected by the Additional Commissioner. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the appellants recording that indisputably the input was received in the factory and was used in the manufacture of final product. Modvat--Rule 57A--Explanation--Modvat credit allowed as long as inputs are used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and are not specifically excluded from the scope of the benefit in the explanation clause in Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 or by exclusion in Notification No. 177/86-CE. "There is no requirement that inputs should be present in the final product or it should be consumed in order to qualify for modvat benefit. It is clear that to become input it must be used in or in relation to the manufacture of goods. If lead is used in the process of manufacture of final product, there cannot be any doubt in availing modvat credit as per Explanation to Rule 57-A. As long as they are used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and are not specifically excluded from the scope of the benefit......in the explanation clause in Rule 57-A of the Central Excise Rules or by exclusion in Notification No. 177/86-CE, dated 1st March, 1986, modvat credit has to be allowed."

Modvat--credit is not admissible as no duty leviable on the final product (PSE) cleared by the appellants. "A reading of the various Central Excise Rules and the Scheme of the MODVAT set out therein shows that the facility of MODVAT Credit is available in respect of duty paid on inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the specified final product and for utilizing the credit so allowed towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final product. When, therefore, there is no duty leviable on the final products which have been cleared from the appellants' factory, the question of allowing them the MODVAT Credit on the inputs would not arise. Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules clearly envisages that no credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nit rate of duty. ...In view of above, we hold that there is no force in the appellants' plea......."

The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which stated as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation (c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which results in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f ) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw-material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. The instant case fell in clause (c) and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) even before 16-3-1995

Modvat - Phospheric acid added to cane juice to make up deficiency of phosphate is an input for quality sugar--Eligible. CE Rule 57A. "Modvat scheme does not restrict input duty relief only to essential raw materials or components. It is available to any item used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. The only restriction is that it is not to be an item of machinery/tool, appliance etc. Here the undisputed fact is that phosphoric acid is required to be added, where-ever P. 205 content is low in the cane juice for achieving whiteness of sugar. Hence, it is an input needed in the manufacture of the desired quality sugar......It is a chemical added to the product mix for achieving proper clarification of cane juice. Hence it goes as an input for the clarification of cane juice. Hence we cannot appreciate the stand taken by the Collector (Appeals) that the phosphoric acid is a tool or appliance. We also carefully considered the Boards' clarification......in a case where the cane juice does not have the desired level of P. 205 content and on account of that phosphoric acid is necessarily to be added for purpose of clarification, it cannot be dismissed as not an input.....Viewed in this context, the addition of phosphoric acid is a necessity and hence we could not agree with the clarification given by the Board."

Modvat--Inputs used "in relation to manufacture"--Graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used in relation to the manufacture of diamond drilling bits and not directly in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits, as these are not used as raw material or component parts of the finished goods, but the process in which they are used is so integrally connected with the ultimate production of goods that but for it the manufacture or processing of goods would be impossible or commercially inexpedient. "The Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that manufacture involves series of processes. Process in manufacture or in relation to manufacture implies not only the production but the various stages through which the raw material is subjected to change by different operations. It is the cumulative effect of the various processes to which the raw material is subjected to, manufactured product emerges. Therefore, each step towards such production would be a process in relation to the manufacture. Where any particular process is so integrally connected with the ultimate production of goods that but for that process manufacture or processing of goods would be impossible or commercially inexpedient that process is one in relation to the manufacture.......In the case before us graphite rods converted into graphite-moulds are used not as raw material or component part of the finished product--diamond drilling bits. We have, however, taken a view that they are used in relation to the manufacture of the diamond drilling bits."

2. Modvat--Appliances excluded from applicability of Rule 57A CE Rules--Graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used as "appliances", as these moulds are applied in one heat/sintering process in the furnace to bind particles of powdered metals to form the bits. Hence, graphite rods are excluded from the applicability of Rule 57A and are not eligible for Modvat credit. "The appellants themselves have called the material used in the furnace as graphite-mould. These moulds are used for one heat/sintering process. These moulds as such are not used in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits, for the purposes of Rule 57D of the Rules. These graphite moulds processed from graphite rods are applied in the furnace to bind particles of the powdered metals to form the bits. In this process referred to by the party as sintering process, the graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used as an 'appliance'. As appliances used for producing or processing of any goods or for bringing about any change in any substance in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products, are excluded from the applicability of Rule 57A, the graphite rods used in relation to the manufacture of diamond drilling bits are not the inputs for the purposes of that Rule........Accordingly, we hold that the credit of the duty of excise paid on graphite-rods is not allowed for utilisation towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the diamond "drilling bits."

3. Limitation--The show cause notice is not time barred as the limitation laid down under section 11A CESA is not applicable to cases of wrongful availment of Modvat credit under Rule 57I. Section 11A occupies the general field while Rule 57I deals with specific field of wrongful availment of Modvat credit [ratio of Gujarat High Court judgment in Torrent Laboratories Ltd. v. UOI, 1991(32) ECR 381 (Gujarat)]. "In the case - Torrent Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India.......the Hon'ble Gujarat High Court..........did not accept the contention that the provisions of Section 11A of the Act as regards the period of limitation should be read into Rule 57I.......

The assessee-company imported a consignment of paraffin wax on payment of customs duty including additional customs duty (also known as 'counter vailing duty' or 'CVD'), and such inputs were used in relation to manufacture of the finished products namely paraffin wax. There is no dispute to the fact that CVD was actually paid by the assessee at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem because Central excise duty leviable on, such petroleum products manufactured in India was 15 per cent ad valorem and CVD/additional customs duty is levied and collected on goods imported in India at the rate of excise duty applicable to like goods produced or manufactured in India. Thus, all the consignments of paraffin were imported by the assessee has actually suffered incidence of additional customs duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem. [Para 9]

Rule 57A(1) specifies that the Central Government was empowered to issue a notification for specifying duty for which credit was allowed and also the goods, i.e ., inputs and final products for which the credit scheme was applicable. Additional duty leviable under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was specified under rule 57A(1) for allowing its credit and the expression 'paid on' occurring under rule 57A(1) also clarified that the amount of additional duty actually paid was allowed as Modvat credit. [Para 11]

Notification No. 5/94, dated 1-3-1994 was issued under rule 57A; and it was specified at clause (iii) in the first paragraph of this Notification that the additional duty under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was allowed as Modvat credit for imported inputs, and the expression 'paid on inputs' occurring under this clause (iii ) emphasized that Modvat credit of the amount of additional duty actually paid on inputs was allowed. It appears that the assessee took Modvat Credit of additional customs duty actually paid by it while importing paraffin wax. The Modvat credit which was taken by the assessee was 15 per cent on paraffin wax imported by it. Record also reveals that various petroleum products produced in local refineries were governed and their price controlled by the Union Government under administrative/administered price regime APR because petroleum products produced by local refineries were APM products whose price in the domestic market was controlled and regulated by the Union Government through oil pool account. On petroleum products paraffin was produced by local refineries, excise duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem was leviable; but duty burden of 15 per cent on locally produced petroleum products was considered to be very high. As a result of which the Union Government devised a scheme under APM regime thereby directing the local refineries to charge excise duty at the rate of 10 per cent only from the consumers whereas the remaining 5 per cent duty was paid to such local refineries oil pool account, thereby absorbing incidence of excise duty to the extent of 5 per cent in the oil pool account through the APM regime mechanism. As a result of this, though the local refineries used to show in its gate pass/invoice the payment of excise duty on petroleum products at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem, the amount recovered from the consumer was 10 per cent whereas the balance 5 per cent was being adjusted under APM through oil pool account. Consequently, any person purchasing inputs in the nature of petroleum products from a local refinery actually suffered incidence of excise duty at the rate of 10 per cent only though the gate pass or invoice issued by the refinery would indicate total incidence of excise duty at 15 per cent ad valorem. This system, i.e., gate pass/invoice showing excise duty at 15 per cent but the person purchasing the petroleum products from a local refinery actually paying excise duty to the extent of only 10 per cent was applicable only for purchases from the local refineries because only local refineries and their products were governed by APM regime. For importers who directly imported the petroleum products from foreign countries, additional duty (CVD) being equal to excise duty leviable on like goods manufactured in India was levied and collected at 15 per cent ad valorem and, therefore, the importers like the assessee had actually paid additional duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem as such imports from foreign countries and foreign refineries were not governed by APM regime, and no payment towards duty was ever made from the oil pool account for such direct imports made by the citizens on their own. [Para 12]

Modvat - Caustic soda used for cleaning aerated water bottles eligible as cleaning is an important process in the manufacture and bottling of aerated water. CE Rule 57A. "The aerated waters cannot be marketed in unclean and unhygienic bottles. Therefore, the glass bottles are required to be cleaned. The assessee has a separate cleaning plant and first the bottles are cleaned with caustic soda, which is not in dispute. It follows that cleaning is an important process in the manufacture and bottling of aerated water. It is not remotely connected as held by ld. Collector. The proximity between the caustic soda and final product is also not remote but it is very essential and it is a part of a important process of manufacture linking with the bottling of aerated water. Therefore, for marketing aerated bottles, the clean glass bottles being a necessity, the modvat credit claimed for caustic soda cannot be denied, in the light of term "in and in relation to the manufacture of final product" appearing in Rule 57A of Central Excise Rules, 1944."

Rule 57C provides in mandatory and categorical terms that no credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product (of the enumerated categories) shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the instant case, the modvat credit had been taken on LDO and FO in terms of the provisions of rule 57A. The assessee procured inputs in sealed railway rakes from the plants of Indian Oil Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation. The consigned quantity and the received quantity were measured through manual measurement process and the difference between the consigned quantity and the received quantity was on an average 2.42 per cent. The oil is highly volatile in nature and is subject to change in quantum due to change in temperature and other atmospheric conditions. The measurements were taken on the manual basis and there would always be a tolerance error in measurement and the modvat credit could not be denied on such differences in weight or measurements under rule 57A. Once it is ascertained that this credit was allowable irrespective of the fact whether the appellants' actually availed of the credit or not, the appellants' case would fall within the exception of Rule 57H(2). Modvat credit--Rule 57A--assessable value---when inputs are cleared for home consumption on payment of duty at the appropriate rate from the original manufacturer and the assessee is not the manufacturer--the rate of duty applicable will be the rate of duty prevalent at the time of clearance of the goods--No justification for recovery of higher rate of duty. It is to be observed that rule 57B commences with a non obstante clause. It allows credit to be taken by a manufacturer of inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not. In the main body of sub-rule (1) there is no qualification as to where the inputs must be used. Qualifications have been introduced to the extent stated in clauses (i) to (vi), read with the Explanation. Clause (i) provides for inputs which are manufactured and used within the factory of production. Paints, fuel, packing materials and accessories are also treated as inputs without any requirement for user within the factory. Clause (iv) provides for credit on inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used for manufacture of the final products or for any other purposes ‘within the factory of production’. As far as the Explanation is concerned, the inputs are restricted to inputs notified under rule 57A.

There is no dispute that both explosives and limestone are notified under section 57A for manufacture of the final product viz., cement. [Para 4]

Under rule 57F, credit on inputs sent by a manufacturer from the factory to a job worker for test, repair, etc., but ultimately utilized in the final product is allowable. [Para 5]

Rule 57J allows credit on inputs used in manufacture of intermediate products described in column 3 of the Table provided the intermediate products are received by the manufacturer for use in or in relation to the manufacture of final products described in the corresponding Entry in column 4 of the Table. Explosives, limestone and cement are admittedly covered by column 1, 2 and 3 respectively of the Table. [Para 6]

In the case of Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra), the Supreme Court concluded that rule 57A(1) did not in any way specify that the inputs have to be utilized within the factory premises. It was further held that a reading of rule 57J and relevant notification can leave no manner of doubt that even in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of intermediate product which product is then used for the manufacture of a final product, the manufacturer would be allowed credit on the duty paid in respect of the input. On the explosives, duty had been paid and the appellants would be entitled to claim credit because the explosives were used for the manufacture of the intermediate product, namely, limestone which, in turn, was used for the manufacture of cement. The appeal of the manufacturer was, accordingly, allowed and it was held that the MODVAT credit was allowable on the use of the explosives in the manufacture of cement irrespective of the fact that the explosives were used directly in the mines and never entered the factory of the manufacturer of cement. [Para 8]

In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Collector to restrict the demand only to the extent of modvat credit involved on inputs like printing ink and other substances used for lamination and printing but allowing the modvat benefit in respect of duty on aluminium foils and paper."

While the appellants cannot claim the benefit as a matter of right without proper declaration, we also would like to observe that considering the facts and circumstances of this case, where the benefit in respect of the same goods has been subsequently extended, we would deem it proper to allow the modvat credit even during the period in dispute."

Modvat--Input--Paper bags used as packing material is not an Input in or in relation to the manufacture of cement As cement is also admittedly sold in bulk, paper bags are not a pre-requisite for fulling the cement in the market stream. Point of law referred to High Court as to whether bar under sub-rule (9) is applicable to the manufacturer per se for availing benefit of proforma credit under Rule 56A in respect of the same inputs or bar is applicable only if the manufacturer avails of Modvat credit under Rule 57A. Though the Bench decided that proforma credit cannot be availed of if Modvat credit is availed of the applicant's interpretation that the bar was not applicable as the inputs on which Modvat credit was claimed was different from those on which proforma credit was availed of, is worth considering. "The interpretation which he seeks to place on sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A, as it stood then, cannot also be dismissed as of no significance. The main question in the Reference Application to be decided is, whether the bar envisaged in sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A is applicable to the manufacturer per se if he avails of the benefit under the Modvat scheme or whether the bar is applicable only if that manufacturer avails of Modvat scheme in respect of the same inputs, for which proforma credit benefit is also availed of by the manufacturer. The issue, no doubt, bristles with debate and we consider it necessary to refer this point of law to the Hon'ble High Court so as to put the matter beyond any pale of doubt. While the view taken by this Bench that the bar is applicable to a manufacturer who cannot avail of proforma credit, if he opts for Modvat scheme appears to flow from a simple and straight reading of sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A, the other view canvassed by the applicants cannot also be brushed aside, mainly because of the fact that the term used in sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A refers to the availment of credit of duty paid on inputs under Rule 57A."

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

Analysis of Rule 57A :

As per rule 57A, a manufacturer of final products can avail the credit of any duty of excise or the additional duty under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. [Para 20]

Sub-rule (6) of rule 57A commences with a non-obstante clause and it empowers the Central Government to issue notification declaring the inputs on which the duty of excise paid under Section 3A to be deemed to have been paid at such rate or equivalent to such amount as may be specified in the said notification and allow the credit of such duty in respect of the said inputs at such rates or such amount and such conditions as may be specified in the notification. The proviso to the said Rule stipulates that the manufacturer shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that the inputs acquired by him are goods on which the appropriate duty of excise, as indicated in the documents accompanying the goods, has been paid. Thus, what is expected of an assessee is to take reasonable steps that appropriate duty, as indicated in the documents, has been paid. [Para 21]

Provision of Notification No. 58/97 :

Clause (2) of Notification No. 58/97-CE(NT) dated 30.8.1997 spells about the concept of deemed payment of duty on the inputs and further prescribes that it shall be equivalent to the amount calculated at the rate of twelve per cent of the price, as declared by the manufacturer, in the invoice accompanying the said inputs. On a plain reading of clauses (4) and (5), it is clear that there are two mandates to avail the benefit of the said notification -

First part (couched in the affirmative language) : As per the first part it is obligatory on the part of the assessee to produce the invoice declaring that the appropriate duty of excise has been paid on such inputs under the provision of section 3A.

Second part (couched in negative language) : The second command is that the provisions of the said notification shall not apply to inputs where the manufacturer of the said inputs has not declared the invoice price of the said inputs correctly in the documents at the time of their clearance from his factory. [Para 23]

Notification doesn't require assessee to verify actual payment from Department :

In the case at hand, there is no dispute that a declaration was given by the manufacturer of the inputs indicating that the excise duty had been paid on the said inputs under the Act. It is also not in dispute that the said inputs were directly received from the manufacturer but not purchased from the market. There is no cavil over the fact that the manufacturer of the inputs had declared the invoice price of the inputs correctly in the documents. It is perceivable from the factual matrix that the only allegation is that at the time of MODVAT verification it was found that the supplier of the inputs had not discharged full duty liable for the period covered under the invoices. This lapse of the seller is different and not a condition or rather a precondition postulated in the notification. [Para 24]

Rule 57A (6) requires the manufacturer of final products to take reasonable care that the inputs acquired by him are goods on which the appropriate duty of excise as indicated in the documents accompanying the goods, has been paid. The notification has been issued in exercise of the power under the said Rule. The notification clearly states to which of those inputs it shall apply and to which of the inputs it shall not apply and what is the duty of the manufacturer of final inputs. Thus, when there is a prescribed procedure and that has been duly followed by the manufacturer of final products, there is no justifiable reason to hold that the assessee had not taken reasonable care as prescribed in the notification. Due care and caution was taken by the assessee. It is not stated what further care and caution could have been taken. The proviso postulates and requires "reasonable care" and not verification from the department whether the duty stands paid by the manufacturer-seller. When all the conditions precedent have been satisfied, to require the assessee to find out from the departmental authorities about the payment of excise duty on the inputs used in the final product which have been made allowable by the notification would be travelling beyond the notification, and in a way, transgressing the same. This would be practically impossible and would lead to transactions getting delayed. [Para 25]
