[1994] 75 TAXMAN 167 (ART) MODVAT CREDIT ON CAPITAL GOODS - ACCOUNTING TREATMENT

C. Thandava Krishna*

Among the Budget proposals of 1994-95 most widely welcomed in the Indian industrial circles was the one pertaining to the extension of the MODVAT Credit Scheme to capital goods. The proposal has now been put into effect by amendment of the relevant statutory provisions.

In this article, the author examines the salient features of the new provisions and outlines the accounting problems that are likely to arise in the implementation of the extended scheme. He also examines the relevant existing Accounting Standards and Guidance Notes issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) which can be helpful in formulating a suitable method of accounting to achieve the objective underlying the new proposal The author also makes certain suggestions of his own in this context and stresses the necessity for the ICAI to issue a separate accounting Standard or Guidance Note on the subject - EDITOR

An overview of the new provisions

1. The Finance Minister provided a boon to the Indian industry by introduction of MODVAT credit on capital goods in the Budget for 1994-95.

In para 58 of part B of his Budget Speech, the Finance Minister has stated, "availability of capital goods at a reasonable cost is necessary to enhance our competitiveness and promote investment. It is also necessary to ensure that our domestic capital goods industry, which has a tremendous potential, is not at a comparative disadvantage due to anomalies in the tax structure. To further both these objectives, I propose the following package of measures".

The proposals include - reduction of basic customs duty on project imports and general capital goods, reduction of import duty on spares and parts, imposition of countervailing duty on imports of capital goods equal to the excise duty on domestic capital goods, reduction of import duty on machine tools and customs duty on steel, etc.

The major proposal in this package is that of extending the benefit of MODVAT credit to capital goods so that the full credit of excise duty paid on domestic capital goods or countervailing duty paid on imported capital goods will be available at one time.

The Finance Minister hoped that these proposals would give a strong boost to investment in the economy and will help the domestic capital goods industry in particular. This is a very good step taken by the Finance Minister and the proposals have been wholeheartedly welcomed by the entire industry.

It is hoped that the Indian industry will seize the opportunity and take full advantage of these benefits by starting new industrial lines, enhancing the existing capacities, modernising the existing equipment with updated technology and fully equip itself to be more competitive on a global level. Incidentally, the capital goods industry which has been suffering from acute recession in the recent past is bound to recuperate with full vigour.

Rules 57Q to 57U have been introduced in Chapter V of the Central Excise Rules for extending the scheme of MODVAT credit of the duty paid on capital goods. Notification No. 4/94-CE(NT) has been issued for this purpose which came into effect from March 1, 1994. The salient features of these rules and notifications are as follows :

Salient features of New Rules

2.1 Definition of capital goods - The expression 'Capital goods' is defined in rule 57Q as covering :

(i)Machines, machinery, plant, equipment, apparatus, tools or appliances used for producing or processing of any goods and also includes components, spare parts and accessories for such equipment.

( ii)Moulds and dies, generating sets and weigh bridges used in the factory of the manufacturer. It may be noted that duty paid on components, spare parts or accessories intended for these equipments is not eligible for MODVAT credit. It may also be noted that it is enough that these equipments are used in the factory and need not be used for producing or processing of any goods as in the case of machinery and equipment mentioned in sub-clause (i) above.

2.2 Adjustment of credit and exceptions - The credit of duty paid on capital goods can be used for payment of duty on any of the specified manufactured goods mentioned in the Annexure to rule 57Q.

If, however, any capital equipment acquired by the manufacturer is used exclusively for the manufacture of goods which are wholly exempted from excise duty or chargeable at nil rate of duty, no credit shall be allowed in respect of such equipment. Similarly, any components, spare parts or accessories of such items which are used for the production of wholly exempted or nil-rated goods are also not eligible for credit of the duty.

However, if any equipment is used even partly for manufacture of dutiable goods, MODVAT credit will not be denied on such capital goods.

The duty paid on capital goods on or after March 1, 1994, only is eligible for MODVAT credit and not the duty paid earlier.

Section 145A (a) leads to the logical conclusion and the resultant strange situation that a hybrid system can again be followed by the assessee regularly with retrospective effect from April 1, 1986 so long as the principle adumbrated in section 145A (b) with regard to the valuation of purchases, sales and inventories is followed. Section 145A (b) mandates the inclusion of any tax, duty, cess or fee paid or incurred by the assessee. The purchase cost incurred by the assessee at times may include the excise duty paid by a supplier. But such excise duty is not paid by the assessee at all. It is paid by the supplier, an outsider. Such an anomalous situation obviously could not have been intended by the Legislature.

A strange and undesirable consequence is that only purchases and sales which were made on the last day (March 31st) of the accounting year, and the entire closing stock on the aforesaid last day should be valued according to the new statutory formula, while purchases and sales made in the antecedent 364 days do not require to be so valued. Contingent Liability of excise duty for purposes of income-tax

4. Excise duty is normally payable by a company on manufactured goods, and for this purpose the company maintains two different godowns : (1) Duty-unpaid godown for goods in respect of which excise duty is not paid, and (2) Duty-paid godown for goods where excise duty is paid. Excise duty is paid before the removal of goods from the duty unpaid godowns. Generally excise duty liability in respect of goods lying in the duty-unpaid godown is shown by way of contingent liability under the Notes on Account. The liability is shown as ‘Estimated excise duty on goods manufactured but not despatched". As excise duty is not paid, it is not debited to the profit and loss account. The company’s accounts are generally prepared and maintained on the basis of the mercantile system.

The MODVAT Angle

5. Modvat is a procedure whereby a manufacturer can utilise credits for inputs against duty payable on final products. Duty credit taken on inputs is in the nature of a set off available against the payment of excise duty on the final products. This scheme was primarily introduced to arrest the cascading effect of duty paid on the intermediary product. Three situations arise in the application of Modvat, viz, (i) the manufacturer availing Modvat credit on inputs, (ii) the manufacturer transfers finished goods to the depots or sales outlet after the payment of duty, and (iii) the manufacturer not availing of Modvat credit.

The Supreme Court in Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (2) SCC 159, has observed :

(a) Where Modvat credit is availed of on duty paid inputs used in manufacture of exempted final products, crediting duty paid on such inputs and reversing the entry would not bar entitlement to exemption.

(b) The assessee should have maintained separate accounts for duty- free goods and the goods on which duty has to be paid. But a Departmental Circular Letter on this problem in which it has been clarified by the Ministry of Finance is as under :-

ing Standard 2

7. Accounting Standard 2 dealing with ‘Valuation of Inventories’ pres-cribed by the ICAI will be made mandatory soon and it has revised the definition of ‘costs of purchase’ as follows :

"The costs of purchase consist of the purchase price including duties and taxes (other than those subsequently recoverable by the enterprise from the taxing authorities), freight inwards and other expenditure directly attributable to the acquisition, less trade discounts, rebates and other similar items." From the definition, it is clear that Modvat credit is outside the purview of cost of purchase. While the Modvat credit is instantly taken and is available for payment of duty on the finished goods, the availment of credit carries a concurrent obligation for the inputs to be disposed of in the manner specified under rule 57F of the Central Excise Rules. In view of this, till the goods are so disposed of, the assessee has a potential liability and obligation in terms of the credit taken and utilised. Only on the disposal of the goods, in accordance with the rules, would the liability be extinguished and the benefit could be recognised as income in the profit and loss account.

"(4) The appellant’s contention as reflected in the reply to the show-cause notice that their factory was situated at a remote place where no facilities were available for stay of their engineers and workmen, and it was, therefore, necessary to construct a residential colony for the employees for being available on the spot in order to maintain continuity in the process of cement manufacture, has not been disputed. Legislative intent

11. A plain and simple reading of section 145A will show that the intention of the Legislature is to include only items like excise duty and customs duty to avoid one year advance claim under section 43B as per the following comparative analysis: Thus, it can be concluded—

(a)The Modvat benefit should not be added to the value of closing stock even under a plain and independent reading of section 145A as it is not incurred to bring the goods to their present location and condition.

(b)The excise duty and customs duty paid do form part of cost as they are incurred to bring the goods to their present location and condition on the matching concept basis.

Valuation of Fixed Assets and Inventories

12. Under rule 579 of the Excise Rules, the value of fixed assets should be capitalised net of Modvat benefit only. The assessee has to give a declaration and give proof also. This means any payment made from Modvat on capital goods is only an advance payment and should be treated like that only. Under the Income-tax Act also valuation has to be done net of Modvat only.

In case of inventories also, there cannot be any difference in the valuation principle. Any Modvat paid for inventories is also an advance payment only. Further, there is no one-to-one correlation. Thus, on the same logic and following international practices, the inventory should be valued on net basis only and there is no case for valuing it differently.

Gross Method of Valuation and Bank Financing

13. Banks finance the value of inventory held by the assessee. The value of inventory does not and should not include value of Modvat as credit is taken as soon as material reaches the factory. Further, such credits are utilised without one-to-one correlation for payment of excise duty of other manufactured goods. Hence, Modvat cannot and should not enter the stock valuation principles. If banks are financing assets in inventories inclusive of Modvat, they are only making a valuation mistake as the borrower has already received the benefit.

However, the balances in RG23A, 23C and PLA are balances held by the department and are in the nature of ‘temporary’ advances. These balances are highly liquid and, hence, deserve consideration for bank finance on merits and banks should analyse and recognise such items separately and under the head ‘Inventory’.

Conclusion

14. The following points emerge from the foregoing discussion :

(a)The purpose of section 145A is to plug the loopholes of judgments in the cases of Food Specialities Ltd. (supra) and Lakhanpal National Ltd. (supra) of claiming excise duty/customs duty one year in advance. Further, it should be understood that such practice was adopted only in part of the country as the Southern Bench has rejected the same argument in Durametallic (India) Ltd. v. IAC [1991] 38 ITD 24 (Mad.).

This objective is fully served by making AS-2 mandatory from April 1, 1999 as explained earlier

(b)It is quite clear that both gross and net methods of Modvat accounting under the matching concept are revenue neutral. Internationally only the net method of accounting is followed and, hence, we should also follow the same as we are moving towards borderless trading.

(c)No adjustment outside the books is fool-proof. The volume of transactions affecting Modvat is mind-boggling, e.g., number of gate-passes per day will be anywhere between 100 and 1000 per day depending on the volume of transactions.

(d)The companies themselves are extremely careful in accounting and reconciling Modvat as any claim not made adversely affects the bottom line.

(e)There is a regular audit and check by the department on Modvat.

(f)All the requirements in section 145A are fully and squarely met by making AS-2 mandatory.

(g)Hence, the provision of section 145A should be withdrawn immediately.

(h)A suitable safeguard may be introduced in section 43B to avoid advance claim relating to duty on inventories which are governed by AS-2, even though it is not possible to make such claim differently as AS-2 has been made mandatory.

Hence, the provision of section 145A may be deleted in the coming Finance Bill.

Section 145A of the Income-tax Act, 1961

5. Section 145A has been introduced in the Income-tax Act, to make certain adjustments to opening stock, purchases, sales and closing stock for arriving at income under the head ‘Profits and gains for business or profession’ and this will be effective from April 1, 1999. The adjustments to be made pertain to expenses actually incurred or paid towards tax, duty, cess or fee, etc. These are to be grossed up with purchases, sales and valuation of inventory.

Accounting practices

6. Most of the companies are following the ‘exclusive method’ of accounting for purchases, sales and inventory. Under this method, Modvat paid on purchase of inputs will not form part of cost of purchases in all cases wherever the benefit of Modvat credit is allowed to be enjoyed by the manufacturers of excisable goods. This is on the lines of the relevant Accounting Standard in India and International Accounting Standards. Similarly, excise duty and sales tax are also treated as balance sheet items.

Since the provisions of section 145A have been included in the statute effective from April 1, 1999 (assessment year 1999-2000), requirements of this section have to be given effect to by the assessees from April 1, 1998 onwards. For the sake of consistency and in accordance with the accepted accounting practices followed in India and abroad, it is better to continue the existing practice of accounting of purchases, sales and inventory valuation in the books net of sales tax, excise duty and Modvat as applicable. Adjustments as required to be carried out as per section 145A will be done outside the books of account for income-tax purposes.

uOne is the manufacturer can avail common CENVAT credit and pay excise duty equivalent to 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods. Similarly, the provider of output service can avail common CENVAT credit and pay service tax equivalent to 8 per cent of the value of exempted services.

uThe other option is that the manufacturer of goods or provider of output service can avail common CENVAT credit and pay an amount equivalent to CENVAT credit attributable to input goods and services consumed in relation to the manufacturer of exempted goods or the provision of exempted services, as per the procedures and conditions specified in sub-rule (3A) of rule 6. The said sub-rule, in principle, provides that the manufacturer can avail the CENVAT credit common to taxable and exempted goods and services by making a provisional monthly payment of the proportionate credit attributable to the exempted goods and services. The sub-rule further provides a formula to compute the percentage of the CENVAT credit attributable to the exempted goods or services based on the preceding year’s turnover of taxable and exempted goods and services. At the end of the financial year through which such provisional payments have been made, the quantum of the CENVAT credit attributable to the exempted goods or services is to be recomputed on the year’s actuals and the amount paid to the Government provisionally will be adjusted accordingly. The use of the above formula, by and large, would result in an appropriate identification of common input credit in proportion to the value of taxable and exempted output goods or services for that year.

The option to choose either of the above options has to be exercised and intimated to the department at the beginning of the year and once the option is exercised, it would be in force throughout the relevant financial year.

These options are significantly different from the option available, particularly to the service provider, under the erstwhile provisions. Supreme Court’s decision

8. The Court held that it felt it is appropriate that cost of excisable product for the purpose of assessment of excise duty under section 4(1)(b) read with rule 6 of the Valuation Rules should be reckoned as it would be reckoned by a man of commerce. It held that such realism must inform the meaning that the courts give to words of a commercial nature, like cost, which are not defined in the statutes which use them. A man of commerce would, in our view, look the matter thus : "I paid Rs. 100 to the seller of the raw material as the price thereon. Consequent upon purchasing the raw material and by virtue of the Modvat Scheme, I have become entitled to the credit of Rs. 10 with the excise authorities and can utilise this credit when I pay excise duty on my finished product. The real cost of the raw material (exclusive of freight, insurance and the like) to me is, therefore, Rs. 90. In reckoning, the cost of the final product would include Rs. 90. This, in real terms, is the cost of the raw material (exclusive of freight, insurance and the like) and that was which, in view of the Supreme Court, should be properly included in computing the cost of the excisable product.

The view the Supreme Court took about the cost of the raw material is also borne out by the Guidance Note of the Indian Institute of Chartered Accountants. In arriving at the above-mentioned decision it also acknowledged the fact that there can be no doubt that the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India is an authoritative body in the matter for laying down accountancy standards. Thus, in determining the cost of the excisable product covered by the Modvat Scheme under section 4(1)(b) read with rule 6 of the Valuation Rules, the excise duty paid on raw material also covered by the Modvat Scheme is not to be included.

It also held that by reason of clause (i) of the Explanation where there is an exemption ‘notification or order’ giving exemption in respect of excisable goods, it shall be given effect to and the excise duty leviable under the concerned Central Excise Statute shall be reduced to the extent of such exemption provided the notification or order is not ‘for giving credit with respect to, or reduction of duty of excise under such Act on such goods equal to any duty of excise under such Act, or the additional duty under section 3 of the Custom Tariff Act, 1975 already paid on the raw material or component parts used in the production or manufacture of such goods.’

It held that it is, therefore, only a notification or order relating to the excisable goods that gives an exemption equal to the excise duty already paid on raw materials used therein that is not to be taken into account for the purpose of computing the effective duty of excisable product. The Court held that it was not concerned in the instant case with a notification or order and that it was no body’s case that the credit that each manufacturer takes on its excisable product is equal to the excise duty paid on the raw materials used therein. In view thereof, the revenue could not draw any assistance from the Explanation to section 4(4)(d)( ii).

Conclusion

9. In view of the above-mentioned decision, the long drawn-legal controversy has been settled in favour of the assessee. This decision of the Supreme Court will go a long way in reducing the hardship of the manufacturers.

Therefore, the expression ‘in relation to’ which can be found in various grammatical situations in different legislative texts and contexts will have to be construed in a manner consistent with the scheme of the law. One has got to understand the definitions under rule 2 by keeping in mind the Cenvat credit scheme as a whole. Hence, there was no point in saying that the main part of the definition of ‘input service’ has to be interpreted without reference to the inclusive part of the definition.

Query – We are a private company and liable under reverse charge mechanism. We received security services in March, 2015. We will be making payment to the security agency in May 2015. Answer – As per section 67A of Finance Act, 1994, the rate of service tax is as on date of provision of taxable service. It does not talk of date of invoice or date of payment at all. Further, the preamble is only introduction to the rules. It is not a statutory provision in itself. That preamble was relevant upto 28-5-2012 i.e. till introduction of section 67A. Thus, if security agency service was provided prior to 1-4-2015, the service provider is liable to pay 25% of service tax and as obvious corollary, you will be liable to pay balance 75% of service tax. 8. Sum not eligible for relief under section 90/91 to be allowed as deduction: Mumbai ITAT Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. ACIT - [2020] 121 taxmann.com 190 (Mumbai - Trib.)

Assessee claimed deduction of state taxes paid overseas in the return of income. Assessing Officer (AO) held that the payments were not liable to be allowed as deduction. Assessee contended that as per Section 40(a)(ii) read with Section 2(43) taxes paid overseas are allowable as deduction if same are not eligible for any relief as per Section 90 or Section 91.

On appeal, Mumbai ITAT held that Bombay HC in case of Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. v. CIT - 390 ITR 271 held, since, the meaning of the word "tax" as defined under Section 2(43) would mean only the tax chargeable under the Act, the tax which has been paid abroad would not be covered within the meaning of Section 40(a)(ii). Thus, taxes levied overseas which were not eligible for relief either under Section 90 or Section 91, would not come within the purview of section 40(a)(ii). Pertinently, unlike Section 91 read with Explanation (iv), Section 90 does not provide for inclusion of tax levied by any State/local authority of that country within the expression 'income tax'.

Relying on said decision, AO was directed to verify whether the State taxes paid by the assessee overseas were eligible for any relief under section 90 and if it is not found to be so, assessee's claim of deduction should be allowed.

Clarification is required here about 50 per cent plus 50 per cent, when it is available?

( a)First 50 per cent of Cenvat credit is available in first year itself. Rule 4(2a) says :

From the above, it is clear that assessee wants to avail Cenvat credit which is less than 50 per cent in first year, then such credit will be allowed. However, total claim of Cenvat credit cannot in any case exceed 50 per cent of the total duty paid on ‘such capital goods’.

3. We are manufacturers of plastic containers and have manufactured 200 pieces of bottles (5 litre) capacity, which are lying in our premises and also in RG1 register (daily stock account). Same are also shown as closing balance in ER 1 return filed. However, due to urgent requirement of 1 litre bottles, we will have to regrind 5 litre bottles and use the same for the manufacturing of 1 litre bottles. How should we account for the same in ER-1 return as well as in RG1 register (daily stock account) ?

Since 5L bottles are lying in stock with you, they must be non-duty-paid stocks.

As per rule 4, read with rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, in case excisable goods (5L bottles) are used for further manufacture of excisable goods (1L bottles), then these would termed as 'captive consumption' and as per the exemption notifications in force, no duty is payable thereon. There is no bar that finished goods cannot be used as 'inputs'. In fact, rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 stipulates such situation, though in the context of finished goods removed and subsequently returned for remaking. Hence, assuming that process of converting 5L bottles into 1L bottles is manufacture, no duty is payable. You may account for the same as issue for captive consumption and duty may be paid on value of 1L bottles.

However, if process of converting 5L bottles into 1L bottles is not manufacture you may pay duty on value of 5L bottles (normal transaction value) and after processing into 1L bottles, clear them. In records, the stock of 5L bottles may be shown to have been cleared as per rule 4 of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000.

Transfer Pricing Impact:

This downturn in the industry will have a significant impact in the transfer price both in the internal pricing policy as well to adhering to the compliance, as discussed below some of them; Royalty Rate - Vendors to the OEM would be the most impacted. Usually such vendors have long term relationship with the OEM and based on the forecast there is quite investment is made in the dies & tools. Also, it is true that for some of the vendors the dependency with few / even sole OEM is too highly concentrated, keeping in mind long term relationship there would be lot of push back from the OEM to honour the commitment.

Resulting such vendors may not be profitable or lower than usual with high working capital.

With this above fact, I clearly believe the TP methodology followed earlier to defend the covered transaction may not continue to sustain particularly where profit-based methods have been used. For example – most of the vendors will have either an overseas joint venture partner for technology – hence there is payment of royalty triggers. Typically, royalty is based percentage of sales, in order to benchmark the royalty, rate the company choose either sophisticated database such "royalty stat", etc. or use over aggregate approach using some profit-based method.

In case of transaction-based approach, it may be difficult to rely on such global database, as there may not be significant change in the royalty rates, also it is not possible for the companies renegotiating the royalty rates for such inverted growth which is potentially temporary. Here is a challenge…

Of course, in profit-based method, one may argue that it would apply to the comparable sets and hence the "tested party" can be aligned with market profit. In order to sustain such argument – (a) selection of right comparable is an very important , apart from the routine selection process one must carefully compare the right business model (b) after screening the right set - the importance of various financial ratio's including selection of profit level indicator plays a crucial role (c) apply the permissible economic adjustment . Having said this , based on our experience after applying above you may have set of comparable's below threshold number for application of range plus practical challenge during the time when the return needs to filed the local Indian data based may not have financials of the relevant year, multiple year may throw up wrong number.

Tangible transaction – here in this article, we are only dealing with purchase of goods including raw materials (may be in SKD / CKD) from its associated enterprises. These purchases are made in order to supply to their domestic customers in India. The challenges will be more severe as it would significantly impact their profitability and it may be very difficult for the local subsidiary to renegotiate with their group companies. Once it impacts on profitability, the issues would be the same as described in the previous paragraph under "Royalty rate".

(ii)Is the company obliged to make the adjustments suggested in the section in the company’s books of account or can it be made outside the books for income-tax purpose? The Government has recently issued an ordinance to amend section 211 of the Companies Act, 1956 requiring the companies to follow the accounting standards to be prescribed by the National Advisory Board Committee on A ccounting Standards and till such time as this Committee prescribes the standards, the standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) have to be followed.

The Accounting Standard 2 (AS 2) on valuation of inventories issued by the ICAI (both old and new exposure draft) recognises only exclusion of Modvat credit from the purview of cost of inventories. The valuation of stock will have to be made according to AS 2 and companies will have to continue preparation of accounts as per existing practice of excluding Modvat in purchases and closing stock. Thus, the adjustments as required under section 145A will be made outside the books of account.

(iii)Is it correct to say that the profit figure after making the adjustments in section 145A will be the same ?

The provisions of section 145A can be compared to the second alternative method of accounting as suggested in the Guidance Note on Accounting for Modvat issued by the ICAI. The companies have to identify the Modvat availed in respect of consumption of inputs and pass necessary entries in the books to reduce it from the total cost of inputs consumed. The balance of Modvat credit for the units in stock will be shown as deduction from closing stock so that double accounting of profit is avoided. This will result in the same profit figure both under the existing practice and the proposed method.

(iv)Is it the intention of the Income-tax Act to make the adjustment to both opening and closing stock of inventories ?

The explanatory memorandum on the notes on clauses of the Finance Bill, 1998 prescribes adjustment to both opening and closing stock of inventories. It means that the opening stock of inventories as on April 1, 1998 will be adjusted to include the Modvat content without disturbing the closing stock value as on March 31, 1998. This can be done by a suitable transfer from loans and advances- RG 23A balance as on April 1, 1998. This has to be done in addition to adjustment of Modvat value in the closing stock as on March 31, 1999.

The above-mentioned questions need to be answered to have a clear understanding of the provisions of section 145A either by way of issue of a clarification explaining the abovenoted points or making a suitable amendment to section 145A to the extent of exclusion of Modvat from the purview of adjustments as envisaged in that section.

An example showing the presentation of profit and loss account with adjustment of Modvat on closing stock of inventories is given in the Annexure. The adjustment of M odvat on closing stock has been reduced from the balance of Modvat balance and showing the closing stock inclusive of Modvat content. The profit will be the same under both the traditional and the proposed methods.

Conclusion

4. From the foregoing, it will be seen that we have actually ended up with seeking clarifications on a number of questions on the provisions of section 145A. This being so, we have to conclude that the purpose of ‘rationalisation and simplification’ has not been achieved.

Cenvat eligible as input but availed as capital goods and vice versa

Definition of 'capital goods' under Cenvat is not a conventional definition. Thus, sometimes, it happens that an article is eligible for credit as Cenvat on inputs but is availed as Cenvat on capital goods, or vice versa. In some earlier cases, when Modvat declaration was required, it was held that declaration filed in respect of inputs can be accepted if the goods are found to be capital goods and vice versa. The principle of these decisions will surely apply when Cenvat is available under one head but taken in other head due to mistake. It is true that in capital goods, only upto 50% credit can be availed in current year and balance in any subsequent years. However, this is only a technical lapse.

REVERSAL OF MODVAT CREDIT TAKEN ON INPUTS UNDER RULE 57CC

Kind attention is invited to the provisions of Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules for reversal of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods chargeable to 'nil' rate of excise duty. The provision has been made that where a manufacturer uses inputs which are common to both dutiable goods as well as exempted goods, the manufacturer is required to debit the amount equal to 8% of the value of the exempted goods when they are cleared from the factory.

2. In some cases, the exempted goods cleared by one manufacturer are used as inputs by another manufacturer. The manufacturer of exempted goods indicates the amount of Modvat credit reversed on the invoices issued by him for such exempted goods. In this context, some doubts have been raised whether the amount of Modvat credit so reversed is available as Modvat credit to the user of such exempted goods when he uses them as inputs in his factory.

3. In this context, it is clarified that the amount reversed is not by way of payment of excise duty. Accordingly, the amount of Modvat credit reversed and shown in the invoice by the manufacturer of exempted goods cannot be taken as credit by the user of exempted goods.

4. Reliance Industries Limited

Background: Reliance Industries (RIL), controlled by the Ambanis, commenced operations with a synthetic fabric mill at Naroda, Ahmedabad, where texturising/twisting facilities were set up in 1979. RIL mainly came out in the late 1980s when they progressed from no position among top hundred Indian companies to their present status of India’s top ranking private sector company. This success came through clearly read out forthcoming business opportunities in advance even before the start of the liberalization era. The strength of Reliance lies in its capabilities, largest number of equity base, to introduce innovative financial instruments and initiate novel funding schemes. The philosophy of “think big, grow big” has resulted in RIL building world-size plants in the areas it operates and achieve market dominance. RIL commissioned a PFY project in 1982, a PSF unit in 1986, linear alkyl benzene (LAB) and a PTA unit in 1988, all at Patalganga, Maharashtra. The technical collaborator for PFY and PSF was Du-Pont, US, and for PTA, UOP Processors, US, and ICI, UK. In 1991-92, RIL commissioned a petrochemicals unit to manufacture HOPE and PVC at Hazira, Gujarat, in technical collaboration with Du Pont and BF Goodrich respectively. In 1995-96, it entered the telecom industry through a joint venture with Nynex, US. RIL is a major player in the Indian petrochemicals sector. Its operations capture value addition at every stage from producing crude oil and gas to polyester and polymer products and are vertically integrated to the production of textiles.

Reliance has one of the largest marketing networks in Indian industry. All its brands are market leaders. RIL has obtained ISO 9002 certification from BVQI for its Patalganga and Hazira complexes. RIL is the first private sector company in India to be rated by the international credit rating agencies. During 1999-2000, the company completed its integrated Jamnagar complex, in a record period of less than 3 years. The Jamnagar complex houses the world’s largest grass root refinery (under Subsidiary company Reliance Petroleum), paraxylene and polypropylene project with the capacity of 27 million tons, 1.4 million tons and 6,00,000 tons per annum respectively together with country’s largest all weather port, power plants and all related infrastructure. It has also acquired control over the polyester manufacturing facilities of four relatively large polyester producers over the last two years. This has enhanced the effective production capacity in polyester by nearly 2,00,000 tons per annum to 8,00,000 tons per annum.

208 ELT 211 (CESTAT), assessee purchased some components, took Cenvat credit and cleared as such on payment of duty. It was held that they could do so even as trader and hence no duty is payable even if the activity is not 'manufacture' (It is advisable to show it as 'amount' and not as 'duty') - followed in AB Stampings v. CCE (2010) 259 ELT 299 (CESTAT SMB) In Natural Vitamins v. CCE 2005 (179) ELT 326 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if department collects excise duty on final product, it cannot say that Cenvat is not available as process is not 'manufacture'. Such stand is self-contradictory - same view in CCE v. MP Telelinks v. 2004(178) ELT 167 (CESTAT) * Markwell Paper Plast v. CCE (2012) 285 ELT 76 (CESTAT) * CCE v. North Sun Enterprises (2012) 284 ELT 75 (CESTAT).

In Sterlite Opticals v. CCE (2012) 282 ELT 392 (CESTAT), assessee paid excise duty under bona fide belief that the activity carried out by him is 'manufacture'. He availed Cenvat credit of inputs. The payment of duty was accepted by department. It was held that even if activity is not 'manufacture', it is case of removal of inputs 'as such' and Cenvat credit is reversible. Thus, entire exercise is revenue neutral and demand is not sustainable.

In one case, Tribunal observed that if the activity does not amount to manufacture, there can be no question of levy of duty and if duty is levied, Cenvat credit cannot be denied by holding that there is no manufacture. This view was upheld in CCE v. Creative Enterprises (2009) 235 ELT 785 (Guj HC DB) * Perfo Chem v. CCE (2015) 315 ELT 237 (CESTAT).

If department accepts duty (though not payable), it cannot refuse Cenvat credit on inputs, since department cannot approbate and reprobate, as held in Laxmindco Steel P Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 629 (CESTAT SMB).

In Rico Auto Industries v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 170 = 57 RLT 271 (CEGAT), it was held that inputs can be removed 'as such' or 'after processing' under Cenvat Credit Rules. Hence, even if there is no 'manufacture', no further amount is payable - followed in Sona Koyo Steering Systems v. CCE (2007) 5 STR 15 (CESTAT) [Strictly legally, in such case, it should be shown as 'amount' in invoice and not 'duty'].

If supplier has paid excise duty on wire drawn (though not legally payable during the relevant time), the buyer is eligible to avail Cenvat credit if supplier had not obtained refund of duty paid by them on drawn wire - BCL Springs v. CCE 2005 (185) ELT 56 (CESTAT).

Similarly, in Owens Bilt Ltd. v. CCE 1998(101) ELT 642 (CEGAT), it was held that once duty is paid at the manufacturer's end, the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner at user's end has no jurisdiction to decide whether duty was payable or not - followed in Goa Industrial Products v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 222 (CESTAT).

Duty paid at full rate without availing concession - If assessee has paid duty at tariff rate without availing concessional rate, the buyer can get full Cenvat credit. - CCE v. Noel Pharmaceuticals 1999 (113) ELT 66 (CEGAT).

In Bharat Chemicals v. CCE (2004) 170 ELT 568 (CESTAT), tariff rate was 20%, but effective rate by way of exemption notification was 10%. Assessee was paying duty @ 10% for home clearances, but was paying duty @ 20% for goods exported and claiming rebate of full duty paid on export goods. It was held that he is entitled to full rebate, as rebate is of 'duty paid' and not 'duty payable'. [He was paying higher duty as he had excess balance in Cenvat credit account].

Cenvat credit if process incidental to manufacture - Purification and filtration of chemical to make it marketable in international market is process incidental to manufacture of the product and hence is covered in definition of 'manufacture' and hence is eligible for Cenvat credit - CCE v. Alok Enterprises (2010) 259 ELT 333 (Bom HC DB).

Buyer can avail Cenvat credit, if supplier paid duty, even though not payable - If supplier had paid excise duty (though not payable), buyer is eligible to avail Cenvat credit. See case law in earlier part of this chapter.

9.3-4 Process losses and handling loss are allowable There will be some loss of inputs during manufacturing process. Cenvat (now ITC) is available on entire quantity of input even if part of input goes in process loss, since all inputs are 'used' in the manufacture of final product, even if it is not reflected in final product - Multimetals Ltd. v. ACCE 57 ELT 209 (SC) = 1992 (1) SCC 715 = AIR 1992 SC 1532 = 1992 AIR SCW 1644 - quoted with approval in UOI v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC - 3 member bench order), where it was held that exact mathematical equation between quantity of raw material purchased and the raw material found in finished product is not possible, and should not be looked for. [This judgment is in respect of Proforma Credit, but its ratio is fully applicable to Cenvat (now ITC).]

In CCE v. IPF Vikram India 2002(150) ELT 175 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat on inputs (now ITC) which have gone in waste is not deniable - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC on merits - 2003 (153) ELT A303.

Entire Cenvat credit (now ITC) is available if part of input is contained in waste, refuse or by-product - Mahindra Hinoday Industries v. CCE (2014) 308 ELT 555 (CESTAT), relying on CBE&C circular No. B-4/7/2000-TRU dated 3-4-2000 - same view in Rupa and Co v. CESTAT (2015) 324 ELT 295 (Mad HC DB). * ARS Steels & Alloy International (P.) Ltd. v. State Tax Officer [2021] 86 GST 644 = 127 taxmann.com 787 (Madras HC).

Even if waste is not returned by job worker, Cenvat credit of excise duty (now ITC of GST) contained in such scrap or waste is not required to be reversed - Mukand Ltd. v. CCE (2015) 318 ELT 134 (CESTAT SMB).

Loss of input by evaporation during manufacturing processing is to be treated as ware or loss and Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such loss is not required to be reversed - CCE v. BOC (India) (2008) 223 ELT 33 (Guj HC DB).

Chlorine gas left in cylinder after use of gas in processing can be termed as 'process loss' and its Cenvat credit (now ITC) is available - CCE v. Andhra Paper Mill (2011) 269 ELT 79 (AP HC DB).

Even excess process loss is allowable if any evidence of clandestine removal is not available - Rollex Electro Products v. CCE (2016) 338 ELT 736 (CESTAT).

Loss of inputs during handling eligible - In or in relation to the manufacture covers the entire manufacturing process starting from initial stage of handling of inputs. Thus, if wastage of input at the initial handling from tank discharge due to various reasons like spillage, pipeline losses, handling losses etc., it is 'in or in relation to manufacture' and Cenvat (now ITC) cannot be denied. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 943 (CEGAT) - followed in CCE v. Hydrogas Plg (I) P Ltd. 2006 (196) ELT 167 (CESTAT) - same view in Zeneca ICI Agro Chemicals v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 770 (CESTAT).

9.3-5 No credit on short received inputs but natural losses allowable

If inputs are short received and there is loss during transit, the goods short received cannot be termed as 'used in or in relation to manufacture'. Hence, Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such short received inputs is not available - Asea Brown Boveri Ltd. v. CCE 1994 (74) ELT 897 (CEGAT) - same view in Bombay Dyeing v. the matter, the amendment, as such does not Affect valuation of inventory of raw material, etc. As discussed, for purchases, a purchaser pays a price for the goods. Such price would have various components including Cost, Duties, Taxes, profits etc. The price is lump sum or composite price and cannot be divided into its components.

Further, the Duty, etc. embedded in purchase price is not incurred by the purchaser.

MODVAT Credit is not available as a consequence of payment. Finally, the credit available under the Rule is in respect of purchase price, which includes Duties. The credit is quantified with reference to the amount of Duty. That is only a basis for quantifying the amount.

Accordingly, it is not a credit for Duty. In this connection, a useful reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. P.J. Chemicals [1994] 210 ITR 830 wherein it is held that a subsidy granted as incentive cannot be reduced from actual cost of the assets merely because it is quantified on the basis of the value of Fixed Assets. Accordingly, in purchase cost of raw material, in spite of the amendment, there is no requirement to adjust MODVAT.

One of the arguments against such a view could be that 'mischief sought to be cured', as explained in the Memorandum, is to provide for such adjustment. It seems, the provision and the Memorandum are at variance. The provision, as said above, aims at including Duty, etc., incurred or paid for bringing the goods to its location and conditions so as to neutralize Special Bench Decision and Gujarat High Court Decision. Had the intention been otherwise, the language would have been different and section 145A(b), possibly would have read "further adjusted to include any set-off, credit or any other entitlement in respect of any Tax, Duty ..., actually paid or incurred by the assessee, whether as a part of the price or otherwise, to bring the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation".

CIRCULAR NO. 283/117/96-CX, DATED 31-12-1996

UTILISATION OF CENVAT CREDIT IN RESPECT OF INPUTS ON WHICH CREDIT IS AVAILED BUT THE INPUTS ARE EXPORTED AS SUCH UNDER BOND

It has been represented to the Board that the field formations have taken a view that credit on inputs cleared as such for export under bond cannot be allowed to be utilised for payment of duty on final products cleared for home consumption nor can it be refunded in cash. In this regard, it has been stated that aforesaid facilities are available where inputs are used in the manufacture of export products and not in the case where inputs have themselves been exported. This doubt has arisen on account of the proviso to rule 57F(4) according to which duty availed on inputs used in the manufacture of final product exported under bond could be utilised towards payment of duty on goods cleared for home consumption or refunded in cash.

2. The matter has been examined by the Board.

3. Rule 57A(1) provides for the general scheme of MODVAT given in section V(AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and it indeed mentions that credit of duty will be allowed for utilising towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final products. Whereas rule 57F is a more specific provision regarding manner of utilisation of the inputs and the manner of utilisation of the credit allowed in respect of duty paid thereon. Rule 57F(1)(ii) permits removal of the inputs as such for export under bond. Proviso to rule 57F(4) deals with manner of utilisation of credit in cases of export of 'final products' or 'intermediate products' under bond. Export of inputs as such under bond were treated as 'final product' by virtue of 'deemed manufacture' clause (i.e., the expression as if such inputs have been manufactured in the same factory) under the erstwhile rule 57F(1)(ii) which covered all such cases within the ambit of proviso to rule 57F(4). This expression was omitted by Notification No. 28/95-C.E.(N.T.), dated 29-6-1995 with a view to simplify the clearance procedure, which has created a doubt in respect of utilisation of credit in such cases. It is not the intention of the Government to debar such manufacturer-exporters from utilising credit. Clearance of inputs as such for export under bond can still be treated at par with 'final product' and the manner of utilisation of credit in such cases will be governed by the provisions of the proviso to rule 57F(4).

4. It is also observed that in case such inputs are cleared on payment of duty by debit in RG-23A Part II account by virtue of rule 57F(4)(iii), the manufacturer will be entitled for rebate under rule 12(1)(a) of the Central Excise Rules. He is however, put to disadvantage if he opts for export under bond procedure.The exports under 'claim of rebate' and 'export under bond' should be at parity, since, intention of both the procedures is to make duty incidence 'nil'. It is also an established principle that rules should be interpreted in a manner which do not render them redundant.

5. Accordingly, it is clarified that the Modvat credit in RG-23A Part II account against the export of inputs as such under bond can be utilised in the same manner as is provided for a final product under proviso to rule 57F(4). Obviously, it follows from this that such inputs should be allowed to be exported under bond without any reversal of the credit.

FACT: The assessee used Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) and furnace oil as fuel for generating electricity which in turn was captively consumed for production of final products such as caustic soda and cement. The assessee claimed MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) of rule 57A on LSHS. In civil appeal challenging the entitlement of assessee to MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

orem because Central excise duty leviable on, such petroleum products manufactured in India was 15 per cent ad valorem and CVD/additional customs duty is levied and collected on goods imported in India at the rate of excise duty applicable to like goods produced or manufactured in India. Thus, all the consignments of paraffin were imported by the assessee has actually suffered incidence of additional customs duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem. [Para 9] Rule 57A(1) specifies that the Central Government was empowered to issue a notification for specifying duty for which credit was allowed and also the goods, i.e ., inputs and final products for which the credit scheme was applicable. Additional duty leviable under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was specified under rule 57A(1) for allowing its credit and the expression 'paid on' occurring under rule 57A(1) also clarified that the amount of additional duty actually paid was allowed as Modvat credit. [Para 11]

Notification No. 5/94, dated 1-3-1994 was issued under rule 57A; and it was specified at clause (iii) in the first paragraph of this Notification that the additional duty under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was allowed as Modvat credit for imported inputs, and the expression 'paid on inputs' occurring under this clause (iii ) emphasized that Modvat credit of the amount of additional duty actually paid on inputs was allowed. It appears that the assessee took Modvat Credit of additional customs duty actually paid by it while importing paraffin wax. The Modvat credit which was taken by the assessee was 15 per cent on paraffin wax imported by it. Record also reveals that various petroleum products produced in local refineries were governed and their price controlled by the Union Government under administrative/administered price regime APR because petroleum products produced by local refineries were APM products whose price in the domestic market was controlled and regulated by the Union Government through oil pool account. On petroleum products paraffin was produced by local refineries, excise duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem was leviable; but duty burden of 15 per cent on locally produced petroleum products was considered to be very high. As a result of which the Union Government devised a scheme under APM regime thereby directing the local refineries to charge excise duty at the rate of 10 per cent only from the consumers whereas the remaining 5 per cent duty was paid to such local refineries oil pool account, thereby absorbing incidence of excise duty to the extent of 5 per cent in the oil pool account through the APM regime mechanism. As a result of this, though the local refineries used to show in its gate pass/invoice the payment of excise duty on petroleum products at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem, the amount recovered from the consumer was 10 per cent whereas the balance 5 per cent was being adjusted under APM through oil pool account. Consequently, any person purchasing inputs in the nature of petroleum products from a local refinery actually suffered incidence of excise duty at the rate of 10 per cent only though the gate pass or invoice issued by the refinery would indicate total incidence of excise duty at 15 per cent ad valorem. This system, i.e., gate pass/invoice showing excise duty at 15 per cent but the person purchasing the petroleum products from a local refinery actually paying excise duty to the extent of only 10 per cent was applicable only for purchases from the local refineries because only local refineries and their products were governed by APM regime. For importers who directly imported the petroleum products from foreign countries, additional duty (CVD) being equal to excise duty leviable on like goods manufactured in India was levied and collected at 15 per cent ad valorem and, therefore, the importers like the assessee had actually paid additional duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem as such imports from foreign countries and foreign refineries were not governed by APM regime, and no payment towards duty was ever made from the oil pool account for such direct imports made by the citizens on their own. [Para 12]

The Union Budget for the year 1996-97 was presented in the Parliament on 22-7-1996 and it was during this budget that the excise duty on locally produced petroleum products except LPG and kerosene was enhanced to 15 per cent (from 10 per cent) but by providing for adjustment of payment of 5 per cent excise duty from oil pool account by operating APM so that the ultimate burden on the local consumers may not increase by additional 5 per cent excise duty for locally produced petroleum products. Thus, the liability of 5 per cent was absorbed by the Union Government itself through the APM regime. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, read with section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 and section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Credit of duty not to be denied or varied in certain cases - Inputs - Whether section 11A Central Excise Act, would have no application, while construing impact of section 87 of Finance Act - Held, yes - Assessee, a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, paid specified duty - Relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE(NT) dated 1-3-1994 issued under rule 57A, assessee took MODVAT credit on inputs namely, Furnace Oil at rate of ‘15 per cent at valorem’ - This Notification was amended by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT) dated 3-5-1997 - By said amendment, rate of credit on above inputs was restricted to ‘10 per cent ad valorem’ - Said Notification was given retrospective effect from 23-7-1996 by virtue of provisions of section 87 of Finance Act - Whether demand for recovery of MODVAT Credit with interest was justified - Held, yes [Paras 17.2  18.1] [In favour of revenue]GST/Excise  Customs: Where specified duty was paid on inputs and relying upon Notification 5/94-CE (NT) dated 1-3-1994, assesse took MODVAT credit at rate of 15 per cent, in view of restriction imposed on rate of credit at 10 per cent via subsequent Notification 14/97 CE(NT) dated 3-5-1997 which was given retrospective effect, revenue’s demand for recovery was justified

FACT: The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS. HELD: The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which stated as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation (c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which results in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f ) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw-material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. The instant case fell in clause (c) and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) even before 16-3-1995

HEADNOTE: Rule 56A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Proforma Credit - Inputs relief - proforma credit admissible even if end products (tyres) are exempts: U/Notfn. 95/79-CE, since no correlation is required. CE NOTFN. 95/79-CE

FACT: The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

HELD: Set off Since Notfn. No. 95/79-CE does not contain a clause to the effect that proforma credit on inputs should be correlated to the duty payable on outputs, non-payment of duty on finished goods does not make the manufacturer ineligible to proforma credit. "Read by itself this notification does not have any condition that there should be any nexus between the inputs and outputs.... The Ld. JDR's argument that goods mentioned in column 5 (final products) are only those which pay duty is not supported by the wordings of the notification. No condition regarding payment of duty is contained any where in the notification. We are further supported in this view by a judgment of the Cegat (SRB) (CCE Bangalore v. Wipro Information Technology, Bangalore) reported in 1988(14) ECR 490 wherein it was held that proforma credit once allowed cannot be recovered subsequently even if finished goods are exempted later on, making proforma credit ineligible, since no interlinking account is provided for in rule."

Minority view:--Interpretation--as per proviso 2 of the Notfn. availability of proforma credit on inputs is directly proportional to the duty payable on the finished product and since tyres were cleared without payment of duty, set off cannot be allowed on the inputs used in the manufacture of tyres. Proviso 2 of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE ".....the extent of the credit that could be taken in respect of the duty paid on the inputs shall be restricted to the duty payable on the end product if it happens to be less than the credit of duty taken on the inputs. What follows from this therefore, is that if the duty payable on the end product is nil, then the extent of exemption that will be available will also be nil........In as much as, no duty in respect of these tyres has been paid, in terms of proviso 2 to the notification, the availability of the credit on the inputs in respect of these tyres will have therefore, to be nil."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Conditions for allowing of

HELD: Modvat - Phospheric acid added to cane juice to make up deficiency of phosphate is an input for quality sugar--Eligible. CE Rule 57A. "Modvat scheme does not restrict input duty relief only to essential raw materials or components. It is available to any item used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. The only restriction is that it is not to be an item of machinery/tool, appliance etc. Here the undisputed fact is that phosphoric acid is required to be added, where-ever P. 205 content is low in the cane juice for achieving whiteness of sugar. Hence, it is an input needed in the manufacture of the desired quality sugar......It is a chemical added to the product mix for achieving proper clarification of cane juice. Hence it goes as an input for the clarification of cane juice. Hence we cannot appreciate the stand taken by the Collector (Appeals) that the phosphoric acid is a tool or appliance. We also carefully considered the Boards' clarification......in a case where the cane juice does not have the desired level of P. 205 content and on account of that phosphoric acid is necessarily to be added for purpose of clarification, it cannot be dismissed as not an input.....Viewed in this context, the addition of phosphoric acid is a necessity and hence we could not agree with the clarification given by the Board."
