facts.text: The appellants receive duly paid bi-metal strips for use in the manufacture of I.C. Engines and parts thereof. They avail of Modvat Credit for the inputs. The appellants cleared certain parts like plain shaft bearings at nil rate of duty by following Chapter X procedure. The Assistant Collector held that credit could not be allowed on inputs used in the manufacture of parts cleared at nil rate of duty as per provisions of Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. This was upheld by the Collector (Appeals).

The assessee used Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) and furnace oil as fuel for generating electricity which in turn was captively consumed for production of final products such as caustic soda and cement. The assessee claimed MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) of rule 57A on LSHS. In civil appeal challenging the entitlement of assessee to MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

Besides manufacturing chlorine, the appellant company also manufactures hydrochloric acid, essential for the treatment of effluents generated during the process of manufacture of chlorine. The appellants claimed Modvat credit under Rule 57A on hydrochloric acid in terms of Notfn. 217/86-CE, as hydrochloric acid used has to be considered as an input for the finished product (chlorine).

The appellants manufacture metal containers claiming Modvat benefit for lacquered sheets used us input. Duty-paid plain tin sheets were bought and sent direct for lacquering. They were charged for having taken credit in RG-23A register without declaring plain tin sheets as inputs and getting them lacquered without following the procedure under Rule 57F(2) till January 1987, in contravention of Rule 57G. The credit of Rs. 2,28,521.64 was negatived. The Collector (Appeals) upheld the order.
The Department ordered reversal of Modvat under Explanation to Rule 57A, CE on wire netting and felt as the items are parts of paper making machine.

The assessee was engaged in manufacture of paper and was availing the benefit of the Modvat Scheme under rule 57A. The assessee was also manufacturing pulp which was chargeable to nil rate of duty. The said pulp was captively consumed for the manufacture of paper. A small quantity of said pulp was sent to its sister unit without payment of requisite duty thereon on the ground that it was the case of stock transfer and not a sale and, therefore, rule 57CC was not applicable in its case. The department was of view that the assessee should have taken into account 8 per cent of the selling price of pulp sold by the assessee’s sister units in other States for reversal of Modvat credit on inputs on which credit was taken by applying rule 6(b)(i ) of the Central Excise (Valuation) Rules, 1975. The department issued show-cause notice alleging that if comparable prices obtained by the sister units were taken into consideration, then the total duty payable at the rate of eight per cent would work out to Rs. 4.58 lakh (approx.) whereas the assessee had paid duty of Rs. 2.67 lakh (approx.) and, therefore, the assessee had evaded payment of duty and was also liable to pay penalty under rule 57-I(4), read with rule 173C of the 1944 Rules. However, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s contention that in the case of ‘stock transfer’ there is no ‘sale’ and, therefore, rule 57CC was not applicable.

On revenue’s appeal to the Supreme Court :

The applicants utilised Modvat credit under Rule 57A CE Rules on kraft paper used for packing the final product Linoleums. The Department held that under Notification No. 177/86-CE dt. 1.3.1986 credit in respect of paper used "in the manufacture of final product" was to be restricted to Rs. 800/- per tonne. The applicants' case is that they used the kraft paper "in relation to the manufacture of the final product", as "packing material" is recognised as an input under Explanation to Rule 57A. The Tribunal upheld the Department's view but found the Notice time-barred. In this Reference Application, the main question raised by applicants for reference is whether the expression "in relation to the manufacture" used in Rule 57A is synonymous to the expression "in the manufacture" used in the abovesaid notification. By the Cross Objection, the Department wants reference of the question whether the time limit prescribed in amended Rule 57-I is applicable in respect of an offence committed earlier to the amendment.

The respondent are manufacturers of electrical stampings and laminations out of hot-rolled and cold-rolled electrical steel and silicon steel sheets etc. and availed deemed Modvat credit in respect of the inputs as specified under Rule 57A, which were purchased from market and were not covered by any duty paying documents. The G.O.I. modified its earlier instructions and respondent's inputs became illegible with effect from 2.11.1987 for deemed Modvat credit without production of duty paying documents.

Iron & Steel products are manufactured by the appellants. They filed a declaration under Rule 57G of CE Rules for availing MODVAT benefit in respect of inputs used in relation to their manufacture of finished products. The Assistant Collector held that the refractory products are not covered by the explanation in Rule 57A of CE Rules. This order was upheld by Collector (Appeal).

The appellants manufacture duplicating paper, stencil paper, etc. and avail proforma credit under Rule 56A for tissue paper, maplitho paper, printing paper etc. used as inputs in their manufacture. While continuing to avail of proforma credit they opted for Modvat credit in respect of inputs used, other than those on which the Modvat scheme had been extended from 1.3.1986. This was objected to by the department on the ground of sub-rule (9) of 56A which totally bars an availment of benefit under 56A if Modvat credit is availed of under 57A hence they filed the appeal claiming the amount of proforma credit taken under Rule 56A. In 1988, this Bench held that sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A as it stood prior to 15.4.1987 indicated two categories of manufacturers, one under the purview of Rule 56A and the other opting for Modvat credit and that it was not applicable only in respect of the very same inputs on which Modvat credit had been availed of. That if the manufacturer avails Modvat credit under Rule 57A, proforma credit under Rule 56A shall not apply. Reference application has been filed against this decision for referring certain points of law before the High Court.

The appellants manufacture welding electrodes for which they receive wire rods as inputs. Modvat scheme was availed in respect of these goods after filing the requisite declaration. During the period 1.3.1986 to 30.9.1986, the inputs were received against gate passes indicating that the goods were cleared at 'nil' rate of duty under Notfn. No. 208/83. However, the supplier subsequently paid duty on the subject goods on 6.4.1987. Thereafter, in December 1987, the appellants filed a claim for refund of duty in cash as provided for under Rule 57E. The Asstt. Collector rejected their claim. On appeal, the Collector allowed their appeal holding that the appellants were entitled to avail Modvat credit of the duty paid subsequently on the said inputs under Rule 57A and that Rule 57E was inapplicable in their case. Since the appellants' factories have been sold, their object is to get a cash refund as provided for under Rule 57E. Hence this appeal.

The appellants are manufacturers of vegetable product They receive Tin Sheets as packaging material, in respect of which they were taking Modvat Credit. Tin Sheets are converted without the aid of power into metal containers which in turn are used for packing their product. The Collector held that credit taken in respect of Tin Sheets was inadmissible as the sheets were used for conversion into exempted metal containers. He confirmed the demand for Rs. 6,44,906. under Rule-57-I read with S. 11A(1) of CESA, and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 50,000.

Rule 57I is a special provision under the Modvat scheme for the recovery of wrongly availed credit. Prior to its amendment with effect from 6.10.1988, no specific period of limitation was prescribed, for such recovery. Dismissing five Revenue appeals directed against the order-in-original of the CCE (Appeals), the Bench vide its common order No. 2310-14/90-WRB dated 24.10.1990, held that Rule 57I being complementary to CESA S. 11A, the time limit prescribed under S. MA is to be imported into Rule 57I. Through this application, the Department has sought reference to the High Courts of Bombay and Gujarat as a point of law, the question whether for the recovery of irregular credit relating to a period prior to the amendment of Rule 57I, a show cause notice was required to be issued within the period of limitation prescribed under section 11A, CESA, 1944.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the respondents holding that they were entitled to avail of Modvat credit in respect of tinplate used by them for manufacturing tins used for packing their final product, vegetable product for paying duty on the said final product. Revenue have submitted a Reference Application raising the point as to whether the Tribunal's interpretation is legal and proper in view of the fact that Rule 57A, C.E. does not include raw materials for packaging materials if the final product is not container for packaging but some other goods which require a container for packaging. The Department's stand is that Modvat credit is available only on ready to use containers and not on raw materials to be used for containers.

Without filing a declaration under Rule 57G, CER, the respondents were paying duty on the final product "Cables complete" through RG-23A, Part II, by utilising Modvat credit taken on the input, cables. The product was, however, being made through job workers with the permission taken under Rule 57F(2). Classification lists and price lists filed. The department held that in the absence of declaration under Rule 57G, duty could be paid only through PLA or in cash and not through RG-23A Demands were therefore raised taking the clearances as made without payment of proper duty.

The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

In this background, on 1-11-1997, a show cause notice was issued to the Appellant/Assessee raising a demand in the sum for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 2-5-1997, along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent to be calculated on the said amount for the period commencing from 12-8-1997 and ending on the date of payment. Furthermore, via the very SCN, a proposal was also made for imposing penalty.

In the reply, the assessee took stand that, for the period falling between 3-5-1997 and 19-6-1997, it had already 'expunged' MODVAT credit, in consonance with Notification No. 14/97 CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. In so far as the demand for interest was concerned, it was stated that it was premature, as under section 87(2)(c) of the Finance Act, interest would be payable, only, if, the amount demanded was not paid within ninety (90) days of the enactment of the Bill.

The stand, which, the Appellant /Assessee appeared to have taken with respect to penalty was that the alleged infraction was not an offence prior to the enactment of the Finance Act.

The Adjudicating authority sustained the demand in sum, equivalent to the excess credit availed of by the Appellant/Assessee for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 to 3-5-1997. Furthermore, the Appellant/Assessee was directed to pay interest at the rate of 18 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals), allowed the appeal of the Appellant/Assessee, albeit, partially. While the Commissioner (Appeals), confirmed the demand of duty for the period 23-7-1996 to 28-2-1997, along with interest, he set aside the demand of duty for the period spanning between 1-3-1997 and 3-5-1997.

The appellants manufacture aluminium conductors and double paper covered aluminium strips falling under heading 8544.02 of CET 1985. They use aluminium rods as raw material and availed proforma credit under Rule 56A and also benefit of MODVAT Scheme simultaneously for the period 1.3.1986 to 31.7.1986. They paid duty on the intermediate product i.e. bare aluminium strips used captively which was exempt under Notification No. 217/86 dated 2.4.1986. Notional credit under Rule 57B of MODVAT Scheme was taken. Both these practices were objected to by the department and recovery of erroneously availed MODVAT benefits ordered and penalty imposed.

The respondents claimed the benefit of Modvat credit in respect of Graphite rods and A.P.C. Powder, used for the manufacture of castings etc. The original authority denied the claim on the ground that Graphite rods are in the nature of appliance or equipment and the other is not an input under CE Rule 57A. But the Collector of Central Excise (Appeals Madras ordered that the Graphite rods and the A.P.C. Powder are eligible for the benefit of Modvat credit. The Department is in appeal.

The appellants had availed modvat credit for the full amount of duty paid on Kraft Paper used as packaging material for their final product linoleum. The Collector ordered reversal of the credit in excess of Rs. 800/- per mtr. The issues involved in this appeal were (i) interpretation of the terms 'Manufacture' used in Notification No. 149/87-CE vis-a-vis the expression "in relation to" figuring in Rule 57A, and (ii) applicability of extended limitation under Rule 57I when notice was issued after amendment of the Rule and there was no suppression.

The question for consideration in this appeal is whether plaster of paris for moulds used by the appellant for the manufacture of ceramic insulators could be considered to be an 'input' within the meaning of Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 for eligibility of Modvat credit.

The appellants manufacture paper and paperboards and availed of Modvat credit on gum tapes received as inputs from an SSI Unit, availing concession in terms Notification No. 175/86 dated 1.3.1986. The Department held that by virtue of Notification No. 177/86 dated 1.3.1986 the Modvat credit shall be restricted to Rs. 800 per MT and demanded repayment of credit availed in excess of that amount. The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which stated as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation (c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which results in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f ) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw-material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. The instant case fell in clause (c) and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) even before 16-3-1995

Modvat--Inputs used "in relation to manufacture"--Graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used in relation to the manufacture of diamond drilling bits and not directly in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits, as these are not used as raw material or component parts of the finished goods, but the process in which they are used is so integrally connected with the ultimate production of goods that but for it the manufacture or processing of goods would be impossible or commercially inexpedient. "The Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that manufacture involves series of processes. Process in manufacture or in relation to manufacture implies not only the production but the various stages through which the raw material is subjected to change by different operations. It is the cumulative effect of the various processes to which the raw material is subjected to, manufactured product emerges. Therefore, each step towards such production would be a process in relation to the manufacture. Where any particular process is so integrally connected with the ultimate production of goods that but for that process manufacture or processing of goods would be impossible or commercially inexpedient that process is one in relation to the manufacture.......In the case before us graphite rods converted into graphite-moulds are used not as raw material or component part of the finished product--diamond drilling bits. We have, however, taken a view that they are used in relation to the manufacture of the diamond drilling bits."

2. Modvat--Appliances excluded from applicability of Rule 57A CE Rules--Graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used as "appliances", as these moulds are applied in one heat/sintering process in the furnace to bind particles of powdered metals to form the bits. Hence, graphite rods are excluded from the applicability of Rule 57A and are not eligible for Modvat credit. "The appellants themselves have called the material used in the furnace as graphite-mould. These moulds are used for one heat/sintering process. These moulds as such are not used in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits, for the purposes of Rule 57D of the Rules. These graphite moulds processed from graphite rods are applied in the furnace to bind particles of the powdered metals to form the bits. In this process referred to by the party as sintering process, the graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used as an 'appliance'. As appliances used for producing or processing of any goods or for bringing about any change in any substance in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products, are excluded from the applicability of Rule 57A, the graphite rods used in relation to the manufacture of diamond drilling bits are not the inputs for the purposes of that Rule........Accordingly, we hold that the credit of the duty of excise paid on graphite-rods is not allowed for utilisation towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the diamond "drilling bits."

UOI, 1991(32) ECR 381 (Gujarat)]. "In the case - Torrent Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India.......the Hon'ble Gujarat High Court..........did not accept the contention that the provisions of Section 11A of the Act as regards the period of limitation should be read into Rule 57I.......

The assessee-company imported a consignment of paraffin wax on payment of customs duty including additional customs duty (also known as 'counter vailing duty' or 'CVD'), and such inputs were used in relation to manufacture of the finished products namely paraffin wax. There is no dispute to the fact that CVD was actually paid by the assessee at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem because Central excise duty leviable on, such petroleum products manufactured in India was 15 per cent ad valorem and CVD/additional customs duty is levied and collected on goods imported in India at the rate of excise duty applicable to like goods produced or manufactured in India. Thus, all the consignments of paraffin were imported by the assessee has actually suffered incidence of additional customs duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem. [Para 9]

Rule 57A(1) specifies that the Central Government was empowered to issue a notification for specifying duty for which credit was allowed and also the goods, i.e ., inputs and final products for which the credit scheme was applicable. Additional duty leviable under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was specified under rule 57A(1) for allowing its credit and the expression 'paid on' occurring under rule 57A(1) also clarified that the amount of additional duty actually paid was allowed as Modvat credit. [Para 11]

Notification No. 5/94, dated 1-3-1994 was issued under rule 57A; and it was specified at clause (iii) in the first paragraph of this Notification that the additional duty under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was allowed as Modvat credit for imported inputs, and the expression 'paid on inputs' occurring under this clause (iii ) emphasized that Modvat credit of the amount of additional duty actually paid on inputs was allowed. It appears that the assessee took Modvat Credit of additional customs duty actually paid by it while importing paraffin wax. The Modvat credit which was taken by the assessee was 15 per cent on paraffin wax imported by it. Record also reveals that various petroleum products produced in local refineries were governed and their price controlled by the Union Government under administrative/administered price regime APR because petroleum products produced by local refineries were APM products whose price in the domestic market was controlled and regulated by the Union Government through oil pool account. On petroleum products paraffin was produced by local refineries, excise duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem was leviable; but duty burden of 15 per cent on locally produced petroleum products was considered to be very high. As a result of which the Union Government devised a scheme under APM regime thereby directing the local refineries to charge excise duty at the rate of 10 per cent only from the consumers whereas the remaining 5 per cent duty was paid to such local refineries oil pool account, thereby absorbing incidence of excise duty to the extent of 5 per cent in the oil pool account through the APM regime mechanism. As a result of this, though the local refineries used to show in its gate pass/invoice the payment of excise duty on petroleum products at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem, the amount recovered from the consumer was 10 per cent whereas the balance 5 per cent was being adjusted under APM through oil pool account. Consequently, any person purchasing inputs in the nature of petroleum products from a local refinery actually suffered incidence of excise duty at the rate of 10 per cent only though the gate pass or invoice issued by the refinery would indicate total incidence of excise duty at 15 per cent ad valorem. This system, i.e., gate pass/invoice showing excise duty at 15 per cent but the person purchasing the petroleum products from a local refinery actually paying excise duty to the extent of only 10 per cent was applicable only for purchases from the local refineries because only local refineries and their products were governed by APM regime. For importers who directly imported the petroleum products from foreign countries, additional duty (CVD) being equal to excise duty leviable on like goods manufactured in India was levied and collected at 15 per cent ad valorem and, therefore, the importers like the assessee had actually paid additional duty at the rate of 15 per cent ad valorem as such imports from foreign countries and foreign refineries were not governed by APM regime, and no payment towards duty was ever made from the oil pool account for such direct imports made by the citizens on their own. [Para 12]

It is to be observed that rule 57B commences with a non obstante clause. It allows credit to be taken by a manufacturer of inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not. In the main body of sub-rule (1) there is no qualification as to where the inputs must be used. Qualifications have been introduced to the extent stated in clauses (i) to (vi), read with the Explanation. Clause (i) provides for inputs which are manufactured and used within the factory of production. Paints, fuel, packing materials and accessories are also treated as inputs without any requirement for user within the factory. Clause (iv) provides for credit on inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used for manufacture of the final products or for any other purposes ‘within the factory of production’. As far as the Explanation is concerned, the inputs are restricted to inputs notified under rule 57A.

There is no dispute that both explosives and limestone are notified under section 57A for manufacture of the final product viz., cement. [Para 4]

Under rule 57F, credit on inputs sent by a manufacturer from the factory to a job worker for test, repair, etc., but ultimately utilized in the final product is allowable. [Para 5]

Rule 57J allows credit on inputs used in manufacture of intermediate products described in column 3 of the Table provided the intermediate products are received by the manufacturer for use in or in relation to the manufacture of final products described in the corresponding Entry in column 4 of the Table. Explosives, limestone and cement are admittedly covered by column 1, 2 and 3 respectively of the Table. [Para 6]

In the case of Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra), the Supreme Court concluded that rule 57A(1) did not in any way specify that the inputs have to be utilized within the factory premises. It was further held that a reading of rule 57J and relevant notification can leave no manner of doubt that even in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of intermediate product which product is then used for the manufacture of a final product, the manufacturer would be allowed credit on the duty paid in respect of the input. On the explosives, duty had been paid and the appellants would be entitled to claim credit because the explosives were used for the manufacture of the intermediate product, namely, limestone which, in turn, was used for the manufacture of cement. The appeal of the manufacturer was, accordingly, allowed and it was held that the MODVAT credit was allowable on the use of the explosives in the manufacture of cement irrespective of the fact that the explosives were used directly in the mines and never entered the factory of the manufacturer of cement. [Para 8]

In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Modvat--Intermediate product--soda ash used in the purification of brine is not an intermediate product and is also exempted from duty under Notification 154/68-CE. Therefore, Modvat is inadmissible on inputs used for soda ash consumed in the purification of brine. "It is an admitted position that fully manufactured soda ash is cleared under exemption for captive use. For construing this as an intermediate product as per Rule 57D, that product should have come into existence during the course of manufacture of final product and such intermediate product is for the time being, exempted. In this case, there is a considerable force in the argument of the learned SDR that soda ash removed for brine purification does not occur in the manufacture of final product viz. soda ash. Hence, applying provisions of Rule 57D to the present facts and circumstances is to be ruled out. The Collector has erred in applying Rule 57D. The Rule applicable, is only Rule 57C and hence on merits, such soda ash removed for brine purification is not eligible for Modvat benefit; because it is exempted from whole of the duty payment."

Modvat--Input--Paper bags used as packing material is not an Input in or in relation to the manufacture of cement As cement is also admittedly sold in bulk, paper bags are not a pre-requisite for fulling the cement in the market stream. In this view of the matter, we uphold the order of the lower appellate authority."

Point of law referred to High Court as to whether bar under sub-rule (9) is applicable to the manufacturer per se for availing benefit of proforma credit under Rule 56A in respect of the same inputs or bar is applicable only if the manufacturer avails of Modvat credit under Rule 57A. Though the Bench decided that proforma credit cannot be availed of if Modvat credit is availed of the applicant's interpretation that the bar was not applicable as the inputs on which Modvat credit was claimed was different from those on which proforma credit was availed of, is worth considering. "The interpretation which he seeks to place on sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A, as it stood then, cannot also be dismissed as of no significance. The main question in the Reference Application to be decided is, whether the bar envisaged in sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A is applicable to the manufacturer per se if he avails of the benefit under the Modvat scheme or whether the bar is applicable only if that manufacturer avails of Modvat scheme in respect of the same inputs, for which proforma credit benefit is also availed of by the manufacturer. The issue, no doubt, bristles with debate and we consider it necessary to refer this point of law to the Hon'ble High Court so as to put the matter beyond any pale of doubt. While the view taken by this Bench that the bar is applicable to a manufacturer who cannot avail of proforma credit, if he opts for Modvat scheme appears to flow from a simple and straight reading of sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A, the other view canvassed by the applicants cannot also be brushed aside, mainly because of the fact that the term used in sub-rule (9) of Rule 56A refers to the availment of credit of duty paid on inputs under Rule 57A."

in the present case. ............When these articles are referred to as machines or part of machines in the Tariff itself, their Tariff classification outside Section XVI is no impediment to their identity as such machines, appliances or parts of machines. Such is not the case with felts and wire netting. They are neither machines nor parts thereof and they are also not known as such machines/parts. The question posed is one of fact which does not require to be referred to the High Court." 7. Tribunal's order holding felt and wire-netting for paper making machinery, and chemicals used for water treatment, as eligible for modvat benefit was based on several factors and ratio of several judgment of Supreme Court and High Courts. Criteria laid down by Supreme Court in Ballarpur judgment are satisfied, and there is no justification for making reference to the High Court Reference application and stay applications are dismissed/rejected. "The order granting modvat benefit is based on several factors following the ratio of several decisions discussed therein. As far as felt and wire netting are concerned, it has been held that these are neither the excluded items in the Explanation under Rule 57A nor parts of such items. Not being machines, machinery etc. which are the excluded items, they qualify for modvat benefit. .............We have now considered the contentions raised by the Collector citing the Ballarpur judgment of the Supreme Court wherein the criterion of utilisation in the manufacturing process as distinct from the manufacturing apparatus had been laid down. We have found that this criterion is satisfied by the inputs in question which are not used as manufacturing apparatus. We have held them to be outside the zone of exclusion spelt out in Rule 57A...... ........The enlarged scope of "in relation to" would, without any doubt, bring the process of water treatment carried out in relation to the manufacture of paper within the requirements of Rule 57A. The use of the inputs in any anterior process and not directly in the manufacturing process of paper had been adequately covered by the Ballarpur judgment. ......Respectfully following the decisions of the Supreme Court and the various High Courts on the issues involved as well as on the question of reference, we dismiss the present Reference Applications. ....In view of our orders on the Reference Applications, the Stay Petitions preferred by the Collector do not merit consideration and are rejected as such.

8. Observations contained in the Collector's Reference Applications stretched beyond reasonable limits meaning of expression 'inputs' are viewed with total disapproval. "Before parting with the case, we have to express our total disapproval of the observations contained in the Reference Applications about stretching the meaning of the expression 'inputs' to limits beyond reason by incomplete examination of statutory provisions and overlooking/misinterpreting the exclusion provisions. .......While it is entirely open to the Collector to point out errors in the order requiring a Reference, to call into question the order with snide references to stretching the meaning to limits beyond reason by incomplete examination etc. is totally unwarranted. While we would certainly welcome applications to have doubtful questions of law referred to the High Courts for obtaining the benefit of their advice, the scope of such a reference in the present case does not exist, for the reasons exhaustively dealt with by us. For that matter, the order also has followed several decisions discussed elaborately. The effect of these have been totally missed by the Collector and an offensive Reference Application has been made, incidentally, stretching the meaning beyond reason, misinterpreting etc. by itself may not give rise to questions of law requiring reference but only if, by such aberrations or otherwise, doubtful or faulty conclusions are drawn."

of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B. Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

Analysis of Rule 57A :

As per rule 57A, a manufacturer of final products can avail the credit of any duty of excise or the additional duty under section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. [Para 20]

Sub-rule (6) of rule 57A commences with a non-obstante clause and it empowers the Central Government to issue notification declaring the inputs on which the duty of excise paid under Section 3A to be deemed to have been paid at such rate or equivalent to such amount as may be specified in the said notification and allow the credit of such duty in respect of the said inputs at such rates or such amount and such conditions as may be specified in the notification. The proviso to the said Rule stipulates that the manufacturer shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that the inputs acquired by him are goods on which the appropriate duty of excise, as indicated in the documents accompanying the goods, has been paid. Thus, what is expected of an assessee is to take reasonable steps that appropriate duty, as indicated in the documents, has been paid. [Para 21]

Provision of Notification No. 58/97 :

Clause (2) of Notification No. 58/97-CE(NT) dated 30.8.1997 spells about the concept of deemed payment of duty on the inputs and further prescribes that it shall be equivalent to the amount calculated at the rate of twelve per cent of the price, as declared by the manufacturer, in the invoice accompanying the said inputs. On a plain reading of clauses (4) and (5), it is clear that there are two mandates to avail the benefit of the said notification -

First part (couched in the affirmative language) : As per the first part it is obligatory on the part of the assessee to produce the invoice declaring that the appropriate duty of excise has been paid on such inputs under the provision of section 3A.

Second part (couched in negative language) : The second command is that the provisions of the said notification shall not apply to inputs where the manufacturer of the said inputs has not declared the invoice price of the said inputs correctly in the documents at the time of their clearance from his factory. [Para 23]

Notification doesn't require assessee to verify actual payment from Department :

In the case at hand, there is no dispute that a declaration was given by the manufacturer of the inputs indicating that the excise duty had been paid on the said inputs under the Act. It is also not in dispute that the said inputs were directly received from the manufacturer but not purchased from the market. There is no cavil over the fact that the manufacturer of the inputs had declared the invoice price of the inputs correctly in the documents. It is perceivable from the factual matrix that the only allegation is that at the time of MODVAT verification it was found that the supplier of the inputs had not discharged full duty liable for the period covered under the invoices. This lapse of the seller is different and not a condition or rather a precondition postulated in the notification. [Para 24]

Rule 57A (6) requires the manufacturer of final products to take reasonable care that the inputs acquired by him are goods on which the appropriate duty of excise as indicated in the documents accompanying the goods, has been paid. The notification has been issued in exercise of the power under the said Rule. The notification clearly states to which of those inputs it shall apply and to which of the inputs it shall not apply and what is the duty of the manufacturer of final inputs. Thus, when there is a prescribed procedure and that has been duly followed by the manufacturer of final products, there is no justifiable reason to hold that the assessee had not taken reasonable care as prescribed in the notification. Due care and caution was taken by the assessee. It is not stated what further care and caution could have been taken. The proviso postulates and requires "reasonable care" and not verification from the department whether the duty stands paid by the manufacturer-seller. When all the conditions precedent have been satisfied, to require the assessee to find out from the departmental authorities about the payment of excise duty on the inputs used in the final product which have been made allowable by the notification would be travelling beyond the notification, and in a way, transgressing the same. This would be practically impossible and would lead to transactions getting delayed. [Para 25]

LDPE/HDPE granules fed into extrusion machines for testing the same do not quality as inputs for manufacture and are, therefore, not eligible for MODVAT credit as per Rule 57-A of the Central Excise Rules. "...having regard to the scope of Rule 57-A, we are unable to agree with the respondents that materials used for testing the fully finished machines would also be materials used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product, namely, the extrusion machine."

Limitation--recovery of wrongly availed Modvat credit under Rule 571 is subject to the provisions of Sec. 11A--demand for the period beyond six months is time barred--extended period inapplicable as non-declaration by the appellants that the inputs had been cleared at 'nil' rate of duty does not amount to suppression.".....the fact of non-declaration by the appellants as to whether they have received the inputs from the manufacturing units after being cleared at Nil rate of duty will not amount to suppression. The Collector (Appeals) has discussed this aspect of alleged suppression in paragraph 5 of the impugned order by holding that since the appellants suppressed the fact that the inputs received by them were actually subject to nil duty the 5 year period prescribed under the proviso to Section 11-A would be applicable. In view of a subsequent finding on merits that the inputs cannot be treated as charged to nit rate of duty, the question of suppression does not arise. On the other aspect viz. whether the provisions of Section 11-A apply to a demand under Rule 571 prior to its amendment we find that this issue has been settled by the Hon'ble Karnataka High Court in the case Tungabhadhra Steel Products v. Superintendent of Central Excise and another.........we hold that the demand under Rule 57-1 can only be raised subject to the time limit prescribed under Section 11-A. Therefore, the demand of Rs. 4,73,782.50 forming part of the subject matter in E/59/89-NRB is barred by limitation."

Demands set aside as goods that are charged to rates of duty as set forth in the First Schedule, but are exempted from payment of duty by way of an exemption Notification under CK Rule 8(1), cannot be construed as goods 'charged to nil rate of duty' [ratio of earlier decision in Arun Auto Spring Mfg. Co. v. CCE 1990 (29) ECR 458 (Cegat WRB)]. "The goods in question were cleared under an exemption notification and, therefore, cannot be treated as non-duty paid. The Tribunal has field in the Arun Auto Spring Mfg. Co.......that the goods cleared after availing of exemption legitimately available to a manufacturer cannot be construed to be non-duty paid and they should be considered as goods having been legally cleared availing of the exemption. Therefore, the Department cannot deny MODVAT credit in terms of Government of India order dated 2.11.1987. The demand in this case is set aside........As a result we set aside the impugned order and allow the appeals with consequential relief if any."

Modvat - Control panels and circuit breakers, procured from others, are component parts of diesel generators. Credit admissible [ratio of Supreme Court decisions in Eastend Paper Industries 1990 (26) ECR 10 (SC) and J.K. Cotton Spg. & Wvg. Mills Co. Ltd.] CE Rule 57A. "The ratio of the Supreme Court decisions would clearly establish the appellants' case for granting of Modvat benefit in respect of the specified duty paid on the inputs, Control Panel and Air Circuit Breaker used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product, diesel generating sets......Not only is the inclusion of the value of the inputs in question in the assessable value of the final product the material factor but the fact that these inputs are actually fitted in the generating sets and perform specific functions therein to make it properly functional will remove any doubt in this regard"

The specific inclusion, for purpose of MODVAT Credit, of inputs manufactured and consumed captively for the production of final product in amending Notification No. 197/86 (which is of a clarificatory nature, and defines the term 'inputs' in respect of Rule 57-A), does not preclude the availment of MODVAT credit on such inputs prior to the issuing of the notification. "......the Explanation to the Rule brought about by the amending Notification dated 14.3.1986 could appropriately be considered in the nature of a clarificatory amendment regarding the scope of the term 'input' used in Rule 57-A. So long as the material is admittedly used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product and declared as such, and duty had been paid on it, about which also there are no two opinions, the fact that such inputs are captively manufactured and consumed would not, in our view, make any difference to the framework of Rule 57-A relating to credit of duty paid on excisable goods used as inputs."

Modvat--Input credit is not allowable to aluminium castings received without payment of duty. "It is observed that the learned Collector (Appeals), while taking note of this has also taken note of the fact that in the same notification issued by the Govt. of India it has also been stated that no such credit shall be allowed if such inputs are clearly recognisable as being non-duty paid or charged to nil rate of duty or wholly exempt from duty. The learned Collector (Appeals) in his order has observed that since the Aluminium castings in respect of which input credit has been claimed were received without payment of duty, in view of the proviso to the Notification in F. No. 822/5/86-TRU dated 7.4.1986 the appellants were not eligible for the benefit of the input credit as claimed..........In the MODVAT Scheme since the benefit of credit is sought to be given for that quantum of duty which has been paid towards the goods or which is otherwise directed to be given in terms of the Rules, it has to be held the term "non-duty paid" refers to the goods where numerically no duty has been paid. As it is under Rule 57C no credit of duty is to be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of excise duty leviable thereon or if chargeable to Nil rate of duty. Thus if the inputs are used for the exempted goods, the inputs are not eligible for the benefit of MODVAT credit and the question of carrying forward the duty paid on the inputs, which resulted in the production of the exempted goods and which in turn are used in the manufacture of specified finished product, cannot arise."

Simultaneous benefit of proforma credit under Rule 56A and MODVAT under Rule 57A, not admissible upto 15.4.1987. ".........on a reading of sub-rule (9) along with its amendment on 15.4.1987 it is clear that there was a total restriction until 15.4.1987 on simultaneous availment of the proforma credit under Rule 56A and MODVAT under Rule 57A. Therefore,........on the above interpretation of the Rule 56A, sub-rules (8) and (9), the order of the lower authorities barring the appellants from enjoying both the facilities simultaneously is valid till 15.4.1987."

2. Notional credit under Notification 175/86-CE of duty paid on intermediate product not available if Classification List for payment of duty on such intermediate products is not filed by the assessee. "....... the assessee has not filed a Classification List for payment of duty on goods used captively. It is, therefore, not open to the assessee to pay duty at a lesser rate on the intermediate product for captive usage, which is exempted in terms of Notification and avail higher notional credit on the same goods in terms of Notification 175/86. This observation of the Deputy Collector (Appeals) is valid and is accepted........"

Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. [Para 9]

Modvat - Caustic soda lye is an in-process material for caustic soda and is therefore eligible for Modvat credit. CE Rule 57A [ratio of Tribunal decision in CCE v. DCW Ltd.--1992(39) ECR 108].The Bench in respect of the same input in question has observed as under:

"...We observe that as to what is intermediate or final product, the Scheme of Modvat has to be read in the context of the manufacturing process of a particular assessee. So long as it can be shown that the inputs have been used for manufacture of any in process materials which are used in the manufacture of final product, the said material manufactured out of the inputs before it is finally used in the manufacture of the declared final product will have to be treated as intermediate product There is nothing on record to show nor is there any plea that caustic soda lye and caustic soda flakes which emerged during the manufacturing process by use of the inputs were not used as in process material for the manufacture of de-dared final product ..."

Following the ratio of the ruling we set aside the impugned order and allow the appeal."

Modvat--Rule 57C vis-a-vis Notfn. 217/86-CE--Modvat scheme is to avoid cascading effect of input taxation. The purpose of Notfn. 217/86-CE is to avert scriptory work and duty payment at every stage from basic materials to manufacture of final products in the same factory or in other units of the same manufacturer. When considering the application of Rule 57C, Notfn. 217/86-CE stands on a different footing as compared to other exemption notifications. No need to refer to the Larger Bench. "Under the Modvat scheme, credit of duty paid on notified inputs is to be given for payment of duty on the notified final products, if such inputs are used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and such inputs are not hit by explanation to Rule 57A. This same concept is clearly discernable in Notfn. 217/86. This Notification is mainly intended to avert payment of duty at each intermediate stage and take credit of such duty at each subsequent stage, starting from the basic materials, turning out components and finally ending with the ultimate final product. Such a vertical integration of production line can be in one and the same factory or spread over two or more factories of the same manufacturer. In such cases Notfn. 217/86 can be availed. They also can take Modvat credit on primary inputs used in the manufacture of secondary inputs (M.V. parts, I.C. engines) so long as the final product namely Motor vehicle pays duty. Hence, we are to agree with the ld. counsel Shri Lodha that Notification 217/86 stands on a different footing, when it comes for consideration for purposes of applying Rule 57C. It is not like any other exemption, where intention is to forego the levy on the products cleared from the factory. .......Hence, the scope of Rule 57C in a situation like the present one, is to be construed in the context of the Modvat scheme and not to destroy that concept. Any interpretation in such a situation has to be to give effect to Notification 217/86 and not to take away the benefit of averting duty payment at each stage in the line of production. Hence, a mechanical application of Rule 57C, is to be avoided, since it destroys the very benefit, which is otherwise available under the scheme right from stage one to the final stage. ........Thus viewed from all angles, we are not persuaded to accept the plea of the ld. JDR to interpret Rule 57C in the manner as pleaded by him. We are also not persuaded to treat the facts as well as the issue in this case as analogous to the case of Kirloskar Oil Engines calling for a reference to the larger Bench."

Modvat credit--availment of Modvat credit cannot be permitted when the inputs have not been specifically mentioned in the declaration filed under Rule 57G [ratio of earlier decision in Paro Food Products v. CCE 1988 (19) ECR 127]. "........in interpreting the scope and ambit of Rule 57G(2) the Tribunal has in a number of decisions taken the view that the manufacturer who fails to file a declaration under Rule 57G specifying the particular input would not be entitled to take credit of duty paid on the inputs received by him under the MODVAT Scheme. .......in view of the decisions quoted above........the appeal is allowed."

Notification No. 175/86--Not obligatory to avail Modvat even if a Declaration under Rule 57G is filed--Payment of duty at concessional rate of 10% or filing of Modvat declaration does not debar subsequent claim for full exemption under para a(ii) of the Notification.

2. Notfn. No. 175/86--It is the option of the appellants either to avail Modvat benefit or not even if Declaration is filed opting for Modvat.

3. Notification No. 175/86--Para 5 does not require a manufacturer to pay concessional rate only after availing Modvat credit.

4. Rule 57B--Para 5 of Notification 175/86--Allegation about deliberate payment of duty at concessional rate for enabling the buyer to avail notional higher credit, remains in the realm of conjecture in the absence of any finding that any buyer actually availed of higher credit as per Rule 57B.

ruling.text:
is to whether the case on hand cannot fall under the rigours of erstwhile Rules 57CC, 57AD and present Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules and whether appellants are obligated to pay the amount equal to 8% of the Central Excise duty supply of Sulphuric Acid and Phosphoric Acid made to the fertilizer units as demanded by the Commissioner of Central Excise, Tirunelveli vide order dated 27.3.2003. 8. They also brought on record the scenario that prevailed prior to the introduction of modvat regime 21/3/86 to 3/9/94 (prior to the introduction of Rule 57C) and scenario after 4.9.96 (after introduction of Rule 57CC) by stating as follows:

1. SCENARIO PRIOR TO INTRODUCTION OF MODVAT CREDIT

The Supreme Court in its landmark judgment in the case of Swadeshi Polytex Limited vs. Collector of Central Excise 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC) was pleased to hold as follows :

This was a decision rendered under the proforma regime (set off duty on inputs) wherein provision similar to Rule 57D which permits retention of modvat credit on inputs even if the same is used in the manufacture of dutiable final products and emergence of by-products, waste or refuse is not to be denied.

Para 20

"It is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible.

It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantum of polyester fibre. Thus the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wontedly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. The Tribunal erred when it held that appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of the duty since ethylene glycol when it reacts with DMT also gives rise to Methanol."

2. SCENARIO UNDER THE MODVAT REGIME BETWEEN 01/03/86 TO 03/09/94

Bearing the spirit of the decision of the Supreme Court in Swadeshi Polytex the lawmakers when they introduced Modvat Scheme, brought into force a specific provision in the form of Rule 57D(1) of the Central Excise Rules which reads as under :

Credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs shall not be denied or varied on the ground that part of the inputs is contained in any waste, refuse or by product arising during the manufacture of the final product, whether or not such waste, refuse or by product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty or is not specified as a final product under Rule 57A.

WHILE INTRODUCING RULE 57D CENTRAL GOVT ALSO BROUGHT INTO FORCE RULE 57C WHICH READS AS UNDER :

Credit to duty not to be allowed if final products are exempt. No credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty.

be cleared on payment of duty under Rule 57 F18 which GTC did not do so

They claimed nil rate of duty benefit under 2401.10

Under such circumstances, the department did not deny the input credit on cut tobacco but demanded duty of an amount of 8% on dust and winnowings, since no duty was paid as waste and scrap under Rule 57 F18.

In short, the facts of the case are totally different and therefore cannot be relied upon. Dujodwala Resins Terpenes Ltd. vs. Collector of Central Excise, Chandigarh - 1996 (14) RLT 650 (CEGAT-NB)=1997 (93) ELT 451 (Tribunal)

Kirloskar Oil Engines Ltd. vs. Collector of Central Excise, Pune - 1994 (4) RLT 296 (CEGAT-WRB)=1994 (73) ELT 835 (Tribunal)

Orissa Extrusions vs. Collector of Central Excise, Bhubaneswar - 2000 (115) ELT 30 (SC).

14. They further submitted that all these decisions have been rendered only under Rule 57C and not under Rule 57CC and they have no application. The decision of the Supreme Court in Orissa Extrusions was one considering the applicability of Rule 57C vis a vis Notification No. 180/88 and therefore they have no relevance to the facts of the case. As regards the other two tribunal rulings, these are again decisions under Rule 57C and not Rule 57CC and further more, these decisions are no longer good law in the light of two Larger Bench decisions in the case of CCE vs. Ashok Iron and Steel Fabricators 2002 (48) RLT 789 (CEGAT-LB)=RLT (L.B.-CEGAT)-2202=2002 (140) ELT 277 and Raghuvar India Ltd. vs. Commissioner 2002 (48) RLT 792 (CEGAT-L.B.)=RLT (L.B.-CEGAT)-2205=2002 (140) ELT 280.

15. It is the plea of the appellants that copper concentrate is employed only in the smelter which gives rise to copper anodes and emissions of sulphur-dioxide in gaseous form. No other inputs are added at this stage. When this emissions of sulphur dioxide is processed into sulphuric acid and phosphoric acid, there is an addition of various inputs such as caustic soda, Ferric sulphate, ferric Chloride, Indion, Magnafloc, etc. The Commissioner of Central Excise, Tirunelveli in para 13 had observed that appellants have availed Modvat credit on some of these inputs also which the appellants deny. It is their case that appellants have not taken any credit at any point of time on any of these inputs. To this effect, a certificate dated 19.9.2003 issued by the Superintendent of Central Excise, SIPCOT Range was produced which confirmed that for the period September 2000 to July 2002 appellants have not taken any input credit on any of the inputs such as water treatment chemicals, magnafloc, .ferric chloride, ferric sulphate, caustic soda flakes, deformer, sodium silicate, hydrogen hydrade, active silica, spak and maxtreat. The certificate confirms having verified the same with RG23A Part Ii register. No credit has been availed on any of these inputs except maxtreat but this input has been used only in the smelter and not in the sulphuric acid/phosphoric acid plants. In other words, certificate confirms that no credit has been taken on any of the inputs employed in the sulphuric acid/phosphoric acid plants. Finally, appellants made submissions as to how the Commissioner's findings are factually incorrect and legally not sustainable.

.e.f. 1.3.92 notwithstanding the clearance of the final product without payment of duty to a unit in a FTZ or 100% EOU, the modvat credit on the inputs would be admissible. The reference has been made to the Larger Bench to determine the question whether the aforesaid amendment dt. 1.3.92 of Rule 57C was clarificatory in nature and whether it would have retrospective effect in the absence of any specific provision. 3. Shri Prakash Shah, Ld. Advocate appearing for the appellants M/s. Larsen & Toubro contended that notwithstanding the provisions of Rule 57C, the clearances by the manufacturers of excisable goods to the units in FTZ and 100% EOU without payment of duty were always treated to be on different footings and credit had not been denied on the inputs. He placed reliance on the decision of CEGAT, West Regional Bench in the case of Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE Bombay 1995 (78) ELT 595 (T). In this decision the Bench relied on the judgment of Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corporation 1981 (8) ELT 642 (Del.) and the Board's clarification issued on the scope of proviso (i) to sub-rule (2) of Rule 56A (analogous to the provisions of Rule 57C) in which it is advised that the said proviso to Rule 56A (2) would not stand attracted, where the final products were exported under bond, since such removals could neither be construed to be exempted nor be regarded as goods charged to nil rate of duty. The same view is earlier endorsed by the East Regional Bench of CEGAT in Orissa Synthetics Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bhubaneswar 1994 (69) ELT 585 (T). In the Reliance Industry's case the Bench held the view that the removal of goods to FTZ & 100% EOU are governed by exemption notification either under Rule 8 or Section 5A. Third proviso to Rule 57F (3) allowing credit in respect of such removals to FTZ & 100% EOU was introduced w.e.f. 1.3.92 simultaneously with the amendment of Rule 57C removing the bar on allowing credit to such removals. Since these are exempted goods, a specific mention in both the rules was necessary to give effect to the govt, 's intention. But in this case, all clearances for export under bond are covered by the first proviso to Rule 57F (3). If the Govt's intention is not to allow credit in respect of removals under bond for export in terms of Rule 191B or 191BB, a specific exclusion in the said proviso is called for. In the absence of such a specific exclusion, the first proviso itself takes care of all such removals of final products under bond for export. Since credit earned by inputs used in such export product is permitted to be utilised for similar goods cleared for home consumption, sub rule (5) of Rule 57F would not be attracted.

4. The Ld. Advocate of the appellants further contends that though the goods supplied to the units in FTZ or to 100% EOU are exempt from payment of duty (in this case exemption Notification is No. 272/79 dt. 18.10.79 issued under Rule 8 (1) for the goods supplied to the units in Kandla FTZ) this is not an exemption like that in other notifications. It is the contention of Ld. Advocate that in this case the duty liability gets shifted to the unit in FTZ/100% EOU to whom the duty free goods are supplied and in case the conditions of the notification are not complied with, the duty is liable to be recovered from the receiving unit. "9. MODVAT is basically a duty-collecting procedure, which aims at allowing relief to a manufacturer on the duty element borne by him in respect of the inputs used by him. It was introduced w.e.f. 1-3-1986. The said Scheme was regulated under Rules 57-A to 57-J of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. Rule 57-A entitled a manufacturer to take instant credit of the Central excise duty paid on the inputs used by him in the manufacture of the finished product, provided that the input and the finished product were excisable commodities and fell under any of the specified chapters in the Tariff Schedule. Under Rule 57-G, every manufacturer was required to file a declaration before the jurisdictional Assistant Collector, declaring his intention to take MODVAT credit after paying duty on the inputs. The object behind Rule 57-A read with Rule 57-G and Rule 57-I was utilisation of credit allowed towards payment of duty on any of the final products in relation to manufacture of which such inputs were intended to be used in accordance with the declaration under Rule 57-G. 10. The object of the MODVAT Scheme was to reduce cost of final product by taking credit for the duty paid on the inputs."

13. The Supreme Court has held that the Modvat scheme is a duty-collecting procedure, which aims at allowing relief to a manufacturer on the duty element borne by him in respect of the inputs used by him. The said Scheme entitles a manufacturer to take instant credit of the Central excise duty paid on the inputs used by him in the manufacture of the finished product, provided that the input and the finished product were excisable commodities and fell under any of the specified chapters in the Tariff Schedule. The object of the MODVAT Scheme is to reduce the cost of the final product by taking credit for the duty paid on the inputs.

However, we see no merit in the submission. Clause (d) to the explanation to Rule 57A clearly refers to "inputs used for generation of electricity". Thus the reference is not confined to inputs used as fuel for generation of electricity. Therefore, while a non-fuel input would not be covered by clause (c) to Explanation to Rule 57A, the input used for generation of electricity would be covered by clause (d) introduced on 16.3.95. This according to us is the scope of the first leg of explanation clause (d); the second leg of explanation to clause (d) refers to electricity used in the factory for manufacture of final product or for any other purpose. After 16.3.95, as long as electricity is used within the factory of production, it does not matter whether it was used for purpose of manufacture of final product or for some other purpose. But prior to 16.3.95, for an input used for generation of electricity to qualify for credit under Rule 57A, it should be shown that the electricity so generated has in turn been used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product, and if the electricity generated by use of fuel has not been used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product, it will not be eligible for credit. Therefore, that it is not correct to contend that prior to 16.3.95 inputs used as fuel for generation of electricity are not covered as inputs under Rule 57A. Para 67(3) of the Explanatory Notes to the Finance bill 1995-96 states that the Notification 11/95 seeks to amend the Central Excise Rules so as to inter alia expand the scope of inputs under the Modvat Scheme. Therefore, no inference can be drawn from the Budget Explanatory Notes that the fuel used for generation of electricity was not an input prior to 16.3.95.

3. In terms of proviso to Notification 5/94, credit of specified duty in respect of any inputs produced or manufactured; (a).............(b) by 100% Export Oriented Undertaking or........and used in the manufacture of final products in any place in India shall be restricted to the extent of duty which is equal to the additional duty leviable on like goods under Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.......paid on such inputs. This view is supported by the recent decision of the Apex Court in the case of Collector of Customs Vs. Presto Industries reported in 2001 (43) RLT 1 (SC)=2001 (128) ELT 321 wherein the Supreme Court has held that the additional duty is in addition to customs duty leviable under the Customs Act, and not a countervailing duty and since the additional duties of customs were not paid on waste and scrap of imported cellulose acetate sheets under Section 3 (I) of the Customs Tariff Act 1975, benefit of exemption underNotificationl6/83-CE dated 11.2.83 is not available since the condition of the Notification has not been fulfilled.

4. Following the ratio of the Supreme Court judgment cited supra, we uphold the impugned order and reject the appeal.

(a)

Final product should be specified in a notification issued under rule 57A.

(b)

Inputs should also be specified in that notification.

(c)

Duty of which credit is allowed should also be specified in that notification.

(d)

'Input' should be used in or in relation to manufacture of the final product.

(e)

The 'final product' should be dutiable.

If any of the aforesaid ingredients is missing in any particular case, modvat credit scheme is not applicable. 4.4 Rule 57C makes it further clear that "no credit of specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product (.......) shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty." It may be stated that the rule does not make a distinction whether exemption from duty or chargeability to nil rate of duty of the final product occurs at what stage - whether at the time of receipt of inputs or subsequently. Disallowance of credit, on the inputs becomes automatic, the moment final product is so exempt or chargeable to nil rate. If any credit already taken contrary to such statutory embargo shall stand disallowed and if such a credit has already been utilised, it will be liable to be recovered under Rule 57I, subject of course to limitation of time spelt out therein. It follows from the premise that utilisation can be made only of a valid credit and not of credit wrongly allowed.

4.5 Rule 57F is an important rule in the modvat scheme. It is to be noted that Rule 57F (1) has not been noticed either in Premier Tyres or East India (supra), which is my opinion is very important because it speaks of the manner of utilisation of the input. Clause (i) of Rule 57F stipulates that the 'input' of which credit has been allowed under rule 57A be used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products for which such inputs have been brought into the factory. Rule 57A, as already observed, envisages a 'dutiable' excisable product and not one which is exempt or chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the present case, 'inputs' cannot at all be said to have been used in the dutiable final product, because 'dutiability' is determined at the time of removal of goods. Operation of modvat scheme comes to a halt the moment final product becomes exempted. Credit was allowed at the initial stage under rule 57A subject to the provisions of other rules. It follows, therefore, that if provisions of any of the rules are not followed in respect of any input, credit ab-initio allowed will become void and therefore would be recoverable subject to period of limitation if any.

4.6 Rule 57F (3) (i) read with rule 57G also points to the aforesaid.

4.7 It is true that there is no strict correlationship between final product and the input contained therein, so far as utilisation of credit is concerned, but, as discussed above, it is an essential ingredient of the 'modvat scheme' that 'input' must be used in the dutiable final product. If any 'input' has not been so used, credit initially allowed would be wrong and subject to recovery.

4.8 In view of the foregoing discussion, I reject the appeal.
