1998 taxmann.com 1393 (CEGAT- NEW DELHI)[28-11-1997] Reliance Industries Ltd. vs. Collector of Central Excise, Bombay

Modvat - Control panels and circuit breakers, procured from others, are component parts of diesel generators. Credit admissible [ratio of Supreme Court decisions in Eastend Paper Industries 1990 (26) ECR 10 (SC) and J.K. Cotton Spg. & Wvg. Mills Co. Ltd.] CE Rule 57A. "The ratio of the Supreme Court decisions would clearly establish the appellants' case for granting of Modvat benefit in respect of the specified duty paid on the inputs, Control Panel and Air Circuit Breaker used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product, diesel generating sets......Not only is the inclusion of the value of the inputs in question in the assessable value of the final product the material factor but the fact that these inputs are actually fitted in the generating sets and perform specific functions therein to make it properly functional will remove any doubt in this regard"

The specific inclusion, for purpose of MODVAT Credit, of inputs manufactured and consumed captively for the production of final product in amending Notification No. 197/86 (which is of a clarificatory nature, and defines the term 'inputs' in respect of Rule 57-A), does not preclude the availment of MODVAT credit on such inputs prior to the issuing of the notification. "......the Explanation to the Rule brought about by the amending Notification dated 14.3.1986 could appropriately be considered in the nature of a clarificatory amendment regarding the scope of the term 'input' used in Rule 57-A. So long as the material is admittedly used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product and declared as such, and duty had been paid on it, about which also there are no two opinions, the fact that such inputs are captively manufactured and consumed would not, in our view, make any difference to the framework of Rule 57-A relating to credit of duty paid on excisable goods used as inputs."

Modvat--Input credit is not allowable to aluminium castings received without payment of duty. "It is observed that the learned Collector (Appeals), while taking note of this has also taken note of the fact that in the same notification issued by the Govt. of India it has also been stated that no such credit shall be allowed if such inputs are clearly recognisable as being non-duty paid or charged to nil rate of duty or wholly exempt from duty. The learned Collector (Appeals) in his order has observed that since the Aluminium castings in respect of which input credit has been claimed were received without payment of duty, in view of the proviso to the Notification in F. No. 822/5/86-TRU dated 7.4.1986 the appellants were not eligible for the benefit of the input credit as claimed..........In the MODVAT Scheme since the benefit of credit is sought to be given for that quantum of duty which has been paid towards the goods or which is otherwise directed to be given in terms of the Rules, it has to be held the term "non-duty paid" refers to the goods where numerically no duty has been paid. As it is under Rule 57C no credit of duty is to be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of excise duty leviable thereon or if chargeable to Nil rate of duty. Thus if the inputs are used for the exempted goods, the inputs are not eligible for the benefit of MODVAT credit and the question of carrying forward the duty paid on the inputs, which resulted in the production of the exempted goods and which in turn are used in the manufacture of specified finished product, cannot arise."

The respondent are manufacturers of electrical stampings and laminations out of hot-rolled and cold-rolled electrical steel and silicon steel sheets etc. and availed deemed Modvat credit in respect of the inputs as specified under Rule 57A, which were purchased from market and were not covered by any duty paying documents. The G.O.I. modified its earlier instructions and respondent's inputs became illegible with effect from 2.11.1987 for deemed Modvat credit without production of duty paying documents.

Simultaneous benefit of proforma credit under Rule 56A and MODVAT under Rule 57A, not admissible upto 15.4.1987. ".........on a reading of sub-rule (9) along with its amendment on 15.4.1987 it is clear that there was a total restriction until 15.4.1987 on simultaneous availment of the proforma credit under Rule 56A and MODVAT under Rule 57A. Therefore,........on the above interpretation of the Rule 56A, sub-rules (8) and (9), the order of the lower authorities barring the appellants from enjoying both the facilities simultaneously is valid till 15.4.1987."

2. Notional credit under Notification 175/86-CE of duty paid on intermediate product not available if Classification List for payment of duty on such intermediate products is not filed by the assessee. "....... the assessee has not filed a Classification List for payment of duty on goods used captively. It is, therefore, not open to the assessee to pay duty at a lesser rate on the intermediate product for captive usage, which is exempted in terms of Notification and avail higher notional credit on the same goods in terms of Notification 175/86. This observation of the Deputy Collector (Appeals) is valid and is accepted........"

Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. [Para 9]

Iron & Steel products are manufactured by the appellants. Modvat--Rule 57C vis-a-vis Notfn. 217/86-CE--Modvat scheme is to avoid cascading effect of input taxation. The purpose of Notfn. 217/86-CE is to avert scriptory work and duty payment at every stage from basic materials to manufacture of final products in the same factory or in other units of the same manufacturer. When considering the application of Rule 57C, Notfn. 217/86-CE stands on a different footing as compared to other exemption notifications. No need to refer to the Larger Bench. "Under the Modvat scheme, credit of duty paid on notified inputs is to be given for payment of duty on the notified final products, if such inputs are used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and such inputs are not hit by explanation to Rule 57A. This same concept is clearly discernable in Notfn. 217/86. This Notification is mainly intended to avert payment of duty at each intermediate stage and take credit of such duty at each subsequent stage, starting from the basic materials, turning out components and finally ending with the ultimate final product. Such a vertical integration of production line can be in one and the same factory or spread over two or more factories of the same manufacturer. In such cases Notfn. 217/86 can be availed. They also can take Modvat credit on primary inputs used in the manufacture of secondary inputs (M.V. parts, I.C. engines) so long as the final product namely Motor vehicle pays duty. Hence, we are to agree with the ld. counsel Shri Lodha that Notification 217/86 stands on a different footing, when it comes for consideration for purposes of applying Rule 57C. It is not like any other exemption, where intention is to forego the levy on the products cleared from the factory. .......Hence, the scope of Rule 57C in a situation like the present one, is to be construed in the context of the Modvat scheme and not to destroy that concept. Any interpretation in such a situation has to be to give effect to Notification 217/86 and not to take away the benefit of averting duty payment at each stage in the line of production. Hence, a mechanical application of Rule 57C, is to be avoided, since it destroys the very benefit, which is otherwise available under the scheme right from stage one to the final stage. ........Thus viewed from all angles, we are not persuaded to accept the plea of the ld. JDR to interpret Rule 57C in the manner as pleaded by him. We are also not persuaded to treat the facts as well as the issue in this case as analogous to the case of Kirloskar Oil Engines calling for a reference to the larger Bench."

[Para 8] In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

1.The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on mobile phone services in respect of the phones used by its own employees and officers. The department sought to deny the benefit on the ground that the phones were not installed in the factory premises and, therefore, could not be treated as input service in terms of the Board’s Circular No. 59/8/2003 dated 20-6-2003. 2.The assessee was exporting some portion of its goods and was availing services of Cargo Handling Agency (CHA). Its claim of Cenvat credit of service tax paid for use of such services was rejected by the department on the ground that services of CHA were engaged in relation to the activity after removal from the factory and in the port area. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that the definition of ‘input service’ under rule 2(1) is extended one and it includes activities relating to business; that the service of CHA availed by them should be treated as relating to their business activity and, therefore, credit should be extended.

3.The assessee had got certain circles/gardens prepared and put-up signboards for advertising its products. For this purpose, it had availed the services of construction service providers. The assessee claimed construction service as input service and sought credit of service tax paid on such services. The department denied the assessee’s claim on the ground that availing of construction services for the aforesaid purpose could not be treated as part of activity relating to advertising services.

The Tribunal held :

1.In view of decision of the Tribunal in the case of Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 6 STT 328 (Mum. - CESTAT), the assessee was eligible to input credit on mobile services.

2.The CHA services availed in respect of export did not have any nexus with the manufacture and clearance of the product from the factory. The business activities, which were sought to be included in the extended definition, could not include the services rendered in the port area. Therefore, the appeal on this aspect was to be rejected.

3.Setting up of circles/gardens away from the factory for the purpose of putting signboards cannot be considered as relating to activity in relation to advertisement. This can lead to a situation where any massive building built away from the factory premises where signboards were also put up can be treated in relation to advertisement of the product. While putting up a signboard is definitely a part of advertisement services, the same cannot be, unrealistically, extended to various activities like setting up circles/gardens with the help of construction service providers. Thus, the Tribunal rejected the assessee’s appeal.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57AA of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Inputs - Whether CENVAT scheme brought in year 2000 is only a substitute of earlier Modvat scheme - Held, yes - Supreme Court in Jaypee Rewa Cement v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. 2004 (171) ELT 289(SC) taking a contrary view, is not good law - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant was owner of a limestone mine which was situated at some distance from factory premises. Explosives and other inputs were used in quarrying limestone in the mine. Limestone was, in turn, used for manufacture of cement and clinkers in the factory. The revenue denied the CENVAT Credit availed by the appellant on explosives, etc.

The Supreme Court in a similar case of Jaypee Rewa Cement v. CCE 2001 (133) ELT 3 held that MODVAT credit would be allowable on the use of explosives in the manufacture of cement irrespective of the fact that explosives were directly used in mines and never entered the factory manufacturing cement. However, in the case of CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. 2004 (171) ELT 289 (SC), it was observed that schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT are different and, therefore, the decision of Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra) would have no application to the CENVAT Rules and credit would be allowable only on the inputs which are received in factory of manufacture of final product.

In the instant reference, the broader question arose for consideration as to whether there was a difference in substance between the MODVAT and the CENVAT schemes.

HELD: It is to be observed that rule 57B commences with a non obstante clause. It allows credit to be taken by a manufacturer of inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not. In the main body of sub-rule (1) there is no qualification as to where the inputs must be used. Qualifications have been introduced to the extent stated in clauses (i) to (vi), read with the Explanation. Clause (i) provides for inputs which are manufactured and used within the factory of production. Paints, fuel, packing materials and accessories are also treated as inputs without any requirement for user within the factory. Clause (iv) provides for credit on inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used for manufacture of the final products or for any other purposes ‘within the factory of production’. As far as the Explanation is concerned, the inputs are restricted to inputs notified under rule 57A.

There is no dispute that both explosives and limestone are notified under section 57A for manufacture of the final product viz., cement. [Para 4]

Under rule 57F, credit on inputs sent by a manufacturer from the factory to a job worker for test, repair, etc., but ultimately utilized in the final product is allowable. [Para 5]

Rule 57J allows credit on inputs used in manufacture of intermediate products described in column 3 of the Table provided the intermediate products are received by the manufacturer for use in or in relation to the manufacture of final products described in the corresponding Entry in column 4 of the Table. Explosives, limestone and cement are admittedly covered by column 1, 2 and 3 respectively of the Table. [Para 6]

In the case of Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra), the Supreme Court concluded that rule 57A(1) did not in any way specify that the inputs have to be utilized within the factory premises. It was further held that a reading of rule 57J and relevant notification can leave no manner of doubt that even in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of intermediate product which product is then used for the manufacture of a final product, the manufacturer would be allowed credit on the duty paid in respect of the input. On the explosives, duty had been paid and the appellants would be entitled to claim credit because the explosives were used for the manufacture of the intermediate product, namely, limestone which, in turn, was used for the manufacture of cement. The appeal of the manufacturer was, accordingly, allowed and it was held that the MODVAT credit was allowable on the use of the explosives in the manufacture of cement irrespective of the fact that the explosives were used directly in the mines and never entered the factory of the manufacturer of cement. HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Modvat - Co-relation of input to final product not necessary so long as utilisation is proved. CE Rule 57A allows credit; CE Rule 57F allows utilisation. The two cover separate stages. Reversal of credit not justified

FACT: The respondents are manufacturers of tyres. After filing a declaration under Rule 57G, they took Modvat credit for inputs specified in Rule 57A. Part of the finished goods were cleared free of duty under a notification. The issue for consideration is whether credit on the inputs going into that portion of the finished product, which is cleared free of duty under exemption notification has to be reversed.

HELD: No one-to-one co-relation has been prescribed between the inputs and finished product for the purpose of utilisation of Modvat credit All that is required is that credit should be utilized for discharging the duty liability on finished product. "It has to be observed that no one-to-one correlation has been prescribed between the inputs and the finished product for the purpose of utilisation of the MODVAT credit and all that is required is that the credit should be utilised for discharging the duty liability on the finished product which has been declared under Rule 57G(1) in respect of the inputs for which the MODVAT credit was taken."

2. The event of taking credit is provided for under Rule 57A and event of utilization of credit is provided for separately under Rule 57F. Each event has to be dealt with separately. "The Rules as are worded clearly provide for the utilisation of the credit taken in respect of the inputs for payment of duty towards the final product irrespective of when the final product is cleared and whether a particular batch of inputs have gone into that particular batch of the final product. In the Rules, it is seen, so far as an event of taking credit is concerned that is provided for separately under Rule 57A and the event of utilisation of the credit has been provided for separately under Rule 57F and if the credit has been wrongly taken, the same can be reversed or recovered within a period of six months or 5 years as provided for under Rule 57I. The same would apply in case the said credit has been wrongly utilised. But each event will have to be dealt with separately."

3. Respondents cannot be called upon to pay back the credit utilised as pleaded by the revenue. "...............there is no dispute in regard to the taking of the credit and since we have held that the credit has been correctly utilised, the respondents cannot be called upon to pay back the credit utilised as pleaded by the Revenue."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - OE goods cleared without duty under Chapter X procedure--Whether Modvat admissible--Referred to Larger Bench in view of conflicting decisions

HELD: Though one to one co-relation of inputs with final product is not prescribed, there appears to be a tacit requirement of reading Rule 57C into the provisions of Rule 57F(3)(i). However in view of the fact that decisions of two Benches run somewhat contrary to each other, the issue "whether credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of declared final product part of which is cleared without payment of duty could be disallowed" should be placed before a Larger Bench for decision. "Though one to one co-relation is not prescribed under Rule 57F(3)(i), there appears to be a tacit requirement of reading Rule 57C into the provisions of Rule 57F(3)(i). This is the view taken by the East Regional Bench, which we also share to a certain extent. .......Since the issues involves consideration of these points of law and the decisions for two Benches run somewhat contrary to each other, we consider it fit for placing before the larger Bench, for deciding on the following questions.

"Whether, in the context of the provisions of Rule 57C vis-a-vis Rule 57F(3)(i) of the Central Excise Rules, Modvat credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of declared final products, part of which are cleared free of the whole of duty of excise leviable thereon, in terms of an exemption Notification, could be disallowed by way of reversal of credit of duty on such inputs, which have been used in the manufacture of final products cleared free of duty"?"

HEADNOTE: Section Rule 57A and Section Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Graphite rods used for making moulds for manufacturing diamond drilling bits not eligible as moulds are appliances - Limitation-Modvat--SC notice for wrongful availment of Modvat, not hit by time bar

FACT: The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits. For this purpose they bring graphite rods from outside on payment of duty and convert them into graphite moulds of different sizes and shapes which are used in the process of sintering in the furnace at high temperature for manufacture of diamond drilling bits. They availed of Modvat credit on graphite rods. The Asstt. Collector held that they were not entitled to Modvat credit on graphite rods as these are used in the manufacture of graphite moulds which, in turn, are used as "appliances", and not in relation to manufacture of diamond drilling bits. The appellants also pleaded that the show cause notice was hit by limitation under section 11A, CESA. On appeal, the Collector (Appeals) upheld the order of the Asstt. Collector. Hence this appeal.

HELD: Modvat--Inputs used "in relation to manufacture"--Graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used in relation to the manufacture of diamond drilling bits and not directly in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits, as these are not used as raw material or component parts of the finished goods, but the process in which they are used is so integrally connected with the ultimate production of goods that but for it the manufacture or processing of goods would be impossible or commercially inexpedient. "The Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that manufacture involves series of processes. Process in manufacture or in relation to manufacture implies not only the production but the various stages through which the raw material is subjected to change by different operations. It is the cumulative effect of the various processes to which the raw material is subjected to, manufactured product emerges. Therefore, each step towards such production would be a process in relation to the manufacture. Where any particular process is so integrally connected with the ultimate production of goods that but for that process manufacture or processing of goods would be impossible or commercially inexpedient that process is one in relation to the manufacture.......In the case before us graphite rods converted into graphite-moulds are used not as raw material or component part of the finished product--diamond drilling bits. We have, however, taken a view that they are used in relation to the manufacture of the diamond drilling bits."

2. Modvat--Appliances excluded from applicability of Rule 57A CE Rules--Graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used as "appliances", as these moulds are applied in one heat/sintering process in the furnace to bind particles of powdered metals to form the bits. Hence, graphite rods are excluded from the applicability of Rule 57A and are not eligible for Modvat credit. "The appellants themselves have called the material used in the furnace as graphite-mould. These moulds are used for one heat/sintering process. These moulds as such are not used in the manufacture of diamond drilling bits, for the purposes of Rule 57D of the Rules. These graphite moulds processed from graphite rods are applied in the furnace to bind particles of the powdered metals to form the bits. In this process referred to by the party as sintering process, the graphite rods converted into graphite moulds are used as an 'appliance'. As appliances used for producing or processing of any goods or for bringing about any change in any substance in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products, are excluded from the applicability of Rule 57A, the graphite rods used in relation to the manufacture of diamond drilling bits are not the inputs for the purposes of that Rule........Accordingly, we hold that the credit of the duty of excise paid on graphite-rods is not allowed for utilisation towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the diamond "drilling bits."

3. Limitation--The show cause notice is not time barred as the limitation laid down under section 11A CESA is not applicable to cases of wrongful availment of Modvat credit under Rule 57I. Section 11A occupies the general field while Rule 57I deals with specific field of wrongful availment of Modvat credit [ratio of Gujarat High Court judgment in Torrent Laboratories Ltd. v. UOI, 1991(32) ECR 381 (Gujarat)]. "In the case - Torrent Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India.......the Hon'ble Gujarat High Court..........did not accept the contention that the provisions of Section 11A of the Act as regards the period of limitation should be read into Rule 57I.......

Question raised is of academic nature and one of fact, needing no reference to High Court "This again is an academic question having no practical application in the present case. ............When these articles are referred to as machines or part of machines in the Tariff itself, their Tariff classification outside Section XVI is no impediment to their identity as such machines, appliances or parts of machines. Such is not the case with felts and wire netting. They are neither machines nor parts thereof and they are also not known as such machines/parts. The question posed is one of fact which does not require to be referred to the High Court."

7. Tribunal's order holding felt and wire-netting for paper making machinery, and chemicals used for water treatment, as eligible for modvat benefit was based on several factors and ratio of several judgment of Supreme Court and High Courts. Criteria laid down by Supreme Court in Ballarpur judgment are satisfied, and there is no justification for making reference to the High Court Reference application and stay applications are dismissed/rejected. "The order granting modvat benefit is based on several factors following the ratio of several decisions discussed therein. As far as felt and wire netting are concerned, it has been held that these are neither the excluded items in the Explanation under Rule 57A nor parts of such items. Not being machines, machinery etc. which are the excluded items, they qualify for modvat benefit. .............We have now considered the contentions raised by the Collector citing the Ballarpur judgment of the Supreme Court wherein the criterion of utilisation in the manufacturing process as distinct from the manufacturing apparatus had been laid down. We have found that this criterion is satisfied by the inputs in question which are not used as manufacturing apparatus. We have held them to be outside the zone of exclusion spelt out in Rule 57A...... ........The enlarged scope of "in relation to" would, without any doubt, bring the process of water treatment carried out in relation to the manufacture of paper within the requirements of Rule 57A. The use of the inputs in any anterior process and not directly in the manufacturing process of paper had been adequately covered by the Ballarpur judgment. ......Respectfully following the decisions of the Supreme Court and the various High Courts on the issues involved as well as on the question of reference, we dismiss the present Reference Applications. ....In view of our orders on the Reference Applications, the Stay Petitions preferred by the Collector do not merit consideration and are rejected as such.

8. Observations contained in the Collector's Reference Applications stretched beyond reasonable limits meaning of expression 'inputs' are viewed with total disapproval. "Before parting with the case, we have to express our total disapproval of the observations contained in the Reference Applications about stretching the meaning of the expression 'inputs' to limits beyond reason by incomplete examination of statutory provisions and overlooking/misinterpreting the exclusion provisions. .......While it is entirely open to the Collector to point out errors in the order requiring a Reference, to call into question the order with snide references to stretching the meaning to limits beyond reason by incomplete examination etc. is totally unwarranted. While we would certainly welcome applications to have doubtful questions of law referred to the High Courts for obtaining the benefit of their advice, the scope of such a reference in the present case does not exist, for the reasons exhaustively dealt with by us. For that matter, the order also has followed several decisions discussed elaborately. The effect of these have been totally missed by the Collector and an offensive Reference Application has been made, incidentally, stretching the meaning beyond reason, misinterpreting etc. by itself may not give rise to questions of law requiring reference but only if, by such aberrations or otherwise, doubtful or faulty conclusions are drawn."

FACT: The applicants utilised Modvat credit under Rule 57A CE Rules on kraft paper used for packing the final product Linoleums. The Department held that under Notification No. 177/86-CE dt. 1.3.1986 credit in respect of paper used "in the manufacture of final product" was to be restricted to Rs. 800/- per tonne. The applicants' case is that they used the kraft paper "in relation to the manufacture of the final product", as "packing material" is recognised as an input under Explanation to Rule 57A. The Tribunal upheld the Department's view but found the Notice time-barred. In this Reference Application, the main question raised by applicants for reference is whether the expression "in relation to the manufacture" used in Rule 57A is synonymous to the expression "in the manufacture" used in the abovesaid notification. By the Cross Objection, the Department wants reference of the question whether the time limit prescribed in amended Rule 57-I is applicable in respect of an offence committed earlier to the amendment.

HELD: Reference--Question of law--The question whether the expression "in or in relation to the manufacture of final products" used in Rule 57A, and the expression "in the manufacture of final products" used in Notification No. 177/86-CE are synonymous does not arise from the Tribunal's order which examined the statutory definition of "manufacture" and concluded that kraft paper has been used in this case "in the manufacture" of the final product, as wrapping paper. (Ratio of Supreme Court's judgment in CCE v. East End Paper Industries Ltd. and in J.K. Cotton Spg. Wvg. Mills Co. Ltd. v. S.T.O.). "In view of the categoric finding in the order in question that Kraft Paper has been used in the manufacture of final product, linoleum, rejecting the contention to the contrary that it is not so used but only in relation to the manufacture of such final product, the questions of law suggested for reference lose their significance. Thus, for example, Question A in the application is as to whether the two expressions "goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products" appearing in Rule 57A and the expression "goods used in the manufacture of final products" appearing in the 3rd proviso to Notification 177/86 dated 1.3.1986 are synonymous is an academic question with the answer self-evident. It does not arise from the Tribunal's order which also did not proceed on the basis that the two expressions were synonymous. The order also did not seek to apply the restriction in the quantum of modvat benefit applicable under the Notification in question to inputs used only in relation to the manufacture by equating both the expressions. It was, on the contrary, held on the strength of the statutory definition of the expression "manufacture" that the use was only in the manufacture and their contention was rejected on this score only".

The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

In this background, on 1-11-1997, a show cause notice was issued to the Appellant/Assessee raising a demand in the sum for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 2-5-1997, along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent to be calculated on the said amount for the period commencing from 12-8-1997 and ending on the date of payment. Furthermore, via the very SCN, a proposal was also made for imposing penalty.

In the reply, the assessee took stand that, for the period falling between 3-5-1997 and 19-6-1997, it had already 'expunged' MODVAT credit, in consonance with Notification No. 14/97 CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. In so far as the demand for interest was concerned, it was stated that it was premature, as under section 87(2)(c) of the Finance Act, interest would be payable, only, if, the amount demanded was not paid within ninety (90) days of the enactment of the Bill.

The stand, which, the Appellant /Assessee appeared to have taken with respect to penalty was that the alleged infraction was not an offence prior to the enactment of the Finance Act.

The Adjudicating authority sustained the demand in sum, equivalent to the excess credit availed of by the Appellant/Assessee for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 to 3-5-1997. Furthermore, the Appellant/Assessee was directed to pay interest at the rate of 18 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals), allowed the appeal of the Appellant/Assessee, albeit, partially. While the Commissioner (Appeals), confirmed the demand of duty for the period 23-7-1996 to 28-2-1997, along with interest, he set aside the demand of duty for the period spanning between 1-3-1997 and 3-5-1997.

3.2-4 Reversal of Cenvat credit in respect of obsolete capital goods written off without use

As per rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules (inserted w.e.f. 11-5-2007), if (i) inputs or (ii) capital goods before being put to use, are written of fully or provision is made in books of account to write off fully, the manufacturer is required to pay an 'amount' equal to Cenvat credit taken in respect of such inputs or capital goods. If these are subsequently used in manufacture of final products, manufacturer can take Cenvat credit of amount which was paid earlier.

The provision does not apply if capital goods were used even for a short time.

Recovery if the 'amount' not paid - If the 'amount' payable under rule 3(5), 3(5A) or 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not paid, the same can be recovered in the manner provided in rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, as if it is recovery of Cenvat credit wrongly taken - Explanation to rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2013.

3.2-5 Capital goods manufactured within the factory

As per Rule 2(k) of Cenvat Credit Rules (as effective from 1-4-2011), "input" means– (i) all goods used in the factory by the manufacturer of the final product.

Thus, if some goods are purchased and capital goods are manufactured within the factory, these will be 'inputs' eligible for Cenvat credit.

It may be noted that capital goods manufactured within the factory and used within the factory are exempt from excise duty vide notification No. 67/1995-CE dated 16-3-1995 - See Appendix for text of the Notification.

Cenvat eligible as input but availed as capital goods and vice versa

Definition of 'capital goods' under Cenvat is not a conventional definition. Thus, sometimes, it happens that an article is eligible for credit as Cenvat on inputs but is availed as Cenvat on capital goods, or vice versa. In some earlier cases, when Modvat declaration was required, it was held that declaration filed in respect of inputs can be accepted if the goods are found to be capital goods and vice versa. The principle of these decisions will surely apply when Cenvat is available under one head but taken in other head due to mistake. It is true that in capital goods, only upto 50% credit can be availed in current year and balance in any subsequent years. However, this is only a technical lapse.

REVERSAL OF MODVAT CREDIT TAKEN ON INPUTS UNDER RULE 57CC

Kind attention is invited to the provisions of Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules for reversal of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods chargeable to 'nil' rate of excise duty. The provision has been made that where a manufacturer uses inputs which are common to both dutiable goods as well as exempted goods, the manufacturer is required to debit the amount equal to 8% of the value of the exempted goods when they are cleared from the factory.

2. In some cases, the exempted goods cleared by one manufacturer are used as inputs by another manufacturer. The manufacturer of exempted goods indicates the amount of Modvat credit reversed on the invoices issued by him for such exempted goods. In this context, some doubts have been raised whether the amount of Modvat credit so reversed is available as Modvat credit to the user of such exempted goods when he uses them as inputs in his factory.

3. In this context, it is clarified that the amount reversed is not by way of payment of excise duty. Accordingly, the amount of Modvat credit reversed and shown in the invoice by the manufacturer of exempted goods cannot be taken as credit by the user of exempted goods.

4. Reliance Industries Limited

Background: Reliance Industries (RIL), controlled by the Ambanis, commenced operations with a synthetic fabric mill at Naroda, Ahmedabad, where texturising/twisting facilities were set up in 1979. RIL mainly came out in the late 1980s when they progressed from no position among top hundred Indian companies to their present status of India’s top ranking private sector company. This success came through clearly read out forthcoming business opportunities in advance even before the start of the liberalization era. The strength of Reliance lies in its capabilities, largest number of equity base, to introduce innovative financial instruments and initiate novel funding schemes. The philosophy of “think big, grow big” has resulted in RIL building world-size plants in the areas it operates and achieve market dominance. RIL commissioned a PFY project in 1982, a PSF unit in 1986, linear alkyl benzene (LAB) and a PTA unit in 1988, all at Patalganga, Maharashtra. The technical collaborator for PFY and PSF was Du-Pont, US, and for PTA, UOP Processors, US, and ICI, UK. In 1991-92, RIL commissioned a petrochemicals unit to manufacture HOPE and PVC at Hazira, Gujarat, in technical collaboration with Du Pont and BF Goodrich respectively. In 1995-96, it entered the telecom industry through a joint venture with Nynex, US. RIL is a major player in the Indian petrochemicals sector. Its operations capture value addition at every stage from producing crude oil and gas to polyester and polymer products and are vertically integrated to the production of textiles.

Reliance has one of the largest marketing networks in Indian industry. All its brands are market leaders. RIL has obtained ISO 9002 certification from BVQI for its Patalganga and Hazira complexes. RIL is the first private sector company in India to be rated by the international credit rating agencies. During 1999-2000, the company completed its integrated Jamnagar complex, in a record period of less than 3 years. The Jamnagar complex houses the world’s largest grass root refinery (under Subsidiary company Reliance Petroleum), paraxylene and polypropylene project with the capacity of 27 million tons, 1.4 million tons and 6,00,000 tons per annum respectively together with country’s largest all weather port, power plants and all related infrastructure. It has also acquired control over the polyester manufacturing facilities of four relatively large polyester producers over the last two years. This has enhanced the effective production capacity in polyester by nearly 2,00,000 tons per annum to 8,00,000 tons per annum.

208 ELT 211 (CESTAT), assessee purchased some components, took Cenvat credit and cleared as such on payment of duty. It was held that they could do so even as trader and hence no duty is payable even if the activity is not 'manufacture' (It is advisable to show it as 'amount' and not as 'duty') - followed in AB Stampings v. CCE (2010) 259 ELT 299 (CESTAT SMB) In Natural Vitamins v. CCE 2005 (179) ELT 326 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if department collects excise duty on final product, it cannot say that Cenvat is not available as process is not 'manufacture'. Such stand is self-contradictory - same view in CCE v. MP Telelinks v. 2004(178) ELT 167 (CESTAT) * Markwell Paper Plast v. CCE (2012) 285 ELT 76 (CESTAT) * CCE v. North Sun Enterprises (2012) 284 ELT 75 (CESTAT).

In Sterlite Opticals v. CCE (2012) 282 ELT 392 (CESTAT), assessee paid excise duty under bona fide belief that the activity carried out by him is 'manufacture'. He availed Cenvat credit of inputs. The payment of duty was accepted by department. It was held that even if activity is not 'manufacture', it is case of removal of inputs 'as such' and Cenvat credit is reversible. Thus, entire exercise is revenue neutral and demand is not sustainable.

In one case, Tribunal observed that if the activity does not amount to manufacture, there can be no question of levy of duty and if duty is levied, Cenvat credit cannot be denied by holding that there is no manufacture. This view was upheld in CCE v. Creative Enterprises (2009) 235 ELT 785 (Guj HC DB) * Perfo Chem v. CCE (2015) 315 ELT 237 (CESTAT).

If department accepts duty (though not payable), it cannot refuse Cenvat credit on inputs, since department cannot approbate and reprobate, as held in Laxmindco Steel P Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (202) ELT 629 (CESTAT SMB).

In Rico Auto Industries v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 170 = 57 RLT 271 (CEGAT), it was held that inputs can be removed 'as such' or 'after processing' under Cenvat Credit Rules. Hence, even if there is no 'manufacture', no further amount is payable - followed in Sona Koyo Steering Systems v. CCE (2007) 5 STR 15 (CESTAT) [Strictly legally, in such case, it should be shown as 'amount' in invoice and not 'duty'].

If supplier has paid excise duty on wire drawn (though not legally payable during the relevant time), the buyer is eligible to avail Cenvat credit if supplier had not obtained refund of duty paid by them on drawn wire - BCL Springs v. CCE 2005 (185) ELT 56 (CESTAT).

Similarly, in Owens Bilt Ltd. v. CCE 1998(101) ELT 642 (CEGAT), it was held that once duty is paid at the manufacturer's end, the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner at user's end has no jurisdiction to decide whether duty was payable or not - followed in Goa Industrial Products v. CCE 2005 (181) ELT 222 (CESTAT).

Duty paid at full rate without availing concession - If assessee has paid duty at tariff rate without availing concessional rate, the buyer can get full Cenvat credit. - CCE v. Noel Pharmaceuticals 1999 (113) ELT 66 (CEGAT).

In Bharat Chemicals v. CCE (2004) 170 ELT 568 (CESTAT), tariff rate was 20%, but effective rate by way of exemption notification was 10%. Assessee was paying duty @ 10% for home clearances, but was paying duty @ 20% for goods exported and claiming rebate of full duty paid on export goods. It was held that he is entitled to full rebate, as rebate is of 'duty paid' and not 'duty payable'. [He was paying higher duty as he had excess balance in Cenvat credit account].

Cenvat credit if process incidental to manufacture - Purification and filtration of chemical to make it marketable in international market is process incidental to manufacture of the product and hence is covered in definition of 'manufacture' and hence is eligible for Cenvat credit - CCE v. Alok Enterprises (2010) 259 ELT 333 (Bom HC DB).

Buyer can avail Cenvat credit, if supplier paid duty, even though not payable - If supplier had paid excise duty (though not payable), buyer is eligible to avail Cenvat credit. See case law in earlier part of this chapter.

The manufacturer need not be registered as dealer - In Mittal Pigments v. CCE (2013) 296 ELT 531 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that manufacturer removing inputs as such on reversal of Cenvat credit is not required to be registered as dealer [In my view, this would be so if he is removing inputs occasionally. However, if wants to regularly trade in goods, he should be registered as a dealer]. Cenvat credit on GTA service available even if inputs/capital goods removed as such and the credit is not required to be reversed - Cenvat credit on GTA service is allowable even if inputs/capital goods removed as such - CCE v. Simplex Castings (2010) 25 STT 106 = 253 ELT 640 (CESTAT SMB) - relying on Chitrakoot Steel v. CCE - 2008 (10) STR 118 CESTAT SMB) - same view in CCE v. Punjab Steels (2010) 7 taxmann.com 55 = 29 STT 168 = 260 ELT 521 (P&H HC DB) * Seven Star Steels v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 228 = 32 taxmann.com 186 = 60 VST 264 (CESTAT).

In A R Castings v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 244 = 256 ELT 420 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that rule 3(5) uses the word 'inputs' which applies to input goods and not input services. Hence, Cenvat credit of input services used in bringing the inputs in the factory is not required to be reversed - same view in CCE v. Precision Drawwell (2011) 31 STT 134 (CESTAT SMB) * Industrial Enterprises v. CCE (2012) 284 ELT 444 (CESTAT SMB).

Reversal of input services utilised in respect of inputs removed as such is not required. There is no such provision in rules - Bansal Alloys v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 529 (CESTAT SMB) - followed in Bassi Alloys v. CCE (2010) 29 STT 242 (CESTAT SMB)

This view has been confirmed in para B.26 of CBE&C instruction F No. 96/85/2015-CX.1 dated 7-12-2015, where it was observed that the input services get consumed and become cost of business. Hence, reversal of Cenvat credit of service tax on input services is not required.

Excise duty cannot be paid on removal of such inputs - The assessee is not manufacturer of those inputs. Hence, he cannot and need not pay excise duty on transaction value, even if the inputs are sold at higher price. In CCE v. Inductotherm (2013) 39 STT 141 = 29 taxmann.com 281 = 283 ELT 359 (Guj HC DB), assessee paid excise duty on removal of inputs as such (activity which was not manufacture), through Cenvat credit (presumably to utilise Cenvat credit which was otherwise not utilisable). It was held that duty collected from purchaser is payable under section 11D of CEA and Cenvat credit is not available (double whammy).

Removal of scrapped input is not removal of input 'as such' - If input becomes waste and sold as scrap, it cannot be said that input is cleared 'as such' under rule 57F(3). What is cleared is 'waste' and duty will be payable as if waste has been removed - Tata Oil Mills Co. Ltd. v. CCE 1998(102) ELT 479 (CEGAT) * Fluid Line v. CCE 2002(142) ELT 673 (CEGAT SMB).

In Nagpal Electric v. CCE 2005 (179) ELT 346 (CESTAT SMB), input of copper tubes became waste during manufacture. It was held that it cannot be said that inputs are cleared 'as such' and hence, duty is payable only on scrap value. - same view in Ericsson India v. CCE (2016) 334 ELT 107 (CESTAT).

If input becomes waste during manufacture, Cenvat credit is not required to be reversed - Foil Pack India v. CCE (2007) 216 ELT 616 (CESTAT) * Monika Electronics v. CCE (2006) 204 ELT 468 (CESTAT SMB) * Titan Industries v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 730 (CESTAT).

In CST v. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (1992) 2 SCC 220 = 85 STC 220 (SC), it was held that a refinery will be entitled to full set off (now ITC) even if part goes in sludge.

9.3-4 Process losses and handling loss are allowable There will be some loss of inputs during manufacturing process. Cenvat (now ITC) is available on entire quantity of input even if part of input goes in process loss, since all inputs are 'used' in the manufacture of final product, even if it is not reflected in final product - Multimetals Ltd. v. ACCE 57 ELT 209 (SC) = 1992 (1) SCC 715 = AIR 1992 SC 1532 = 1992 AIR SCW 1644 - quoted with approval in UOI v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC - 3 member bench order), where it was held that exact mathematical equation between quantity of raw material purchased and the raw material found in finished product is not possible, and should not be looked for. [This judgment is in respect of Proforma Credit, but its ratio is fully applicable to Cenvat (now ITC).]

In CCE v. IPF Vikram India 2002(150) ELT 175 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat on inputs (now ITC) which have gone in waste is not deniable - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC on merits - 2003 (153) ELT A303.

Entire Cenvat credit (now ITC) is available if part of input is contained in waste, refuse or by-product - Mahindra Hinoday Industries v. CCE (2014) 308 ELT 555 (CESTAT), relying on CBE&C circular No. B-4/7/2000-TRU dated 3-4-2000 - same view in Rupa and Co v. CESTAT (2015) 324 ELT 295 (Mad HC DB). * ARS Steels & Alloy International (P.) Ltd. v. State Tax Officer [2021] 86 GST 644 = 127 taxmann.com 787 (Madras HC).

Even if waste is not returned by job worker, Cenvat credit of excise duty (now ITC of GST) contained in such scrap or waste is not required to be reversed - Mukand Ltd. v. CCE (2015) 318 ELT 134 (CESTAT SMB).

Loss of input by evaporation during manufacturing processing is to be treated as ware or loss and Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such loss is not required to be reversed - CCE v. BOC (India) (2008) 223 ELT 33 (Guj HC DB).

Chlorine gas left in cylinder after use of gas in processing can be termed as 'process loss' and its Cenvat credit (now ITC) is available - CCE v. Andhra Paper Mill (2011) 269 ELT 79 (AP HC DB).

Even excess process loss is allowable if any evidence of clandestine removal is not available - Rollex Electro Products v. CCE (2016) 338 ELT 736 (CESTAT).

Loss of inputs during handling eligible - In or in relation to the manufacture covers the entire manufacturing process starting from initial stage of handling of inputs. Thus, if wastage of input at the initial handling from tank discharge due to various reasons like spillage, pipeline losses, handling losses etc., it is 'in or in relation to manufacture' and Cenvat (now ITC) cannot be denied. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 943 (CEGAT) - followed in CCE v. Hydrogas Plg (I) P Ltd. 2006 (196) ELT 167 (CESTAT) - same view in Zeneca ICI Agro Chemicals v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 770 (CESTAT).

9.3-5 No credit on short received inputs but natural losses allowable

If inputs are short received and there is loss during transit, the goods short received cannot be termed as 'used in or in relation to manufacture'. Hence, Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such short received inputs is not available - Asea Brown Boveri Ltd. v. CCE 1994 (74) ELT 897 (CEGAT) - same view in Bombay Dyeing v. CCE 1999 (113) ELT 331 (CEGAT) * Sterlite Industries v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 193 (CESTAT) * Carborandum Universal v. CCE (2008) 227 ELT 535 (CESTAT SMB).

the matter, the amendment, as such does not Affect valuation of inventory of raw material, etc. As discussed, for purchases, a purchaser pays a price for the goods. Such price would have various components including Cost, Duties, Taxes, profits etc. The price is lump sum or composite price and cannot be divided into its components.

Further, the Duty, etc. embedded in purchase price is not incurred by the purchaser.

MODVAT Credit is not available as a consequence of payment. Finally, the credit available under the Rule is in respect of purchase price, which includes Duties. The credit is quantified with reference to the amount of Duty. That is only a basis for quantifying the amount.

Accordingly, it is not a credit for Duty. In this connection, a useful reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. P.J. Chemicals [1994] 210 ITR 830 wherein it is held that a subsidy granted as incentive cannot be reduced from actual cost of the assets merely because it is quantified on the basis of the value of Fixed Assets. Accordingly, in purchase cost of raw material, in spite of the amendment, there is no requirement to adjust MODVAT.

One of the arguments against such a view could be that 'mischief sought to be cured', as explained in the Memorandum, is to provide for such adjustment. It seems, the provision and the Memorandum are at variance. The provision, as said above, aims at including Duty, etc., incurred or paid for bringing the goods to its location and conditions so as to neutralize Special Bench Decision and Gujarat High Court Decision. Had the intention been otherwise, the language would have been different and section 145A(b), possibly would have read "further adjusted to include any set-off, credit or any other entitlement in respect of any Tax, Duty ..., actually paid or incurred by the assessee, whether as a part of the price or otherwise, to bring the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation".

[1994] 75 TAXMAN 167 (ART) MODVAT CREDIT ON CAPITAL GOODS - ACCOUNTING TREATMENT

C. Thandava Krishna*

Among the Budget proposals of 1994-95 most widely welcomed in the Indian industrial circles was the one pertaining to the extension of the MODVAT Credit Scheme to capital goods. The proposal has now been put into effect by amendment of the relevant statutory provisions.

In this article, the author examines the salient features of the new provisions and outlines the accounting problems that are likely to arise in the implementation of the extended scheme. He also examines the relevant existing Accounting Standards and Guidance Notes issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) which can be helpful in formulating a suitable method of accounting to achieve the objective underlying the new proposal The author also makes certain suggestions of his own in this context and stresses the necessity for the ICAI to issue a separate accounting Standard or Guidance Note on the subject - EDITOR

An overview of the new provisions

1. The Finance Minister provided a boon to the Indian industry by introduction of MODVAT credit on capital goods in the Budget for 1994-95.

In para 58 of part B of his Budget Speech, the Finance Minister has stated, "availability of capital goods at a reasonable cost is necessary to enhance our competitiveness and promote investment. It is also necessary to ensure that our domestic capital goods industry, which has a tremendous potential, is not at a comparative disadvantage due to anomalies in the tax structure. To further both these objectives, I propose the following package of measures".

The proposals include - reduction of basic customs duty on project imports and general capital goods, reduction of import duty on spares and parts, imposition of countervailing duty on imports of capital goods equal to the excise duty on domestic capital goods, reduction of import duty on machine tools and customs duty on steel, etc.

The major proposal in this package is that of extending the benefit of MODVAT credit to capital goods so that the full credit of excise duty paid on domestic capital goods or countervailing duty paid on imported capital goods will be available at one time.

The Finance Minister hoped that these proposals would give a strong boost to investment in the economy and will help the domestic capital goods industry in particular. This is a very good step taken by the Finance Minister and the proposals have been wholeheartedly welcomed by the entire industry.

It is hoped that the Indian industry will seize the opportunity and take full advantage of these benefits by starting new industrial lines, enhancing the existing capacities, modernising the existing equipment with updated technology and fully equip itself to be more competitive on a global level. Incidentally, the capital goods industry which has been suffering from acute recession in the recent past is bound to recuperate with full vigour.

Rules 57Q to 57U have been introduced in Chapter V of the Central Excise Rules for extending the scheme of MODVAT credit of the duty paid on capital goods. Notification No. 4/94-CE(NT) has been issued for this purpose which came into effect from March 1, 1994. The salient features of these rules and notifications are as follows :

Salient features of New Rules

2.1 Definition of capital goods - The expression 'Capital goods' is defined in rule 57Q as covering :

(i)Machines, machinery, plant, equipment, apparatus, tools or appliances used for producing or processing of any goods and also includes components, spare parts and accessories for such equipment.

( ii)Moulds and dies, generating sets and weigh bridges used in the factory of the manufacturer. It may be noted that duty paid on components, spare parts or accessories intended for these equipments is not eligible for MODVAT credit. It may also be noted that it is enough that these equipments are used in the factory and need not be used for producing or processing of any goods as in the case of machinery and equipment mentioned in sub-clause (i) above.

2.2 Adjustment of credit and exceptions - The credit of duty paid on capital goods can be used for payment of duty on any of the specified manufactured goods mentioned in the Annexure to rule 57Q.

If, however, any capital equipment acquired by the manufacturer is used exclusively for the manufacture of goods which are wholly exempted from excise duty or chargeable at nil rate of duty, no credit shall be allowed in respect of such equipment. Similarly, any components, spare parts or accessories of such items which are used for the production of wholly exempted or nil-rated goods are also not eligible for credit of the duty.

However, if any equipment is used even partly for manufacture of dutiable goods, MODVAT credit will not be denied on such capital goods.

The duty paid on capital goods on or after March 1, 1994, only is eligible for MODVAT credit and not the duty paid earlier.

Case law under earlier definition which is still relevant

21.3 Most of case law under earlier definition of 'input' is now of doubtful validity. Some case law still relevant is given below.

Process losses and handling loss are allowable

21.3-1 There will be some loss of inputs during manufacturing process. Cenvat is available on entire quantity of input even if part of input goes in process loss, since all inputs are 'used' in the manufacture of final product, even if it is not reflected in final product - Multimetals Ltd. v. ACCE 57 ELT 209 (SC) = 1992 (1) SCC 715 = AIR 1992 SC 1532 = 1992 AIR SCW 1644 - quoted with approval in UOI v. Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. - 1995 (77) ELT 268 (SC - 3 member bench order), where it was held that exact mathematical equation between quantity of raw material purchased and the raw material found in finished product is not possible, and should not be looked for. [This judgment is in respect of Proforma Credit, but its ratio is fully applicable to Cenvat.]

In CCE v. IPF Vikram India 2002 (150) ELT 175 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat on inputs which have gone in waste is not deniable - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC on merits - 2003(153) ELT A303.

Entire Cenvat credit is available if part of input is contained in waste, refuse or by-product - Mahindra Hinoday Industries v. CCE (2014) 308 ELT 555 (CESTAT), relying on CBE&C circular No. B-4/7/2000-TRU dated 3-4-2000 - same view in Rupa and Co v. CESTAT (2015) 324 ELT 295 (Mad HC DB).

Even if waste is not returned by job worker, Cenvat credit of excise duty contained in such scrap or waste is not required to be reversed - Mukand Ltd. v. CCE (2015) 318 ELT 134 (CESTAT SMB).

Loss of input by evaporation during manufacturing processing is to be treated as ware or loss and Cenvat credit on such loss is not required to be reversed - CCE v. BOC (India) (2008) 223 ELT 33 (Guj HC DB).

Chlorine gas left in cylinder after use of gas in processing can be termed as 'process loss' and its Cenvat credit is available - CCE v. Andhra Paper Mill (2011) 269 ELT 79 (AP HC DB).

Even excess process loss is allowable if any evidence of clandestine removal is not available - Rollex Electro Products v. CCE (2016) 338 ELT 736 (CESTAT).

Loss of inputs during handling eligible - In or in relation to the manufacture covers the entire manufacturing process starting from initial stage of handling of inputs. Thus, if wastage of input at the initial handling from tank discharge due to various reasons like spillage, pipeline losses, handling losses etc., it is 'in or in relation to manufacture' and Cenvat cannot be denied. CIRCULAR NO. 283/117/96-CX, DATED 31-12-1996

UTILISATION OF CENVAT CREDIT IN RESPECT OF INPUTS ON WHICH CREDIT IS AVAILED BUT THE INPUTS ARE EXPORTED AS SUCH UNDER BOND

It has been represented to the Board that the field formations have taken a view that credit on inputs cleared as such for export under bond cannot be allowed to be utilised for payment of duty on final products cleared for home consumption nor can it be refunded in cash. In this regard, it has been stated that aforesaid facilities are available where inputs are used in the manufacture of export products and not in the case where inputs have themselves been exported. This doubt has arisen on account of the proviso to rule 57F(4) according to which duty availed on inputs used in the manufacture of final product exported under bond could be utilised towards payment of duty on goods cleared for home consumption or refunded in cash.

2. The matter has been examined by the Board.

3. Rule 57A(1) provides for the general scheme of MODVAT given in section V(AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and it indeed mentions that credit of duty will be allowed for utilising towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final products. Whereas rule 57F is a more specific provision regarding manner of utilisation of the inputs and the manner of utilisation of the credit allowed in respect of duty paid thereon. Rule 57F(1)(ii) permits removal of the inputs as such for export under bond. Proviso to rule 57F(4) deals with manner of utilisation of credit in cases of export of 'final products' or 'intermediate products' under bond. Export of inputs as such under bond were treated as 'final product' by virtue of 'deemed manufacture' clause (i.e., the expression as if such inputs have been manufactured in the same factory) under the erstwhile rule 57F(1)(ii) which covered all such cases within the ambit of proviso to rule 57F(4). This expression was omitted by Notification No. 28/95-C.E.(N.T.), dated 29-6-1995 with a view to simplify the clearance procedure, which has created a doubt in respect of utilisation of credit in such cases. It is not the intention of the Government to debar such manufacturer-exporters from utilising credit. Clearance of inputs as such for export under bond can still be treated at par with 'final product' and the manner of utilisation of credit in such cases will be governed by the provisions of the proviso to rule 57F(4).

4. It is also observed that in case such inputs are cleared on payment of duty by debit in RG-23A Part II account by virtue of rule 57F(4)(iii), the manufacturer will be entitled for rebate under rule 12(1)(a) of the Central Excise Rules. He is however, put to disadvantage if he opts for export under bond procedure.The exports under 'claim of rebate' and 'export under bond' should be at parity, since, intention of both the procedures is to make duty incidence 'nil'. It is also an established principle that rules should be interpreted in a manner which do not render them redundant.

5. Accordingly, it is clarified that the Modvat credit in RG-23A Part II account against the export of inputs as such under bond can be utilised in the same manner as is provided for a final product under proviso to rule 57F(4). Obviously, it follows from this that such inputs should be allowed to be exported under bond without any reversal of the credit.

Mere two separate registrations do not mean that these are separate 'factories' - In Diamond Cement v. CCE (2004) 169 ELT 34 (CESTAT), assessee had two units adjacent to each other. No. B-1/3/2011-TRU dated 25-3-2011 - para 2 of CBE&C Circular No. 943/04/2011-CX dated 29-4-2011 - See Appendix for text of the circular.

[Really this considerably broadens scope of 'input']

Safety appliances like hand gloves, shoes - Gloves used by workers of manufacturer of hot jobs and in handling corrosive material is 'used in manufacture' - Member, Board of Revenue v. Phelps & Co (1972) 4 SCC 121 = 29 STC 101 (SC) - quoted in Pratap Steel Rolling Mills v. State of Punjab (2007) 9 VST 629 (P&H HC DB) * Essel Mining and Industries v. CST (2011) 41 VST 154 (Ori HC DB).

In P Narendra Menon v. State of Kerala (2009) 23 VST 66 (Ker HC DB), it was held that safety gloves used for protection of workmen are 'used in manufacture' and are eligible for concessional rate of sales tax [decision under sales tax but principle fully applicable here].

Safety shoes are eligible for Cenvat credit - Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 301 ELT 592 (CESTAT SMB).

Goods used for testing - Testing is inextricably connected with manufacturing process and until it is carried out, manufacturing process is incomplete, as the goods are not fit for sale and hence not marketable. Hence goods used for testing are eligible for Cenvat credit. Physical presence of inputs in final product is not prerequisite to claim Cenvat credit - Flex Engineering Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 5 SCC 609 = 34 STT 512 = 18 taxmann.com 108 = 276 ELT 153 (SC).

4.1-10 Inputs directly sent to site and fitted there are eligible as input

In CCE v. Central Electronics Ltd. (2011) 271 ELT 586 (CESTAT), inputs (batteries) were directly sent to site and fitted there. Excise duty was paid on entire price. Assessee argued that since the system has to be manufactured at various sites, each such site was to be considered as the part of manufacturing premises for that system and hence inputs received at those sites should be considered as having been received in the factory. This contention was accepted as it was held that Cenvat credit is available on such inputs.

4.1-11 Input goods in respect of service providers

Definition of 'input' of goods in respect service provider is restrictive. Only those inputs used for providing any output service would be eligible.

In Mundra Port & SEZ Ltd. v. CCE (2009) 18 STT 314 = 33 VST 107 (CESTAT), it was held that cement and steel used for construction of jetty is not 'input' for providing taxable port service.

Explanation 2.—Input include goods used in the manufacture of capital goods which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer; but shall not include cement, angles, channels, Centrally Twisted Deform bar (CTD) or Thermo Mechanically Treated bar (TMT) and other items used for construction of factory shed, building or laying or foundation or making of structures for support of capital goods."

Earlier position 3. Prior to this, under rule 57Q of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, Cenvat credit on cement, angles, channels, Centrally Twisted Deform bar (CTD) or Thermo Mechanically Treated bar (TMT) and other items used for construction of factory shed, building or laying foundation or making of structures for support of capital goods was allowed as on ‘capital goods’. However, with the coming into effect of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002, and thereafter CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, credit on cement angles, channels, CTD or TMT bar and other items used for construction of factory shed, building or laying or foundation or making of structures for support of capital goods was still allowed being ‘input’ and not as ‘capital goods’ as the definition of ‘capital goods’ was changed under rule 2 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. However, some assessees were still taking them as ‘capital goods’ and yet getting favourable decisions which have allowed cenvat, on these items, bracketing the items as ‘inputs’ as they were revenue neutral and it was immaterial whether it was treated as ‘inputs’ or ‘capital goods’.

Conclusion

4. This change, however, has left no scope for the assessees to avail cenvat credit on cement, angles, channels, CTD or TMT bar and other items used for construction of factory shed, building or laying or foundation or making of structures for support of capital goods.

It has also been clearly stated and emphasized even if these items are used for foundation or making of structure for support of capital goods. They will not still be eligible for cenvat credit. One good aspect of this change is that it would put to rest a plethora of cases which would have come up in various forums, Tribunals & Courts regarding the admissibility of cenvat credit on these items.

The flip side of this may be the new units would try to bring these items as a last resort under the definition of ‘capital goods’ as per rule 2(a)(iii ) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 under the heading ‘components, spares, accessories of the goods specified at (i) and (ii)’; The task may prove to be futile.

It was found that these provisions are in pari materia with the provisions of rule 57CC and rule 57AD of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. Combined reading of rule 57CC (1) and 57CC (9) would indicate that rule 6(3)(b) has been carved out of a combination of the said sub-rule of rule 57CC. It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts has to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods by way of formula as provided in the rule itself; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It is the settled law that reversal of the credit taken on the inputs is as good as non-availment of the credit on the inputs.

Under the Central Excise Act, 1944, levy is on manufacture but payment is at the time of clearance. It has been decided by the Board that credit of the duty paid on common inputs is admissible when used in the manufacturer of the final product (exempted and dutiable) provided the said credit of duty paid on inputs going into the exempted category of the final product is debited in the RG 23A-Part II account before the removal of exempted final product on actual or pro rata (estimated) basis. The facility of reversing the credit taken is neither explicitly given nor necessarily implied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002. It was held in that context that the credit taken but before utilization reversed, will amount to not taking the credit and the benefit of exemption cannot be denied.

In view of the above reasoning, the Tribunal held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are not applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. In other words, it is equivalent to reversal of credit on inputs. Therefore, according to Tribunal, the appellant had satisfied the requirement of not taking Modvat Credit on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Their case is specifically covered by rule 57CC as well as the decision of Supreme Court with regard to not availing of Modvat Credit on inputs in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v.
