This indicates a patent flow in the drafting of section 145A, and the draftsman has not clearly spelt out the object and purpose of altering the law contained in section 145 for all the assessment years starting from the assessment year 1986—97. Section 145A (a) leads to the logical conclusion and the resultant strange situation that a hybrid system can again be followed by the assessee regularly with retrospective effect from April 1, 1986 so long as the principle adumbrated in section 145A (b) with regard to the valuation of purchases, sales and inventories is followed. Obviously, this was not the intention of the revenue.

Section 145A (b) mandates the inclusion of any tax, duty, cess or fee paid or incurred by the assessee. The purchase cost incurred by the assessee at times may include the excise duty paid by a supplier. But such excise duty is not paid by the assessee at all. It is paid by the supplier, an outsider. Such an anomalous situation obviously could not have been intended by the Legislature.

Yet another mandate of section 145A(b ) is the inclusion of all duties paid or incurred by an assessee ‘to bring the goods to the place of its location and condition as on the date of valuation’. A strange and undesirable consequence is that only purchases and sales which were made on the last day (March 31st) of the accounting year, and the entire closing stock on the aforesaid last day should be valued according to the new statutory formula, while purchases and sales made in the antecedent 364 days do not require to be so valued. In this connection attention of the revenue authorities is invited to rules 57A to 57J of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 that deal with (Modvat) Credit utilised by a manufacturer, and the same could have been offered as taxable income.

Section 145(2) provides for notification of Accounting Standards to be followed by any class of assessees or in respect of any class of income, and in pursuance thereof the Central Government has notified the Accounting Standards to be followed by all the assessees following the mercantile system of accounting. No. 9949 F. No. 132/7 of 1995-TPL dated January 25, 1996. - Vide Taxman Income-tax Rules, 1997-123-125. The Accounting Standards provide that the accounts should represent a ‘true and fair view’ of the business, and that a change in policy shall be made if it is considered that the said change would result in a more appropriate preparation and presentation of financial statements. The question that now baffles an assessee is whether the cumulative effect of section 145A and section 145 (2) is to rewrite their own accounts for the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 in accordance with the statutory accounting policy when it is at variance with the actual policy followed by the assessee.

Contingent Liability of excise duty for purposes of income-tax

4. Excise duty is normally payable by a company on manufactured goods, and for this purpose the company maintains two different godowns : (1) Duty-unpaid godown for goods in respect of which excise duty is not paid, and (2) Duty-paid godown for goods where excise duty is paid. Excise duty is paid before the removal of goods from the duty unpaid godowns. Generally excise duty liability in respect of goods lying in the duty-unpaid godown is shown by way of contingent liability under the Notes on Account. The liability is shown as ‘Estimated excise duty on goods manufactured but not despatched". As excise duty is not paid, it is not debited to the profit and loss account. The company’s accounts are generally prepared and maintained on the basis of the mercantile system.

The MODVAT Angle

5. Modvat is a procedure whereby a manufacturer can utilise credits for inputs against duty payable on final products. Duty credit taken on inputs is in the nature of a set off available against the payment of excise duty on the final products. This scheme was primarily introduced to arrest the cascading effect of duty paid on the intermediary product. Three situations arise in the application of Modvat, viz, (i) the manufacturer availing Modvat credit on inputs, (ii) the manufacturer transfers finished goods to the depots or sales outlet after the payment of duty, and (iii) the manufacturer not availing of Modvat credit.

The Supreme Court in Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (2) SCC 159, has observed :

(a) Where Modvat credit is availed of on duty paid inputs used in manufacture of exempted final products, crediting duty paid on such inputs and reversing the entry would not bar entitlement to exemption.

(b) The assessee should have maintained separate accounts for duty- free goods and the goods on which duty has to be paid. But a Departmental Circular Letter on this problem in which it has been clarified by the Ministry of Finance is as under :-

7. Accounting Standard 2 dealing with ‘Valuation of Inventories’ pres-cribed by the ICAI will be made mandatory soon and it has revised the definition of ‘costs of purchase’ as follows :

"The costs of purchase consist of the purchase price including duties and taxes (other than those subsequently recoverable by the enterprise from the taxing authorities), freight inwards and other expenditure directly attributable to the acquisition, less trade discounts, rebates and other similar items." From the definition, it is clear that Modvat credit is outside the purview of cost of purchase. While the Modvat credit is instantly taken and is available for payment of duty on the finished goods, the availment of credit carries a concurrent obligation for the inputs to be disposed of in the manner specified under rule 57F of the Central Excise Rules. In view of this, till the goods are so disposed of, the assessee has a potential liability and obligation in terms of the credit taken and utilised. Only on the disposal of the goods, in accordance with the rules, would the liability be extinguished and the benefit could be recognised as income in the profit and loss account.

Concept of revenue recognition

9. The Appendix to Accounting Standard 9 issued by the ICAI makes it clear that revenue should not be recognised unless all the conditions attached to the contract are completed. In the case of Modvat on closing stock, the important condition is that raw materials should be consumed for the manufacture of finished goods. Since this has not happened, it will have to be ensured that the set-off for Modvat credit on input not yet consumed is carried forward. 6.3 Different units :— 6.3-1 In SINTEX Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2013 (287) ELT 261 (Guj.) - The appellant had two divisions one was the textile division and the other was plastic division. He got separate registration for both units. But both units were having a common PAN under the Income-tax Act. Both the units were located on the common ground surrounded by a common boundary wall adjoining to each other. The appellant installed DG sets/electricity generation plant to be used in the factory of the appellant and it had been using furnace oil as fuel for the generation of electricity. The appellant had been availing of CENVAT credit on the inputs, viz., furnace oil, used as fuel for the generation of electricity, which was used for captive consumption in their own factory. The appellant supplied part of the electricity so generated to its own plastic division also. The department initiated action on the availing of CENVAT credit. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to credit on the eligible inputs utilized in the generation of electricity to the extent to which it was using the produced electricity within its factory which was registered for that purpose but not to the extent supplied to a factory which was registered for a different unit.

6.3-2 In Maihar Cement Unit No. 2 v. CCE 2013 (293) ELT 239 (Tri. - Delhi) - The mines served to Maiher Cement and also to Maiher Cement Unit No. 2, the appellant. The Commissioner (Appeals) considered that both the units were registered separately with the Central Excise Department. Therefore, the credit of duty paid by the appellants on stone crushers and their parts used in the mines for crushing of limestone and transportation of the same to the appellant's factory was denied. The Tribunal held that the criteria adopted by lower authorities would not advance Revenue's case inasmuch as the registration of different units under Central Excise Law could not be held relevant for finding out the status of the two units. There was no dispute that Maiher Cement and Maiher Cement Unit No. 2 were two units of the same parent company, i.e., M/s Century Textiles & Industries Limited and did not have the independent legal persons. Though the accounting of the two units was separate a common balance sheet was being prepared. As such, the mines which were allotted to Maiher Cement at the time of its incorporation and, subsequently, allowed to be used by the second entity, i.e., Maiher Cement Unit No. 2 had to be treated as captive mines for both the units. The Tribunal set aside the impugned order.

CENVAT CREDIT

AVAILMENT OF CENVAT CREDIT (PART 2)

PL. SUBRAMANIAN*

This write-up comprehensively analyses some case laws that throw some light upon availment of cenvat credit under different heads.

Residential Colony - Maintenance Service

1. Cenvat credit of Rs. 1,07,943 availed by the appellants who are manufacturers of cement, on account of repairs and maintenance of civil construction, etc., in their residential colony during the period from July, 2005 to March, 2006 has been disallowed on the ground that repairs, etc., were not input services used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance thereof from the place of removal as per rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

The Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal held that :

"(4) The appellant’s contention as reflected in the reply to the show-cause notice that their factory was situated at a remote place where no facilities were available for stay of their engineers and workmen, and it was, therefore, necessary to construct a residential colony for the employees for being available on the spot in order to maintain continuity in the process of cement manufacture, has not been disputed. Therefore, service provided is relatable to business and credit of service tax is admissible as the service in respect of repairs and maintenance, civil construction in relation to the residential colony are input services. My view finds support from the Tribunal’s order in the case of Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (4) STR 79 holding that credit is admissible on service tax paid on mobile phones provided to employees to carry out business transactions. Credit has been held to be admissible even though the telephones are not installed within the factory premises. The decisions of the Allahabad High Court in the case of ITAT v. B. Hill & Co. (P.) Ltd. [1983] 142 ITR 185 and the Bombay High Court in the case of Greaves Cotton & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [2005] 279 ITR 42 also lend support to my view - Allahabad High Court has held that expenditure incurred on restoration of buildings and residential quarters or factory was available as revenue expenditure for the reason that repair and reconstruction enable the assessee-company to carry on its Business, while the Bombay High Court held that expenditure incurred on maintenance of transit quarters used for accommodating employees visiting Bombay from outstation for business purpose was to be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head ‘Profit and gain of business or profession’ under the provisions of section 37(I)."

Manikgarh Cement v. CCE&C [Final Order No. A/27 of 2008/WZB/C-IV/SMB, dated December 13, 2007 (Mum. - CESTAT).

Goods exempt but exported, CENVAT credit available

2. The company is the manufacturer of printed books. Printed books attract nil rate of duty. It also manufactures other excisable goods. It exported the printed books and claimed Cenvat credit and the same was disallowed by the department. The Bombay High Court has analysed rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2008 and has come to the decision that the company is entitled to avail Cenvat credit on the inputs which are used for manufacturing exempted goods for export. Repro India Ltd. [Writ Petition No. 6951 of 2007, dated December 6, 2008].

Important observations of the High Court are reproduced below:

17. (1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, for the purpose of calculating the net tax payable by a registered dealer for any tax period after being registered, an input tax credit as determined under this section shall be allowed to such registered dealer for the tax paid or payable in respect of all taxable sales other than sales subject to special additional sales tax to the extent of such additional sales tax or any other sales as may be prescribed, or purchases under section 10 during that period.

(2) The input tax credit to which the registered dealer is entitled to, shall be the amount of tax paid by the registered dealer to the seller, on his turnover of purchases made during the tax period, intended to be used for the purposes and subject to the conditions as specified in sub-section (3), sub-section (4) and sub-section (5) and calculated in such manner as may be prescribed.

Legislative intent

11. A plain and simple reading of section 145A will show that the intention of the Legislature is to include only items like excise duty and customs duty to avoid one year advance claim under section 43B as per the following comparative analysis: Thus, it can be concluded—

(a)The Modvat benefit should not be added to the value of closing stock even under a plain and independent reading of section 145A as it is not incurred to bring the goods to their present location and condition.

(b)The excise duty and customs duty paid do form part of cost as they are incurred to bring the goods to their present location and condition on the matching concept basis.

Valuation of Fixed Assets and Inventories

12. Under rule 579 of the Excise Rules, the value of fixed assets should be capitalised net of Modvat benefit only. The assessee has to give a declaration and give proof also. This means any payment made from Modvat on capital goods is only an advance payment and should be treated like that only. Under the Income-tax Act also valuation has to be done net of Modvat only.

In case of inventories also, there cannot be any difference in the valuation principle. Any Modvat paid for inventories is also an advance payment only. Further, there is no one-to-one correlation. Thus, on the same logic and following international practices, the inventory should be valued on net basis only and there is no case for valuing it differently.

Gross Method of Valuation and Bank Financing

13. Banks finance the value of inventory held by the assessee. The value of inventory does not and should not include value of Modvat as credit is taken as soon as material reaches the factory. Further, such credits are utilised without one-to-one correlation for payment of excise duty of other manufactured goods. Hence, Modvat cannot and should not enter the stock valuation principles. If banks are financing assets in inventories inclusive of Modvat, they are only making a valuation mistake as the borrower has already received the benefit.

However, the balances in RG23A, 23C and PLA are balances held by the department and are in the nature of ‘temporary’ advances. These balances are highly liquid and, hence, deserve consideration for bank finance on merits and banks should analyse and recognise such items separately and under the head ‘Inventory’.

Conclusion

14. The following points emerge from the foregoing discussion :

(a)The purpose of section 145A is to plug the loopholes of judgments in the cases of Food Specialities Ltd. (supra) and Lakhanpal National Ltd. (supra) of claiming excise duty/customs duty one year in advance. Further, it should be understood that such practice was adopted only in part of the country as the Southern Bench has rejected the same argument in Durametallic (India) Ltd. v. IAC [1991] 38 ITD 24 (Mad.).

This objective is fully served by making AS-2 mandatory from April 1, 1999 as explained earlier

(b)It is quite clear that both gross and net methods of Modvat accounting under the matching concept are revenue neutral. Internationally only the net method of accounting is followed and, hence, we should also follow the same as we are moving towards borderless trading.

(c)No adjustment outside the books is fool-proof. The volume of transactions affecting Modvat is mind-boggling, e.g., number of gate-passes per day will be anywhere between 100 and 1000 per day depending on the volume of transactions.

(d)The companies themselves are extremely careful in accounting and reconciling Modvat as any claim not made adversely affects the bottom line.

(e)There is a regular audit and check by the department on Modvat.

(f)All the requirements in section 145A are fully and squarely met by making AS-2 mandatory.

(g)Hence, the provision of section 145A should be withdrawn immediately.

(h)A suitable safeguard may be introduced in section 43B to avoid advance claim relating to duty on inventories which are governed by AS-2, even though it is not possible to make such claim differently as AS-2 has been made mandatory.

Hence, the provision of section 145A may be deleted in the coming Finance Bill.

Section 145A of the Income-tax Act, 1961

5. Section 145A has been introduced in the Income-tax Act, to make certain adjustments to opening stock, purchases, sales and closing stock for arriving at income under the head ‘Profits and gains for business or profession’ and this will be effective from April 1, 1999. The adjustments to be made pertain to expenses actually incurred or paid towards tax, duty, cess or fee, etc. These are to be grossed up with purchases, sales and valuation of inventory.

Accounting practices

6. Most of the companies are following the ‘exclusive method’ of accounting for purchases, sales and inventory. Under this method, Modvat paid on purchase of inputs will not form part of cost of purchases in all cases wherever the benefit of Modvat credit is allowed to be enjoyed by the manufacturers of excisable goods. This is on the lines of the relevant Accounting Standard in India and International Accounting Standards. Similarly, excise duty and sales tax are also treated as balance sheet items.

Since the provisions of section 145A have been included in the statute effective from April 1, 1999 (assessment year 1999-2000), requirements of this section have to be given effect to by the assessees from April 1, 1998 onwards. For the sake of consistency and in accordance with the accepted accounting practices followed in India and abroad, it is better to continue the existing practice of accounting of purchases, sales and inventory valuation in the books net of sales tax, excise duty and Modvat as applicable. Adjustments as required to be carried out as per section 145A will be done outside the books of account for income-tax purposes.

(iii) Availment of credit on common input goods and services used in taxable and exempt output goods and services - As per the amended provisions, where a manufacture of final products or a provider of output service uses common inputs for manufacture of exempted and taxable goods or for providing exempt and taxable services, and opts not to maintain separate books of account, there are two options for the utilisation of the common CENVAT credits.

uOne is the manufacturer can avail common CENVAT credit and pay excise duty equivalent to 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods. Similarly, the provider of output service can avail common CENVAT credit and pay service tax equivalent to 8 per cent of the value of exempted services.

uThe other option is that the manufacturer of goods or provider of output service can avail common CENVAT credit and pay an amount equivalent to CENVAT credit attributable to input goods and services consumed in relation to the manufacturer of exempted goods or the provision of exempted services, as per the procedures and conditions specified in sub-rule (3A) of rule 6. The said sub-rule, in principle, provides that the manufacturer can avail the CENVAT credit common to taxable and exempted goods and services by making a provisional monthly payment of the proportionate credit attributable to the exempted goods and services. The sub-rule further provides a formula to compute the percentage of the CENVAT credit attributable to the exempted goods or services based on the preceding year’s turnover of taxable and exempted goods and services. At the end of the financial year through which such provisional payments have been made, the quantum of the CENVAT credit attributable to the exempted goods or services is to be recomputed on the year’s actuals and the amount paid to the Government provisionally will be adjusted accordingly. The use of the above formula, by and large, would result in an appropriate identification of common input credit in proportion to the value of taxable and exempted output goods or services for that year.

The option to choose either of the above options has to be exercised and intimated to the department at the beginning of the year and once the option is exercised, it would be in force throughout the relevant financial year.

These options are significantly different from the option available, particularly to the service provider, under the erstwhile provisions. With respect to the service provider, the option under the erstwhile provisions was to utilise the common CENVAT credit to the extent of 20 per cent of the output service tax liability with the ability to carry forward the unutilised common CENVAT credit to be utilised at a later date. The new options give the service provider more flexibility.

Supreme Court’s decision

8. The Court held that it felt it is appropriate that cost of excisable product for the purpose of assessment of excise duty under section 4(1)(b) read with rule 6 of the Valuation Rules should be reckoned as it would be reckoned by a man of commerce. It held that such realism must inform the meaning that the courts give to words of a commercial nature, like cost, which are not defined in the statutes which use them. A man of commerce would, in our view, look the matter thus : "I paid Rs. 100 to the seller of the raw material as the price thereon. Consequent upon purchasing the raw material and by virtue of the Modvat Scheme, I have become entitled to the credit of Rs. 10 with the excise authorities and can utilise this credit when I pay excise duty on my finished product. The real cost of the raw material (exclusive of freight, insurance and the like) to me is, therefore, Rs. 90. In reckoning, the cost of the final product would include Rs. 90. This, in real terms, is the cost of the raw material (exclusive of freight, insurance and the like) and that was which, in view of the Supreme Court, should be properly included in computing the cost of the excisable product.

The view the Supreme Court took about the cost of the raw material is also borne out by the Guidance Note of the Indian Institute of Chartered Accountants. In arriving at the above-mentioned decision it also acknowledged the fact that there can be no doubt that the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India is an authoritative body in the matter for laying down accountancy standards. Thus, in determining the cost of the excisable product covered by the Modvat Scheme under section 4(1)(b) read with rule 6 of the Valuation Rules, the excise duty paid on raw material also covered by the Modvat Scheme is not to be included.

It also held that by reason of clause (i) of the Explanation where there is an exemption ‘notification or order’ giving exemption in respect of excisable goods, it shall be given effect to and the excise duty leviable under the concerned Central Excise Statute shall be reduced to the extent of such exemption provided the notification or order is not ‘for giving credit with respect to, or reduction of duty of excise under such Act on such goods equal to any duty of excise under such Act, or the additional duty under section 3 of the Custom Tariff Act, 1975 already paid on the raw material or component parts used in the production or manufacture of such goods.’

It held that it is, therefore, only a notification or order relating to the excisable goods that gives an exemption equal to the excise duty already paid on raw materials used therein that is not to be taken into account for the purpose of computing the effective duty of excisable product. The Court held that it was not concerned in the instant case with a notification or order and that it was no body’s case that the credit that each manufacturer takes on its excisable product is equal to the excise duty paid on the raw materials used therein. In view thereof, the revenue could not draw any assistance from the Explanation to section 4(4)(d)( ii).

Conclusion

9. In view of the above-mentioned decision, the long drawn-legal controversy has been settled in favour of the assessee. This decision of the Supreme Court will go a long way in reducing the hardship of the manufacturers.

But one thing which can be said with certainty is that, insofar as transportation of final products is concerned, the inclusive part of the definition is restrictive as it permits such transportation upto the place of removal only as input service. The scope of the expression ‘in relation to’ used in the main part of the definition of ‘input service’ vide rule 2(l)(ii ) must be understood as circumscribed by the limiting factor as regards transportation of final products. u‘In relation to’ has been used as an adverbial phrase in the definition of ‘input service’ (as well as in the definition of ‘input’) whereas, under Sections 3(1) and 4(1) of the Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Ltd. Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings Act, 1986, considered by the Apex Court in Doypack Systems (P.) Ltd. v. UOI 1988 (36) ELT 201, it was used as an adjectival phrase. The assessees had urged that the said decision of the Supreme Court was to be followed and that the expansive meaning to the phrase ‘in relation to’ used in rule 2(1)( ii) was to be imported. That argument was also not persuasive for more than one reason, viz., (a ) an expression used in a definition (which may be expansive or restrictive depending on the requirements of the scheme of the statute) cannot have the same meaning as it has when used in a deeming provision (which is per se expansive); (b) an adjectival phrase and an adverbial one are not interchangeable equivalents; (c) the General Clauses Act, 1897 has interchangeably used the phrases ‘in relation to’ and ‘as respects’, each intended to restrict the scope of the meaning of the word defined vide definitions of ‘Central Government’ in section 3(8) and ‘State Government’ section 3(60). Therefore, the expression ‘in relation to’ which can be found in various grammatical situations in different legislative texts and contexts will have to be construed in a manner consistent with the scheme of the law. One has got to understand the definitions under rule 2 by keeping in mind the Cenvat credit scheme as a whole. Hence, there was no point in saying that the main part of the definition of ‘input service’ has to be interpreted without reference to the inclusive part of the definition.

uTherefore, the goods transport service used by the assessees for transportation of their final products from factory to customer’s premises could not be considered to have been used, directly or indirectly, in relation to the clearance of the goods from the factory (place of removal).

3.6 What is the classification, excise duty rate applicable and other concessions in rates of duty for period upto 29-2-2016 ? - Presently RMC is classifiable under tariff heading 3824 5010. There are two options available:

Pay excise duty @ 6% availing CENVAT credit

As the exemption is available at the time of clearance, excise duty would be NIL for clearances made on 1-3-2016.

3.9 What are the interest rates for delayed payment of excise duty? - Interest has to be paid at 18% p.a. for each day of delay upto 31-3-2016 and 15% p.a. from 1-4-2016.

(a)

110% of cost of production – in case builder/contractor operating RMC plant for himself at site. For instance, M/s. XYZ Ltd. installed RMC plant at construction site wherein construction work is also being executed by M/s. XYZ Ltd.

(b)

Cost of raw materials + job work charges - in case RMC plant is operated by third party on job work basis and RMC is being used at site by builder/contractor.

Get registered ; and

Pay duty as follows :

Pay excise duty @ 2% on RMC cleared upto midnight of 29-2-2016 without availing CENVAT credit

Query – We are manufacturers of excisable goods. We have balance of education cess and SAHE cess in our Cenvat records as on 1-3-2015, which is non-utilisable as education cess is not payable on excise duty after 1-3-2015. Recently, Central Government has issue Notification No. 12/2015-CE(NT), dated 30-4-2015, amending Cenvat Credit Rules. The notification allows Cenvat credit of education cess and SAHE cess for payment of excise duty in respect education cess and SAHE cess paid on goods or services received after 1-3-2015, for payment of excise duty. However, the notification is silent about utilisation of Cenvat credit of education cess and SAHE cess which is in balance on 1-3-2015. Please advise how we can utilise the same.

Answer – Indeed the amending Notification No. 12/2015-CE(NT), dated 30-4-2015 does not allow utilisation of Cenvat credit of education cess and SAHE cess lying in credit as on 1-3-2015 for utilisation for payment of excise duty on goods cleared on or after 1-3-2015. It is not clear whether it is a deliberate omission or a mistake. In any case, there is no provision so far that the balance will lapse. Hence, you can continue that balance in your Cenvat records and your excise returns. Let us hope that some further amendment to Cenvat Credit Rules will come in due course. If no such amendment comes, you will have to write off the balance, at least in your financial accounts as non-utilisable. If you do not write off, your profit will be over stated. Of course, in your Cenvat records, that balance can continue.

Query – We are a private company and liable under reverse charge mechanism. We received security services in March, 2015. We will be making payment to the security agency in May 2015. We wish to know whether we should pay service tax on 75% of amount or on 100% amount. The doubt is due to rule 4(a) of Point of Taxation Rules. The preamble to the Point of Taxation Rules states that the rules are for determination of rate of service tax.

Answer – As per section 67A of Finance Act, 1994, the rate of service tax is as on date of provision of taxable service. It does not talk of date of invoice or date of payment at all. Further, the preamble is only introduction to the rules. It is not a statutory provision in itself. That preamble was relevant upto 28-5-2012 i.e. till introduction of section 67A. Thirdly, rule 5B of Service Tax Rules, which provided for date of determination of rate of service tax has been omitted w.e.f. 1-7-2012. Thus, point of taxation rules are not relevant to determine rate of service tax at least w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

Thus, if security agency service was provided prior to 1-4-2015, the service provider is liable to pay 25% of service tax and as obvious corollary, you will be liable to pay balance 75% of service tax. This would be generally so even if invoice is issued by security agency after 1-4-2015. However, to avoid controversy and litigation, it is advisable that invoice is issued on 31-3-2015.

8. Sum not eligible for relief under section 90/91 to be allowed as deduction: Mumbai ITAT Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. ACIT - [2020] 121 taxmann.com 190 (Mumbai - Trib.)

Assessee claimed deduction of state taxes paid overseas in the return of income. Assessing Officer (AO) held that the payments were not liable to be allowed as deduction. Assessee contended that as per Section 40(a)(ii) read with Section 2(43) taxes paid overseas are allowable as deduction if same are not eligible for any relief as per Section 90 or Section 91.

On appeal, Mumbai ITAT held that Bombay HC in case of Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. v. CIT - 390 ITR 271 held, since, the meaning of the word "tax" as defined under Section 2(43) would mean only the tax chargeable under the Act, the tax which has been paid abroad would not be covered within the meaning of Section 40(a)(ii). Thus, taxes levied overseas which were not eligible for relief either under Section 90 or Section 91, would not come within the purview of section 40(a)(ii). Pertinently, unlike Section 91 read with Explanation (iv), Section 90 does not provide for inclusion of tax levied by any State/local authority of that country within the expression 'income tax'.

Relying on said decision, AO was directed to verify whether the State taxes paid by the assessee overseas were eligible for any relief under section 90 and if it is not found to be so, assessee's claim of deduction should be allowed.

9. TPO wasn't justified in disallowing higher royalty paid for trademark if same was duly approved by RBI

Mondelez India Foods (P.) Ltd. v. ACIT [2020] 114 taxmann.com 184 (Mumbai - Trib.)

Assessee-company was engaged in business of manufacturing and sale of malted food and drinks as well as chocolates. It paid trademark royalty at rate of 1 per cent and technical know-how royalty at rate of 1.25 per cent to an entity.

The Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) disallowed royalty payment on trademark paid by the assessee @1% while allowing the royalty payment on technical knowhow at 1.25% of net sales on the reasoning that as per earlier agreement approved by Government, the assessee could pay royalty for technical knowhow at the maximum rate of 2%. However, in the year under consideration, the assessee paid aggregate royalty of 2.25%. Forming an opinion that royalty for technical know-how subsumes royalty for trademark and therefore, the separate royalty for trademark paid at 1% would not be allowable to the assessee.

The Mumbai Tribunal, following assessee's own case of earlier year had held that as could be seen from the materials placed on record, the payment of royalty for technical knowhow @ 1.25% has been approved by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. Similarly, payment of royalty for trademark @ 1% has been approved by the Reserve Bank of India.

3. We are manufacturers of plastic containers and have manufactured 200 pieces of bottles (5 litre) capacity, which are lying in our premises and also in RG1 register (daily stock account). Same are also shown as closing balance in ER 1 return filed. However, due to urgent requirement of 1 litre bottles, we will have to regrind 5 litre bottles and use the same for the manufacturing of 1 litre bottles. How should we account for the same in ER-1 return as well as in RG1 register (daily stock account) ?

Since 5L bottles are lying in stock with you, they must be non-duty-paid stocks.

As per rule 4, read with rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, in case excisable goods (5L bottles) are used for further manufacture of excisable goods (1L bottles), then these would termed as 'captive consumption' and as per the exemption notifications in force, no duty is payable thereon. There is no bar that finished goods cannot be used as 'inputs'. In fact, rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 stipulates such situation, though in the context of finished goods removed and subsequently returned for remaking. Hence, assuming that process of converting 5L bottles into 1L bottles is manufacture, no duty is payable. You may account for the same as issue for captive consumption and duty may be paid on value of 1L bottles.

However, if process of converting 5L bottles into 1L bottles is not manufacture you may pay duty on value of 5L bottles (normal transaction value) and after processing into 1L bottles, clear them. In records, the stock of 5L bottles may be shown to have been cleared as per rule 4 of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000.

Transfer Pricing Impact:

This downturn in the industry will have a significant impact in the transfer price both in the internal pricing policy as well to adhering to the compliance, as discussed below some of them; Royalty Rate - Vendors to the OEM would be the most impacted. Usually such vendors have long term relationship with the OEM and based on the forecast there is quite investment is made in the dies & tools. Also, it is true that for some of the vendors the dependency with few / even sole OEM is too highly concentrated, keeping in mind long term relationship there would be lot of push back from the OEM to honour the commitment.

Resulting such vendors may not be profitable or lower than usual with high working capital.

With this above fact, I clearly believe the TP methodology followed earlier to defend the covered transaction may not continue to sustain particularly where profit-based methods have been used. For example – most of the vendors will have either an overseas joint venture partner for technology – hence there is payment of royalty triggers. Typically, royalty is based percentage of sales, in order to benchmark the royalty, rate the company choose either sophisticated database such "royalty stat", etc. or use over aggregate approach using some profit-based method.

In case of transaction-based approach, it may be difficult to rely on such global database, as there may not be significant change in the royalty rates, also it is not possible for the companies renegotiating the royalty rates for such inverted growth which is potentially temporary. Here is a challenge…

Of course, in profit-based method, one may argue that it would apply to the comparable sets and hence the "tested party" can be aligned with market profit. Having said this , based on our experience after applying above you may have set of comparable's below threshold number for application of range plus practical challenge during the time when the return needs to filed the local Indian data based may not have financials of the relevant year, multiple year may throw up wrong number.

(ii)Is the company obliged to make the adjustments suggested in the section in the company’s books of account or can it be made outside the books for income-tax purpose? The Government has recently issued an ordinance to amend section 211 of the Companies Act, 1956 requiring the companies to follow the accounting standards to be prescribed by the National Advisory Board Committee on A ccounting Standards and till such time as this Committee prescribes the standards, the standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) have to be followed.

The Accounting Standard 2 (AS 2) on valuation of inventories issued by the ICAI (both old and new exposure draft) recognises only exclusion of Modvat credit from the purview of cost of inventories. The valuation of stock will have to be made according to AS 2 and companies will have to continue preparation of accounts as per existing practice of excluding Modvat in purchases and closing stock. Thus, the adjustments as required under section 145A will be made outside the books of account.

(iii)Is it correct to say that the profit figure after making the adjustments in section 145A will be the same ?

The provisions of section 145A can be compared to the second alternative method of accounting as suggested in the Guidance Note on Accounting for Modvat issued by the ICAI. The companies have to identify the Modvat availed in respect of consumption of inputs and pass necessary entries in the books to reduce it from the total cost of inputs consumed. The balance of Modvat credit for the units in stock will be shown as deduction from closing stock so that double accounting of profit is avoided. This will result in the same profit figure both under the existing practice and the proposed method.

(iv)Is it the intention of the Income-tax Act to make the adjustment to both opening and closing stock of inventories ?

The explanatory memorandum on the notes on clauses of the Finance Bill, 1998 prescribes adjustment to both opening and closing stock of inventories. It means that the opening stock of inventories as on April 1, 1998 will be adjusted to include the Modvat content without disturbing the closing stock value as on March 31, 1998. This can be done by a suitable transfer from loans and advances- RG 23A balance as on April 1, 1998. This has to be done in addition to adjustment of Modvat value in the closing stock as on March 31, 1999.

The above-mentioned questions need to be answered to have a clear understanding of the provisions of section 145A either by way of issue of a clarification explaining the abovenoted points or making a suitable amendment to section 145A to the extent of exclusion of Modvat from the purview of adjustments as envisaged in that section.

30Tax credit certificate to certain manufacturing companies in certain cases.

280ZB. (1) Where any company engaged in the manufacture or production of any of the articles mentioned in the First Schedule to the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 (65 of 1951), is, in respect of its profits and gains attributable to such manufacture or production, —

(i) liable to pay any tax for the assessment year commencing on the 1st day of April, 1965 (hereinafter referred to as the base year), and for any one or more of the five assessment years next following that year; or

(ii) not liable to pay any tax for the base year but becomes so liable for any succeeding year (hereinafter referred to as the succeeding base year), and also for any one or more of the assessment years following that year, not being an assessment year commencing on the first day of April, 1971, or any subsequent assessment year,

and the tax for any such succeeding year exceeds—

(a) in the case referred to in clause (i), the tax payable for the base year;

(b ) in the case referred to in clause (ii), the tax payable for the succeeding base year,

then the company shall be granted a tax credit certificate for an amount equal to twenty per cent of such excess:

Provided that the amount of the tax credit certificate shall not for any assessment year exceed ten per cent of such tax payable by the company for that year.

(2) 31[The amount shown on a tax credit certificate granted to any company under this section shall, on the certificate being produced before the 31a[Assessing] Officer, be adjusted against any liability of the company under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 (11 of 1922), or this Act, existing on the date on which the certificate was produced before the 31a[Assessing] Officer and where the amount of such certificate exceeds such liability, or where there is no such liability, the excess or the whole of such amount, as the case may be, shall, notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter XIX, be deemed, on the said date, to be refund due to such company under that Chapter and the provisions of this Act, shall apply accordingly:]

Provided that the adjustment or refund, as the case may be, under this sub-section shall be only for such amount, not exceeding the amount of the certificate, as is used within such period as may be specified in the scheme—

(i) for repayment of loans taken by the company from any of the financial institutions notified in this behalf by the Central Government, or

(ii) for redemption of its debentures, or

(iii) for the acquisition of any capital asset in India, including the construction of any building, for the purposes of the business of the company.

Explanation 1 : In this section, "tax" means income-tax payable under this Act and surtax, if any, payable under the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 (7 of 1964).

Explanation 2: The amount of income-tax in respect of the profits or gains attributable to the manufacture or production of the articles referred to in sub-section (1) shall be an amount bearing to the total amount of income-tax payable on the total income (such income-tax being computed in the manner specified hereunder) the same proportion as the amount of such profits or gains bears to the total income. 32[The amount of income-tax payable by the company for any assessment year shall be computed after making allowance for any relief, rebate or deduction in respect of income-tax to which the company is entitled under the provisions of this Act or the annual Finance Act and after deducting from such amount of income-tax—

(a) 33[* * *]

(b) (i) in respect of the assessment year commencing on the 1st day of April, 1965, the amount, if any, by which the rebate of income-tax admissible to the company under the provisions of the Finance Act, 1965 (10 of 1965), is, under the provisions of the said Act, reduced with reference to the face value of any bonus shares or the amount of any bonus issued by the company to its shareholders during the previous year or any previous year prior to that year or with reference to any amount of dividends declared or distributed by it during the previous year or any previous year prior to that year; or

(ii) in respect of the assessment year commencing on the 1st day of April, 1966, or any subsequent assessment year, the amount of income-tax, if any, payable by the company under the provisions of the annual Finance Act with reference to the relevant amount of distributions of dividends by it.]

NOTIFICATION NO. 4/2010-CLEAN ENERGY CESS, DATED 22-6-2010

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 83 of the Finance Act, 2010 (14 of 2010) read with section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 (1 of 1944), the Central Government, on being satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, hereby exempts all goods falling under Central Excise Tariff headings 2701, 2702, 2703 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 (5 of 1986), other than raw coal, raw lignite and raw peat, from the clean energy cess leviable under section 83 of said Finance Act:

(a) This Para is to be prepared for the company as a whole covering excise duty, service tax and VAT (including CST and any other State Tax) for all types of products whether or not covered under cost audit.

(b) The information of indirect taxes is to be given for current year and no previous year's figures are required.

(d) CST and Other State Taxes have been added in the costing taxonomy to show the details relating to them also.

(e) Assessable Value relating to all types of taxes should be taken from the respective Returns submitted with the tax authorities. For example, assessable value for excise duty should be taken from RT 12 (now ER-1), the gross amount (assessable value) for service tax should be taken as gross value of services as mentioned in ST-3 (under section 70 of Finance Act 1994).

(f) The duties and taxes Payable is based on clearances of goods and services against the respective heads.

(g) Duties/Taxes Paid include CENVAT/VAT Credit utilized on inputs, capital goods, input services and other utilization, if any.

(h) Taxes paid through PLA/Cash refer to the payment of Excise Duty, Service Tax, Cess & Others and VAT through debit in PLA account or deposit in to the PLA account or payment in to the bank account by way of cheque or cash through the GAR-7 Challan or the Challan for making the payment of VAT.

(i) Duties/Taxes Recovered should be taken from Books of Account of the company. It is necessary that the gross turnover or the gross billings should be duly accounted under various heads such as net sales, excise duty, sales tax, service tax, etc.

(j) Difference between duties/taxes paid and recovered refer to the amount of total duties/taxes paid and recovered. This may not match due to the following reasons -

♦ Excise duty element in stock of excise duty paid goods at depots, branches, and warehouse or with C & F agents.

♦ The goods lying at depots, etc. are duty paid goods which have not been sold to the customer. Hence, the duty has not been recovered from the customers.

♦ Excise duty/sales tax paid on free issues, samples, where the taxes are not recovered from customers.

♦ Excise Duty paid on inter factory transfers.

♦ Excise Duty paid on the goods captively consumed.

♦ Excise duty/sales tax/service tax/cess and other payments arising out of Order-in-Original or Order-in-Appeal, etc.

(k) The fines, penalties, interest etc. are not a payment of Excise Duty, Service Tax, Cess & Others and VAT. However, sometimes it is paid through PLA or Cash (deposit in to the bank account by way of cheque or cash through Challan) under the separate code as specified in the Challan. In these circumstances, the amount should be identified and shown separately. This amount can be tallied from Monthly ER-1 Return (Excise), Annual Financial Information Statement in ER-4 (Excise), Half Yearly ST-3 Return (Service Tax) and Monthly/Annual VAT return.
